The wording is precise: they would not believe, not they could not understand. The difference matters because the Qur'an uses both kinds of statement, and it distinguishes them carefully. Where the Book speaks of sealed hearts, it has already described the choices that produced the sealing. Here the emphasis falls on the refusal itself, made in a country that had examples within walking distance. The verse therefore prepares its audience for what follows, in which the mockers are imagined being handed a door to the sky and responding to the sight with the language of sorcery. A man who has decided in advance what he is willing to conclude will find a way to keep his conclusion. The Book says so, and then it shows the mechanism, so that no reader can take refuge in the thought that he would have believed.

**The Word Behind "Examples": the Sunnah of the Earlier Peoples**

The phrase rendered *examples of those destroyed before* is, in Arabic, *sunnat al-awwalīn*, the established way of the former peoples, and the noun is worth pausing over. A *sunnah* in the language is a path worn by repeated travel, then a practice followed because it has been followed before, and the Qur'an applies the word to God's own dealing with nations. *“Tell the disbelievers that if they desist, their past will be forgiven. But if they persist, then they have an example in those destroyed before them.”* (8:38), and Sūrah Fāṭir asks the mockers whether they are waiting for anything but *“the fate of those ˹destroyed˺ before”*, adding that *“You will find no change in the way of Allah, nor will you find it diverted ˹to someone else˺.”* (35:43). The fixed formula recurs: *“˹This is˺ Allah's way, already long established ˹in the past˺. And you will find no change in Allah's way.”* (48:23; 33:62). Nothing here is an improvisation. The ruin of the deniers is a road that has been walked many times, and the verse that follows this one describes the response that keeps the traffic moving.
verses.14:
> And even if We opened for them a gate to heaven, through which they continued to ascend

**A Condition Stated to Remove an Excuse**

The verse opens with the particle of hypothesis that Arabic uses for a condition contrary to fact, and the effect is not to promise anything but to dismantle a defence. The mockers had implied that visible proof would settle the matter. The answer grants the proof in the most generous available form and reports the result in advance. Nothing here suggests that God intends to open such a gate; the scene exists to show what the demand was worth. This is the same method Sūrah al-Anʿām uses when it stacks every conceivable sign and then says that its questioners would not have believed (6:111). The point is not that evidence is useless in general but that evidence cannot do the work the mockers assigned to it. A proof changes no one who has already defined what he will accept as proof, and the Book is telling its audience exactly what kind of position they had taken.

**A Gate, Not a Glimpse**

The image is deliberately excessive. What is opened is *bāb*, a gate, not a window; what they do is ascend, not look up. The picture is of sustained access to the place from which revelation comes — the very access the mockers claimed they wanted when they asked why angels were not sent down, and the very thing they said would settle the question of whether a message was true. The verb used for their movement, *yaʿrujūn*, is built from the same root as *miʿrāj*, the ladder or ascent, and the same root describes the motion of the angels in *“˹through which˺ the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit will ascend to Him”* (70:4). Human beings are being imagined making the journey that belongs to the angels. The barrier the verse removes is the last one available: distance, altitude, and the separation between the visible world and the source of the message.

**Who Is Being Imagined Here**

Al-Baghawī identifies the men in this passage with the demanders who wanted an angel brought before them, and the identification fits the movement of the sūrah: a challenge is made in verse 7, answered in verse 8, and here it is followed to its conclusion. The pronoun does not name a new group and does not need to. It refers to the same people, and the point holds whether the reader thinks of the Makkan notables who made the demand or of anyone in any century who rests his decision on the promise of one more sign. That is why the passage is written as a hypothetical rather than as an event: it is a test of the challenger's sincerity, and the Book is confident about the result before the test is run. The demand for proof is answered by showing what the demand was actually worth.

**Seeing Is Not Believing**

The Qur'an distinguishes sharply between what the eye receives and what the heart accepts, and it makes the distinction part of its account of human responsibility. *“I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land. And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them.”* (7:146). The same sūrah that describes the sealing of hearts describes a sight that is covered, not a sky that is empty: *“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered.”* (2:7). The verse under commentary assumes the eye is working perfectly. The travellers are imagined climbing through a gate and looking at what lies beyond, and the sight registers. What fails is the interpretation, and the failure happens where the person is, not where the evidence is.

**The Ceiling of Curiosity**

There is a habit of mind that treats the world as a collection of puzzles and itself as a spectator with no stake in them. The demand in these verses is that habit in religious dress: show me something extraordinary and I will reconsider. The Qur'an's answer is that extraordinary sights are available and always have been — a sky furnished with towers, a body that came from clay, a book recited in the desert — and that the appetite for wonders is not the same as the desire for truth. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ says of the mockers that they only listened for entertainment (21:2). A man who reads the creation as entertainment will read a gate to heaven the same way, and will return to his business with a story to tell. The verse does not deny the wonder. It denies that wonder by itself does anything to the person watching it.

**The End of the Argument About Proof**

This verse closes a line of reasoning that began with the mockers' demand. Once it is granted that even a gate to the sky would leave the position unchanged, the debate about evidence has ended and the question has shifted to the person: what does a man do with what he already has? The sūrah answers by turning, in the very next verse, to what the mockers would actually say, and then by lifting its eyes to the sky that everyone can see. The Book's method here is worth noticing. It never argues that the signs are insufficient; it argues that the refusal was never about the signs. What follows in the sūrah is addressed to a different organ of perception, and to a different audience.

**Doors of the Sky in the Qur'an**

The image of an opening in the sky is not invented for this verse; the Book uses it elsewhere, and always with judgment attached. When the flood came, *“We opened the gates of the sky with pouring rain”* (54:11), and the mercy of that rain was simultaneously the instrument of the punishment. At the Hour, *“The sky will be ˹split˺ open, becoming ˹many˺ gates”* (78:19). And the doors are shut in the face of the arrogant: *“Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.”* (7:40). Set beside these passages, the hypothetical in this verse loses its air of generosity. A gate opened in the sky is not a spectacle arranged for the benefit of spectators; it is the sign of an order being executed. The mockers asked to be taken up through it. The Book's other uses of the same door suggest what such a journey would actually have been.
verses.15:
> still they would say, “Our eyes have truly been dazzled! In fact, we must have been bewitched.”

**The Eyes Blamed, Not the Sky**

The sentence they are imagined speaking relocates the whole event inside their own heads. It is not the sky that has changed, and not the world that has opened; it is *our eyes* that have been dazzled. The Arabic verb behind *dazzled* describes a mind or a faculty overwhelmed, and the construction is passive: something was done to them. Nobody in this sentence accepts responsibility for what he saw. The choice of the passive voice is not a small grammatical detail. It is the same move as the sorcery charge that follows, one step earlier. First the organ is disqualified, then the explanation is supplied, and in both cases the conclusion is preserved by treating the perception as an effect inflicted from outside rather than as information about reality.

**"In Fact, We Have Been Bewitched"**

The Arabic uses *bal*, a particle that corrects a statement and replaces it with a stronger one, so the two clauses escalate: not merely dazzled but actually under a spell. Sorcery in the Qur'an's vocabulary is *siḥr*, and the charge is familiar from the sūrah's own context: the Makkans had already used it against the Prophet when they heard the Qur'an. Sūrah Yūnus reports the reaction to the truth arriving, *“This is certainly pure magic!”* (10:76), and Sūrah al-Zukhruf reports the same dismissive move, *“This is magic, and we totally reject it.”* (43:30). The accusation in this verse takes the pattern one step further. The same men who called the messenger a madman and a sorcerer would, on seeing a gate opened in the sky, apply the sorcery label to their own eyes — anything to avoid the conclusion that the messenger was right.

**The Charge That Followed Every Messenger**

This was not an improvisation by the Makkans. When Mūsā confronted Pharaoh, the chiefs announced, *“He is indeed a skilled magician”* (7:109), and Pharaoh said the same to those around him (26:34). The accusation of magic served as a standard explanation for a prophet's authority in Egypt and in Arabia alike, and it appears in the case of Jesus as well: 5:110 records the favours given to him — the bird of clay, the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead — and the response of those who watched. The accusation survives because it works. It requires no examination of the message, no reckoning with its content, and no change of life. It also explains why the Book places the charge next to the signs, in verse after verse, as the fixed answer of the unpersuaded to anything they cannot account for.

**What a Sorcery Charge Does to the Court**

If the witness is under a spell, the witness is disqualified, and the hearing is over. This is the elegance of the accusation, and the reason the Qur'an returns to it so often. It converts a dispute about the truth of a claim into a claim about the condition of the claimant, and the person who makes that conversion owns the outcome. Anyone can accuse anyone of magic; nothing needs to be demonstrated; and the accused can never produce evidence that proves he is not enchanted, because any such evidence will be read as further enchantment. A community that adopts this habit has decided to live where no argument can reach it. The Book's response to it is not to disprove the spell but to describe the position plainly and leave it in view.

**The Self-Sealing Circle**

Notice the shape of the logic. A stranger comes with a message, and if his words are persuasive they are magic; if he climbs to heaven the climbers are bewitched; if he works wonders, they are tricks; if he is poor, he cannot be a messenger; if he eats food, he cannot be an angel. Each response closes one question and opens none. The Qur'an records this habit in the demand for signs, and it says of those who took the position that they would not believe even if every sign were assembled in front of them unless God willed it (6:111). That is the situation the present verse illustrates in a single image. The gate has been opened, and the debate is already over — not by the power of the evidence, but by the determination of the one who saw it.

**The Answer to the Demand for a Sign**

The mockers began with a reasonable-sounding request: bring the angels if you are truthful. The sūrah's reply has three parts. Angels come only with a decree, and on the day they arrive there is no more time. Proof of that kind is not granted on demand. And if it were granted, the result would not be the submission they promised but an excuse they had already rehearsed. The Book is not refusing to put its claims to the test; the rest of the sūrah, and the rest of the Book, invites exactly that test. What it refuses is to play along with the pretence that the test is only now being offered for the first time, when the same evidence has been standing in front of these men since the day they were born.

**What the Qur'an Says About Magic Itself**

The Book treats sorcery as a real practice rather than a superstition, and it denies it the two things its practitioners claimed: power over the divine will, and success. Mūsā answers Pharaoh's magicians with *“Is this what you say about the truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? Magicians will never succeed.”* (10:77), and on the day of the contest he is told what will happen to their work: *“And magicians can never succeed wherever they go.”* (20:69). Sūrah al-Baqarah gives the fullest account, describing magic taught in Babylon and adding the protection clause that changes the whole story: *“Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved.”* (2:102). Sorcery in this framework is a technique with a limited field, and its limits are the point. It can mislead and divide; it cannot open heaven, and it cannot make a prophet what his enemies claimed he was. Sūrah al-Māʾidah lists the practices that belong to *“Satan's handiwork”* and orders them abandoned (5:90). The men in this verse, imagining that a genuine wonder would be magic, were accusing the truth of being the one thing it demonstrably was not.
verses.16:
> Indeed, We have placed constellations in the sky, and adorned it for all to see

**After the Hypothetical Gate, the Real Sky**

The argument of the previous verses ran on a condition that had no need to be met. Here the sūrah stops arguing about a gate and points at what is already overhead. The shift is deliberate and it is also a rebuke: men were demanding an opening in the sky while standing underneath a sky they had never troubled to examine. The Qur'an often reasons this way. Instead of granting a private sign to a specific challenger, it directs attention to something public, permanent and visible from every rooftop in Makkah. The evidence offered is not scarce and does not need to be transported. It rises in the east every evening, and it has done so for every generation that ever denied a messenger, which makes the verse a quiet continuation of the history lesson that came just before it.

**Towers in the Night**

The word rendered *constellations* is *burūj*, and its basic sense in Arabic is towers or fortresses — the raised, fortified structures of a city wall. Applied to the sky, the word pictures the stars as fixed edifices rather than as scattered points. The Qur'an uses the same noun in Sūrah al-Burūj, where an oath is sworn *“By the sky full of constellations”* (85:1), and Sūrah al-Furqān combines the stars with the two great luminaries: *“Blessed is the One Who has placed constellations in the sky, as well as a ˹radiant˺ lamp and a luminous moon.”* (25:61). Al-Kalabī, among the early exegetes, is reported to have identified the *burūj* with the twelve well-known constellations that mark the path of the sun and moon. Whether the word is read as the stations of those two bodies or as the great star groups generally, the sense of a structured order rather than a random scatter is the same.

**The Sky as Something Built**

The verse's second clause uses the language of craft: the sky was *adorned*. Elsewhere the Qur'an is even more explicit about what was done to it. *“Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with the stars for decoration”* (37:6), and Sūrah Qāf puts the building and the beautifying in a single line: *“Have they not then looked at the sky above them: how We built it and adorned it ˹with stars˺, leaving it flawless?”* (50:6). The verbs are borrowed from architecture and jewellery, which is a considered choice. A reader is not asked to treat the sky as an accident that happens to look impressive. He is asked to notice that it has been constructed and decorated, and that both acts belong to the same agent who is speaking in the verse. The Book's case for its own origin runs along this line: a message from the maker of the sky is not an intrusion into an unrelated world.

**Adorned for the Onlooker**

The verse ends by naming the beneficiary: the sky is decorated *for those who look*. The Arabic participle is plural and indefinite, which widens the audience beyond believers, beyond Arabs, beyond any group with a claim on the message. Beauty here is not a private revelation granted to a mystic; it is a public offer repeated nightly. The Qur'an returns to the same thought when it asks its audience to consider the whole of creation: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Consider all that is in the heavens and the earth!’”* (10:101). Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the conclusion: *“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the day and night there are signs for people of reason.”* (3:190). The onlooker is the addressee of revelation in its widest form, and his looking is treated as the beginning of an argument rather than a distraction from one.

**No Instrument and No Intermediary**

Everything here is available to a person with working eyes. No telescope, no teacher, no lineage and no permission are required; a shepherd in the desert has the same access as a philosopher in a city. That is why the verse lands where it does in the sūrah's flow. Men had asked for a gate to be opened and for angels to be brought down so that they could verify a claim; they were being reminded that a far grander structure was already above them, hung with lamps, and that they had grown so used to it that they no longer saw it. The Qur'an repeatedly treats familiarity as the great anaesthetic of the human mind. What is always there stops being evidence, and the Book's response is to describe the familiar again in the language of construction, so that the reader looks up as though for the first time.

**What the Adornment Argues**

The final claim of the verse is that order and beauty in the sky have an author. The Qur'an states the challenge in a form that invites inspection rather than assent: *“You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate. So look again: do you see any flaws?”* (67:3), and then, *“Then look again and again— your sight will return frustrated and weary.”* (67:4). The Book is unafraid of this test, and it presses the point twice in consecutive verses. Decoration serves no survival purpose in a purely material account of things; a sky covered with luminous towers is not explained by saying that human beings find it pleasant. It is fitted to be seen, and the verse's claim is that being fitted to be seen is itself the signature of a maker who intends to be recognised.

**Signs in the Horizons and in the Self**

The Qur'an does not rely on the sky alone, and it says so in a verse that reads like a programme for everything this passage is doing: *“We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth.”* (41:53). The two arenas named there are the ones the sūrah is about to walk through — the sky with its towers, then the earth with its harvests, then the human being made from clay. The order is deliberate and it runs outward to inward, from what anyone can see with his head tilted back to what he would have to look at in a mirror. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ supplies the summary sentence for the physical half of the evidence: *“Do the disbelievers not realize that the heavens and earth were ˹once˺ one mass then We split them apart? And We created from water every living thing.”* (21:30). The verse under commentary is one panel of that larger display, and the sūrah's confidence is that the display has never been hidden from anybody.
verses.17:
> And We protected it from every accursed devil

**The Sky as a Guarded Space**

The verse attaches a second act to the first. The sky was not only built and decorated; it was also secured. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ states the same fact in a single image: *“And We have made the sky a well-protected canopy, still they turn away from its signs.”* (21:32). Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt describes both halves of the work in consecutive lines, adorning the lowest heaven with stars *“and ˹for˺ protection from every rebellious devil.”* (37:7). The Book consistently presents the visible universe as a bounded and administered place rather than an open field. What reads in one verse as beauty reads in the next as a wall. This is characteristic of the Qur'an's cosmology: whatever is described as gift is also described as governed, and the two accounts never contradict each other because the same hand is said to be behind both.

**What "Accursed" Means in This Vocabulary**

The Arabic word rendered *accursed* is *rajīm*, a passive form describing someone driven away or pelted off, and it is used of Satan in a formula every Muslim recites: *“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed.”* (16:98). The word is not a decoration on the name; it states the being's condition. He is the one banished from the presence he once enjoyed, and the expulsion is what he is working from. Read with that in mind, the verse's protection is not a skirmish between equals at the edge of the atmosphere. It is a boundary enforced against an intruder who has already been expelled from one domain and is refused access to another. The Book never presents the devil as a rival power; it presents him as a trespasser with a long record of failure.

**Satans, Jinn, and the Worlds They Belong To**

The Qur'an uses the word *shayṭān* for agents of corruption drawn from more than one order of being. Sūrah al-Anʿām states that God has appointed for every prophet enemies from *“devilish humans and jinn”* (6:112), and Sūrah Fāṭir warns people that Satan is an enemy who must be treated as one: *“Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy.”* (35:6). The verses immediately following this one speak of the jinn who attempted to listen in, and the Qur'an's own usage allows those beings to be called satans when they behave like the arch-satan. This is not a demotion of the jinn or a confusion of categories. It is a description of a role. The Book is interested in what an agent does and whose order he serves, and the protection announced in this verse is aimed at that behaviour rather than at a species.

**Protecting the Route of Revelation**

The most important function of this guard becomes clear when the verse is read beside the sūrah's earlier promise about the Book. Verse 9 says that the Reminder was sent down by God and will be kept by Him. Verse 17 says the sky is protected. The two statements answer the same anxiety from two directions. One secures the text once it has arrived among human beings; the other secures the channel through which the message travels. A revelation cannot be trusted if anything in the unseen world can tamper with its delivery, and it cannot be trusted if anything can forge a rival version of it. The Qur'an closes both routes: the Book will be preserved, and the way to the Book is guarded. Neither claim is left as a general assurance; both are stated as acts of the same speaker.

**A Limit Set on the Whisperer**

The Qur'an is not vague about where the devil's influence does work. Sūrah al-Nās asks refuge from *“the lurking whisperer— who whispers into the hearts of humankind”* (114:4-5), and the phrase marks the boundary precisely. His access is to the human heart, by suggestion, and to the human community, by the encouragement of wrongdoing. It does not extend to the fabric of the heavens, and it does not extend to the source of revelation. This division runs through the whole Qur'anic understanding of evil: the enemy's power is real and it is aimed at choice, which is why his weapons are whispers, fear and delay rather than control. The verse under commentary places one more line in that map, and it places it above the heads of the men who were accusing the Prophet of being possessed.

**What the Guard Says About the Message**

The verse quietly strengthens everything the sūrah has said about the Book's reliability. If the sky is closed to insinuation from below, then the revelation that descends through it cannot have been doctored on the way down, and the message a listener hears is the message God sent. The Qur'an's own summary of the point appears later in Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt, where the eavesdroppers are described as being driven off from every side, unable to hear the highest assembly, while the revelation continues to arrive at its intended recipients. The purpose of the guard is therefore not to protect heaven from a threat — nothing threatens it — but to protect the difference between revelation and rumour. The moment spirits could carry news from above, every oracle and soothsayer could claim an equal share of the unseen.

**The Same Guard in Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt**

The parallel passage states the whole arrangement in three consecutive verses, and it deserves to be read beside this one. *“Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with the stars for decoration”* (37:6), *“and ˹for˺ protection from every rebellious devil.”* (37:7), *“They cannot listen to the highest assembly ˹of angels˺ for they are pelted from every side”* (37:8). The structure matches the sūrah here exactly: beauty first, then the guard, then the reason for it. Two details are added by the parallel. The protection is described as a function of the stars themselves, so that the decoration of the previous verse and the defence of this one are the same installation seen from two sides. And the exclusion is total: the devils cannot hear the assembly at all, which means the eavesdropping imagined in the next verse of this sūrah is an attempt at something already denied to them. Read together, the two passages leave no room for the idea that revelation competes with other traffic from the unseen world.
verses.18:
> except the one eavesdropping, who is then pursued by a visible flare

**The Theft of a Hearing**

The Arabic phrase describes a person who steals a hearing, and the metaphor is carefully chosen. What happens in the highest company is a conversation; the eavesdropper takes a fragment of it and carries it down as property that does not belong to him. The Qur'an does not dignify the practice by calling it knowledge. It calls it theft, and the theft is of the smallest possible unit: a word, a snatch, whatever can be caught before discovery. Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt explains the impossibility of the attempt: *“They cannot listen to the highest assembly ˹of angels˺ for they are pelted from every side”* (37:8), so that the only gain available is a fragment, *“But whoever manages to stealthily eavesdrop is ˹instantly˺ pursued by a piercing flare.”* (37:10). The verse under commentary belongs to that passage's language, and it makes the point by beginning with the exception that proves the rule.

**The Jinn, the Soothsayers, and the Old Trade**

These verses are traditionally read as dealing with the traffic that fed the fortune-tellers of Arabia. The jinn, who hear something and descend with it before being caught, would add to it a hundred inventions, and the soothsayers would sell the mixture as news of the unseen. Sūrah al-Jinn records the situation from the other side, in the words of the jinn themselves: *“˹Earlier˺ we tried to reach heaven ˹for news˺, only to find it filled with stern guards and shooting stars.”* (72:8), and *“We used to take up positions there for eavesdropping, but whoever dares eavesdrop now will find a flare lying in wait for them.”* (72:9). The testimony is striking because it comes from the group whose business had just been ruined. They describe an established practice that has been shut down, and they describe it as a change they themselves noticed.

**A Flare, Visible and Certain**

The Qur'an describes the pursuit with a single noun, *shihāb mubīn*, a clear burning brand. The adjective carries weight: the flare is not hidden, and the chase is not a matter of chance, so the eavesdropper cannot console himself that he might slip away. Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt uses a slightly different word for the same instrument, calling it a piercing flame, and Sūrah al-Jinn describes it as lying in wait at the points where listening is attempted. The consistent picture across the three sūrahs is a defence that requires no action by its defenders: the travellers are intercepted at the approach, without negotiation or delay. Whatever else the passage teaches, it presents the boundary as total. There is no successful raid on the highest assembly anywhere in the Book.

**Why the Channel Was Closed**

The classical commentators connect the intensity of this guard with the arrival of the prophetic mission, and the Qur'an's own language supports the timing. The jinn in Sūrah al-Jinn say *earlier* they had tried to reach heaven and were met with guards, and describe what used to be possible at their listening posts in the past. On that reading, the closing of the sky is part of the same event as the coming of the Qur'an. Revelation was about to descend in its final and most complete form, and the channel that could be confused with it was sealed. The sūrah under commentary states the fact without explanation; the reader is left to see the logic for himself, and the logic is straightforward. Once a message is the standard by which everything else is judged, nothing else may be allowed to arrive with the appearance of news from the unseen.

**The Difference Between Revelation and Rumour**

The traffic shut down in this verse was small in content and large in consequence. A single stolen word, embellished by imagination and repeated in a market, became a prophecy; a coincidence became a portent; a frightened man's guess became destiny. The Qur'an treats the appetite for such information as a serious moral problem, not an entertainment, because it substitutes an unattributable authority for a known one. The Book is giving a fixed text with a known speaker and an accountable line of transmission. The eavesdropper offers a rumour with no author, no chain and no way to test it. The flare that pursues him is therefore doing something more than punishing a trespass; it is keeping the two channels from merging in the minds of the people who consult them.

**The Certainty of the Pursuit**

Everything in the verse is arranged so that the eavesdropper gains nothing. He may hear, but he is immediately tracked; what he carries away is a fragment that he cannot verify and that will be mixed with his own inventions; and the pursuit means that the practice cannot be sustained. The Book offers this as one more illustration of a theme already stated in the sūrah: the higher domain is not available to those who try to take it by stealth, and no power in creation has ever extracted from God the information He has chosen to withhold. What is given, He gives to whom He wills, through messengers He selects and protects. What is stolen is chased off the field before it can be delivered.

**The People Who Consulted the Jinn**

Sūrah al-Jinn records the other end of the trade, the human clients who were paying for it: *“And some men used to seek refuge with some jinn—so they increased each other in wickedness.”* (72:6). The relation described there is not a transaction between equals but a mutual corruption, in which the human party hands over his fear and the jinn party hands over a rumour, and both are made worse by the exchange. Sūrah al-Māʾidah places the whole apparatus of divination in the same category as intoxicants and gambling, describing them as *“evil of Satan's handiwork”* (5:90). The sūrah's closing picture therefore does more than describe a punishment meted out in the upper air. It dismantles the business model. If the sources of hidden news cannot reach the assembly where the news originates, then the oracle's shelf is empty, and the men paying for a glimpse of the future were buying the jinn's own words — which the jinn themselves admit were lies: *“We certainly thought that humans and jinn would never speak lies about Allah.”* (72:5).
verses.19:
> As for the earth, We spread it out and placed upon it firm mountains, and caused everything to grow there in perfect balance

**The Ground Underneath the Argument**

After the sky, the sūrah looks down. The verse is part of a sequence that answers a demand for extraordinary proof by pointing at ordinary creation, and the earth is the most ordinary thing there is — the surface a man walks on without ever thinking about it. The Arabic verb rendered *spread out* describes a surface laid flat and extended, the way a mat is unrolled, and Sūrah al-Nabaʾ uses the same picture in its description of the earth *“smoothed out ˹like a bed˺”* (78:6). Sūrah Qāf repeats the wording of this verse almost exactly, joining the spreading, the mountains and the growth in one line: *“As for the earth, We spread it out and placed upon it firm mountains, and produced in it every type of pleasant plant—”* (50:7). The Book's habit is consistent here: it draws attention to a habitable surface rather than to an astonishing spectacle, because the habitable surface is the wonder that nobody bothers to wonder at.

**Mountains as Pegs and Anchors**

The mountains are described as *firm*, and the Qur'an elsewhere explains what their firmness does. *“He has placed into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you, as well as rivers, and pathways so you may find your way.”* (16:15), and again in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ: *“And We have placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with them, and made in it broad pathways so they may find their way.”* (21:31). Sūrah al-Nabaʾ uses the image of pegs driven into a tent (78:7), and the classical exegetes, al-Qurṭubī among them, read the verses as a statement about the earth's stability for the people living on it. The claim is practical rather than geological: the ground is held in a condition where human life can continue, with routes across it and rivers through it. Notice that the same sentence gives pathways in the same breath as protection. A world that only held still would be safe and useless; the verse's earth is both anchored and navigable.

**The Disagreement Over a Single Pronoun**

The phrase *caused everything to grow there* contains a pronoun, and the commentators asked what it points to. Al-Zamakhsharī and others take it back to the mountains and read the growth as the minerals and metals buried in them — gold, silver, copper and iron. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī prefer the earth as the referent, and then the growth is vegetation: the fruits, grains and pasture on which the provision of the next verse depends. The second reading fits the sentence's shape better. The mountains have already been given their function in the clause before, and the verb of growth naturally attaches to the ground rather than to the rocks standing on it. It also fits what the Qur'an is doing in this passage, which is answering a challenge about signs by naming things a farmer and a herder would recognise: the soil, its produce, and the fact that both arrive on a schedule nobody negotiates.

**Everything in Due Measure**

The final words state that what grows does so *in perfect balance*, and the Arabic participle suggests something weighed on a scale. Al-Zamakhsharī reads it as a reference to God's wisdom apportioning each thing its quantity, which places the phrase in the same family as *“Indeed, We have created everything, perfectly preordained.”* (54:49) and *“He has created everything, ordaining it precisely.”* (25:2). Sūrah al-Shūrā draws the conclusion for provision: God *“sends down whatever He wills in perfect measure”* (42:27), and adds that if He had given provisions in abundance instead, people would have transgressed across the land. The verse's balance is therefore not merely an aesthetic remark about the natural world. It is a statement about supply: seed, soil, rain and season are calibrated so that life is possible and yet not guaranteed, and the calibration is the work of the same agent who has just been asked to produce a sign.

**The Mountain as a Picture of Firmness**

Commentators have long read the mountains in this verse as something more than geology, and the reading is worth reporting because it has shaped how Muslims have spoken about the religion itself. A mountain is fixed, rooted and immovable while everything around it shifts; the Sacred Law, the prophets and the signs of God are described in the same terms, as realities that anchor human life and keep it from sliding. Sūrah al-Raʿd supports the comparison by listing the mountains beside rivers and fruits of every kind and then concluding that in this there are signs for people who reflect (13:3). The comparison has a limit, and the exegetes are clear about it: the primary sense of the verse is literal, and the spiritual reading is an application rather than the meaning. What the application supplies is the reason the Book chose mountains to describe stability in the first place — they are the most visible example of a thing that holds its place.

**A Sign Nobody Can Claim Not to See**

The verse leaves the sūrah's mockers in an awkward position. They had asked for a gate in the sky; they were reminded of the ground under their feet and the bread on their table. A sign of that kind cannot be dismissed as magic or as a private experience, and it cannot be argued away by people who are standing on it. The Book regularly uses this strategy when the demand for proof becomes a game, and the reasoning behind it is stated elsewhere: the creation itself is the argument that no one can avoid, and the only question is whether a person will allow himself to read it. The earth is spread, the mountains are set, the harvest comes in measured quantities, and the audience of this verse had been walking over that evidence from the day they were born.
verses.20:
> And We made in it means of sustenance for you and others, who you do not provide for

**The Table Was Set Before the Guests Arrived**

The verse speaks of provision placed in the earth, and its word order carries a claim about priority. The means of life were arranged in the world before human beings came to the world to use them: the soil capable of holding seed, the rivers, the grazing, the minerals, the seasons. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf states the arrangement plainly: *“We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.”* (7:10). Read this way, the verse is not describing a system that responds to people but one that was fitted to them in advance, which is why the demand for a sign in the preceding verses is treated as an odd request. A man who asks for proof that God provides for him is standing in a field. The Book's argument is not made from the sky but from the harvest, and the harvest was arranged before the man who eats it was born.

**"For You, and for Those You Do Not Provide For"**

The second half of the verse widens the circle, and the exegetes saw two levels in it. Al-Ṭabarī takes *those you do not provide for* as the livestock and wild creatures that share the earth with their human neighbours; al-Zamakhsharī takes it as the dependants and household members whose upkeep a person imagines he is managing. Both readings are grammatical, and both preserve the point, which is the same in each: the number of mouths being fed is larger than the number of hands that believe they are feeding them. A man with a farm reckons he has provided for his family and his animals. The verse says the provider is someone else, and that among the fed there are creatures he has never counted, cannot name, and would not recognise. The line is not a rebuke of farmers. It is a correction of the ledger.

**Al-Zamakhsharī's Correction of the Provider**

Al-Zamakhsharī gives the point a sharp form: people suppose that they are the ones providing for their dependants, and the supposition is an error, because God is the Provider and He sustains both the supposed provider and the one provided for. He cites the verse in which God describes Himself as *“the Supreme Provider—Lord of all Power, Ever Mighty”* (51:58), and Sūrah Fāṭir presses the same question: *“Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?”* (35:3). What the commentators are guarding against is a habit of speech rather than a doctrine: the parent who says he feeds his children is describing a channel, not a source. The verse under commentary keeps the channel and removes the ownership. A person may cultivate, harvest, store and sell; what he may not do is believe that the supply began with him.

**The Creatures Nobody Counts**

The first reading of this verse — that it includes animals humans do not feed themselves — has a resonance that its first audience could not have measured. Biology now estimates roughly 8.7 million species of eukaryotic life on the planet, with about 6.5 million on land and 2.2 million in the oceans, and by the same analysis some 86 per cent of land species and 91 per cent of marine species have not yet been described. Every one of them is fed, and almost none of them is fed by human beings. The verse does not state a species count, but it does make a claim about the reach of provision, and the modern figure makes the old sentence harder to read as a metaphor. Sūrah Hūd states the guarantee in a single line: *“There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah.”* (11:6).

**The Verse That Answers the Argument About Signs**

Placed where it is, the verse does more than describe a generous world. It pre-empts the deepest objection of the mockers, which was that God was absent and unproven. If the supply of food to every creature is continuous and independent of human management, then the argument for a sustaining agent is not a philosophical guess but a report of something visible in every valley the audience knew. Sūrah Yūnus makes the inference explicit: *“It is Allah Who created you, then gives you provisions, then will cause you to die, and then will bring you back to life.”* (30:40). The sūrah has already answered the demand for an angel by pointing at the delay of judgment and the preservation of the Book. Here it points at dinner. The answer to a request for extraordinary proof is the ordinary fact that the asker is alive and fed.

**Gratitude as the Only Sensible Response**

Everything in the verse points toward one human posture. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf ends its statement of provision with the observation that people seldom give thanks (7:10), and the Qur'an treats ingratitude as the failure that turns abundance into a case against the one enjoying it. Sūrah Ibrāhīm reports the promise attached to the opposite response: *“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.”* (14:7). The logic of the verse is simple enough for a child: food arrives, so someone provides it; the provider is not me, so the thanks belong elsewhere. What the Book adds is the warning that the failure to draw that conclusion is not a small oversight. It is the beginning of the disposition described in the sūrah's opening verses, in which a person eats and enjoys and is diverted by hope until the day he is told what he was eating for.
verses.21:
> There is not any means ˹of sustenance˺ whose reserves We do not hold, only bringing it forth in precise measure

**The Treasuries and Their Owner**

The Arabic word rendered *reserves* is *khazāʾin*, the storehouses of a king, and the Qur'an uses it as a fixed part of its vocabulary for God's relation to the world. Elsewhere the point is put as a rebuke to those who imagine another owner: *“Or do they possess the treasuries of your Lord, or are they in control ˹of everything˺?”* (52:37), and in the story of the hypocrites, who thought withholding their spending would starve the Prophet's community: *“But to Allah ˹alone˺ belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, yet the hypocrites do not comprehend.”* (63:7). The image carries two ideas at once. A treasury implies abundance held in reserve rather than a fixed quantity that might run out, and it implies an owner with the authority to release or withhold. The verse begins there and then applies the idea to everything that exists, so that the whole creation is described as drawing on a supply that is not only sufficient but held by someone.

**Nothing Escapes the Claim**

The construction of the sentence is absolute: *there is not any thing, but that its treasuries lie with Us*. Some of the earliest commentators, al-Kalabī, al-Rāzī and al-Thaʿlabī among them, took the verse as a specific statement about rain, since rain is what makes the crops of the previous verses grow. The broader reading, which al-Bayḍāwī favours, takes it as a statement about every existing thing, with God's treasuries standing for His power and the contents of those treasuries standing for everything that power can bring into being. Both readings are legitimate, and they agree on the essential point: nothing in the created order manufactures itself, and nothing exists on a supply that is outside God's knowledge and control. The specific case of rain is simply the visible instance of a universal rule, and the sūrah's placement of the verse right after a discussion of harvest makes the connection deliberate.

**"We Send It Down": A Metaphor With a Reason**

The verse says that what is held in the treasuries is *sent down*, and the language of descent runs through the Qur'an's account of provision. Rain falls, so descent is exact for water, and the sūrah's next words describe the winds and the rain in those terms. But the Book extends the same verb to things that do not fall, describing Scripture as sent down and, in some passages, creation itself. Al-Rāzī notes that the sending down of a created thing can describe its coming into existence after it had no existence, in the same way that revelation comes down from God's knowledge into the world of human beings. The metaphor is not decorative. It keeps the relation between God and the world pointing in one direction: whatever exists came from above, and whatever is withheld is withheld by decision, not by shortage.

**A World Built to a Measure**

The last phrase, *in precise measure*, is the complement of the treasuries. If the supply were unlimited in its release, the world would be a formless flood; if it were left to chance, there would be no basis for gratitude or complaint. The Qur'an states the principle of measure repeatedly as a feature of creation itself: *“Indeed, We have created everything, perfectly preordained.”* (54:49), and *“He has created everything, ordaining it precisely.”* (25:2). Sūrah al-Shūrā applies it to wealth and provision directly, explaining that God *“sends down whatever He wills in perfect measure”* (42:27), and that boundless abundance would have made people transgress. The measure in this verse is therefore not a limitation on God's generosity. It is the reason the world is livable and the reason human beings can be held responsible for what they do with what arrives.

**Why Rain Is the Right First Illustration**

The rain is the case everyone can verify, and the Book uses it as a lesson in dependence, because water is the one provision that no human being can manufacture at will and no society can store indefinitely. Later in this sūrah the subject returns with the winds that carry and fertilise, and Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah makes the argument in a direct question: *“Have you considered the water that you drink? Is it you who sent it down from the clouds, or is it We Who send down?”* (56:68-69), followed by the warning that God could have made it bitter. The question is unanswerable in the direction the audience would prefer. A cloud is not a machine that a person can start, and a stored reservoir proves only that the water arrived, not that its arrival is owed to the people drinking it. The treasuries announced in this verse are therefore opened by their owner, in quantities He determines, at times He sets.

**What a Believer Owes the Reserved Supply**

The Sufi commentator Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz, who died in 286/899, drew from this verse a conclusion that al-Sulamī preserves: only a person who does not fully believe its truth would place his reliance on anything other than God for his worldly or his otherworldly affairs. The inference runs directly from the text, and it is a statement about ultimate reliance rather than about effort. The Qur'an nowhere commands Muslims to abandon work; Sūrah al-Jumuʿah tells them, once the prayer has ended, to *“disperse throughout the land and seek the bounty of Allah”* (62:10), and the same Book that names God the Provider names Him the one who apportions provision to whom He wills. The distinction is between means and source. A farmer sows because the treasuries are opened through causes; he trusts because holding them closed would defeat every effort he makes.
verses.22:
> We send fertilizing winds, and bring down rain from the sky for you to drink. It is not you who hold its reserves

**Winds That Do a Job**

The Arabic participle rendered *fertilizing* is *lawāqiḥ*, and it is used in two senses that the commentators kept distinct and the Qur'an leaves standing together. In one sense the winds impregnate the clouds, gathering the moisture and driving it to where rain falls; in the other they pollinate the plants, carrying the pollen on which fruiting depends. Al-Ṭabrisī notes that the rain-bearing clouds are what the word describes, and the pairing is not accidental in a sūrah that has just spoken of harvests. Sūrah al-Furqān presents the same winds as *“ushering in His mercy”* (25:48), and Sūrah al-Rūm calls them bearers of good news given so that people may taste mercy and seek provision (30:46). Wind is invisible, uncountable and unowned by anybody; the verse gives it a function, a direction and a purpose, and in doing so it removes the last excuse for treating the world as a place of random events.

**Water Given to a Thirsty Creature**

The second clause states the purpose in the plainest possible phrase: *for you to drink*. Not for irrigation, not for the beauty of the landscape, but for the immediate need of a body, which is how the Qur'an usually grounds its arguments about provision. The Book elsewhere turns the ordinary act of drinking into a question that cannot be answered in the wrong direction: *“Have you considered the water you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:69). The question is put to the whole human species, and it is fair to anyone in any century, because no amount of engineering makes it rain. Wells, canals and pipes are arrangements for moving water that has already arrived. The verse does not deny human ingenuity; it locates it downstream of a supply that has never been under human management.

**"You Are Not the Keepers of Its Stores"**

The final words use the vocabulary of storage: *mā antum lahu bi-khāzinīn*, you are not its treasurers. The same root appeared in the preceding verse, which spoke of the reserves that God holds, and the connection between the two statements is deliberate. One says the supply is held by God; the other says the human being is not the one holding it. Sūrah al-Mu'minūn adds the consequence that ought to keep a person awake: *“We send down water from the sky in a precise measure and cause it to settle into the earth; and surely We are well able to take it away.”* (23:18). What humans call a reservoir is a temporary loan with no guarantee of renewal, and the Qur'an names the situation honestly instead of flattering the tenant.

**The Same Wind That Destroys**

Wind is not always the messenger of mercy, and the Book does not pretend otherwise. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt describes what the same element did to the people of ʿĀd: *“And in ˹the story of˺ ’Âd ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent against them the devastating wind.”* (51:41). Nothing about the wind's nature changed between the two occasions; what changed was the decree it carried. This is the point of the verse's arrangement and the reason it speaks of winds rather than simply of rain. The element that fertilises the fields and fills the cisterns is the same one that can strip a town from the earth, and the difference between outcomes lies entirely with the One who sends it. A person who drinks the water has been given a benefit from the very agent whose restraint he has been depending on without knowing it.

**Why the Verse Ends With a Denial of Control**

The rhetorical shape of the verse is worth noticing. It states two gifts and then closes with a statement about what the recipients are not. That is the pattern of the whole passage, and it answers more than a question about agriculture. It answers the deep assumption that human beings are the managers of their own survival, an assumption that holds comfortably in years of plenty and collapses in a single season of drought. The Qur'an's method is not to argue that people are helpless but to describe accurately what they handle and what they do not. They till, plant, harvest, store and sell; they do not make the wind blow or the cloud break. When that division is stated plainly, the response the Book expects is neither fear nor passivity but gratitude, which is a fair acknowledgement of where the water actually came from.

**From Water to Gratitude**

The sūrah has been building an argument about provision for several verses, and this one turns it toward the human response. Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah makes the transition explicit: after asking who sends the rain, it adds, *“If We willed, We could make it salty. Will you not then give thanks?”* (56:70). The question is not sentimental. It is a claim that the ordinary glass of water on an ordinary day is evidence, and that the evidence has been arranged to be noticed rather than argued. The men who mocked the Prophet wanted angels; they were answered with wind and rain, the two things they could neither produce nor explain, and the verse leaves them holding a cup and a responsibility that no amount of cleverness can transfer to anyone else.

**Why the Qur'an Asks Instead of Asserting**

Other passages take the same material and turn it into a question, and the shift in grammar is instructive. *“Or ˹ask them,˺ ‘Who guides you in the darkness of the land and sea, and sends the winds ushering in His mercy? Is it another god besides Allah?’”* (27:63). Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah puts the same challenge to the water itself: *“Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:69). Sūrah al-Nūr describes the machinery in detail, the clouds driven and joined and piled, the hail poured where God wills and turned aside from where He wills (24:43), and Sūrah al-Raʿd adds the image of valleys flowing each to its own capacity (13:17). The verse under commentary is the plain statement of what those passages ask. The Book prefers the question because the answer is not in dispute until a person is asked directly, and because the audience being addressed already knew who they thanked for rain.
verses.23:
> Surely it is We Who give life and cause death. And We are the ˹Eternal˺ Successor

**Two Acts Held by One Agent**

The Arabic packs its emphasis twice into a short sentence, and the effect is to place the beginning and the end of every living creature in a single pair of hands. Life is given, death is caused, and both verbs have the same subject. This is not a comment on biology; it is a claim about ownership. Everything that draws breath is being actively sustained, and everything that stops drawing it has been stopped by the same authority that started it. Sūrah Ghāfir states the point in its sharpest form: *“He is the One Who gives life and causes death. When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, ‘Be!’ And it is!”* (40:68). The verse's force in this sūrah is directed at the men who doubted the raising of the dead. If life and death are a single gesture from one will, the objection that a scattered body cannot be reassembled loses its weight.

**The Name at the End of the Verse**

The verse closes with a title, *al-Wārith*, the Inheritor, and the image is legal rather than botanical. An heir is the one who remains when the other holders of a property have gone; he does not acquire anything the owner did not have, he simply outlasts every other claim. Applied to God, the name means that everything which exists will pass out of the hands of its temporary holders and return to the One whose it always was. Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ states it plainly: *“Everything is bound to perish except He Himself. All authority belongs to Him. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.”* (28:88), and Sūrah al-Raḥmān puts the two halves of the thought in consecutive verses: *“Every being on earth is bound to perish. Only your Lord Himself, full of Majesty and Honour, will remain ˹forever˺.”* (55:26-27). The name is a statement about the end of the story, and the sūrah has placed it directly after a verse about water.

**Why "Inheritor" and Not Merely "Owner"**

The choice of this name over the simpler language of possession carries a lesson about human beings. Ownership is what a person believes he has over his land, his wealth, his body and his children. Inheritance is what happens to all of it. Sūrah al-Ḥadīd states the pairing of power and mortality in a single breath — to Him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, He gives life and causes death, He is capable of everything (57:2). The name therefore does not add a new attribute to God so much as describe the inevitable outcome for everyone else. Every estate changes hands eventually, and the final hand it reaches is not a human one. A person who internalises the title stops speaking about his property in the language of permanence, which is exactly the correction the Qur'an applies to a merchant city that measured security in stored goods.

**Life and Death in the Sūrah's Argument**

The placement of this verse inside a passage about rain, harvest and sustenance is deliberate. The sūrah has been arguing from the visible to the invisible: the sky is furnished, the earth produces in measure, the water is sent down and its reserves are not held by the people who drink them. Now it names the agent behind all of that as the giver of life and death, and the reasoning becomes visible. Anyone who has watched a dead field turn green after rain has seen the pattern that the resurrection repeats on a larger scale. Sūrah al-Rūm draws the inference explicitly: *“See then the impact of Allah's mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same Creator˺ can raise the dead.”* (30:50). The verse under commentary supplies the principle, and the sūrah's later verses will supply the scene.

**Every Creature Standing Between Two Decrees**

Read on its own, the sentence is a summary of the condition of every living thing. Each of them is between an act that has already happened and an act that has not yet happened, and neither is under its own control. Sūrah al-Mu'minūn ties the same power to the ordinary rhythm of the day: *“And He is the One Who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of the day and night.”* (23:80). The alternation is the point: night falls on everyone at once, without regard for plans. A person who has understood this verse does not become gloomy, because the Qur'an never treats mortality as a reason for despair. What the verse removes is the illusion of self-possession, and what it leaves in its place is a creature who knows whom he is dealing with.

**The Inheritor and the Bread on the Table**

The connection between this verse and its neighbours is easy to miss and important. The Provider who sends the rain is the same Inheritor who will outlast every beneficiary, and the two facts together describe the human condition completely: everything a person receives comes from a hand that is not his, and everything he holds will remain behind when he leaves. The Qur'an draws no conclusion about the worthlessness of the world from this. It draws the opposite conclusion, that gratitude and right use are the only coherent responses to a gift that cannot be owned. The verse is therefore not a verse about death so much as a verse about perspective, and it stands in the middle of a passage about food and water because that is where perspective is hardest to keep. A reader who has followed the sūrah's argument about provision to this point is expected to look at his own table with the same thought in mind: the hand that set it is not his, and it will not follow him out of the room.
verses.24:
> We certainly know those who have gone before you and those who will come after ˹you˺

**Two Readings of Advancing and Lagging**

The Arabic describes two groups, those who go ahead and those who fall behind, and al-Rāzī records two ways of taking the pair. On the first reading the words describe conduct: the ones who press forward are those devoted to obedience, and the ones who lag are those who hold back from it, so that the verse is a statement about God's knowledge of the inner quality of every person, including those not yet born. On the second reading the words describe generations: those who have already passed away and those who are still to come, since the verse stands in a passage about resurrection at the end of the world. Both readings are grammatical, and the second has the stronger claim on the context, which is about the gathering of all people. The force of the sentence is unaffected by the choice: the knowledge described is total, and it reaches every person who exists or ever will.

**The Generations on Both Sides of the Present**

Human beings experience history as a narrow window. A person knows his own decade, remembers something of his parents' generation, and imagines little about the ones behind him or the ones ahead. The verse removes that window as a limit on God's attention, and it does so at the exact point in the sūrah where the audience is being told that the dead will be raised. Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah makes the same distinction in its account of the foremost, of whom *“˹They will be˺ a multitude from earlier generations and a few from later generations.”* (56:13-14). The point is not the arithmetic. It is that the earliest and the latest generations are counted together in one book, and that a person's position on the timeline gives him no advantage in the reckoning.

**Those Who Press Forward and Those Who Hold Back**

Read as a description of conduct, the verse touches a nerve that any religious community recognises. Every assembly contains people who move at very different speeds: some take on the obligations with an appetite, some do the minimum, and some are present in body only. The Book says here that the difference is seen, named and measured. Sūrah al-Tawbah uses the same vocabulary of precedence to describe the earliest believers: *“As for the foremost—the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers—and those who follow them in goodness, Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.”* (9:100). Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah places *“the foremost ˹in faith˺”* first among the ranks of Paradise (56:10). The verse therefore functions as encouragement rather than surveillance alone. To be known as one of those who went ahead is, in the Book's economy, an honour that nobody can confer or withdraw.

**A Knowledge That Makes Anonymity Impossible**

Most wrongdoing is possible because of an audience. A person behaves differently when watched, and he assumes that what is hidden will stay hidden. The Qur'an repeatedly dismantles the assumption, and this verse is one of its cleanest statements: the ones who came before, the ones who are here, and the ones who will come after are all in view. Sūrah al-Mu'minūn adds that God also knows the mechanics of every life: *“No female ever conceives or delivers without His knowledge.”* (35:11). The result is not a surveillance state but a universe in which nothing is actually private, including the intentions behind the acts. The sūrah's mockers were laughing in a public street; the verse quietly informs them that the laughing was not the part that mattered most, and that the audience they had not considered was already in attendance.

**What This Does to the Argument About the Dead**

This verse and the one that follows it form a single argument. The claim of the resurrection was the great stumbling block for the Makkan audience: they could accept a creator in the abstract but found the reassembly of the dead impossible to credit. The answer given here begins with knowledge rather than power. Before saying that God will gather them, the sūrah says that He knows all of them — the ones already turned to dust and the ones not yet born — and knowledge of that scope implies a relation to every particle and every generation. The argument is not that the resurrection is easy, though the Book makes that point elsewhere. It is that the objection presupposes a God whose attention is limited to the living, which is not the God being described.

**Standing in the Line Without Knowing One's Place**

The verse offers the reader a position and no information. He is told that he is one of the ones who came after, that his generation is known, and that he is not the end of the story. What he is not told is where he stands in the ranking of those who press forward and those who hold back, and the Book consistently refuses to settle that question for a person while he still has time to act. That refusal is itself a mercy: it keeps hope alive for the one who has lagged, and fear alive for the one who is pleased with himself. The knowledge announced in this verse is total, and its purpose in the sūrah is not to let anyone calculate his standing but to make the calculation unnecessary, since the one keeping the record never loses it.

**Nothing Small Enough to Escape the Record**

The Qur'an's fullest description of this knowledge appears in Sūrah al-Anʿām, and it reads like an answer to anyone who imagines that God's attention operates at the level of nations rather than persons: *“With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything—green or dry—but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.”* (6:59). The leaf and the grain are the point. If the fall of a single leaf is registered, then the categories of people named in the verse under commentary — the earlier generations and the later ones — are not being tracked as groups. They are known one by one, with what each of them did. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ attaches the same certainty to the daily conduct of a family and ends with the words *“Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you.”* (4:1).
verses.25:
> Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ will gather them together ˹for judgment˺. He is truly All-Wise, All-Knowing

**The Gathering Announced Without a Condition**

The Arabic places the Lord in the foreground by repeating the pronoun: your Lord, He will gather them. The construction leaves no room for a delegated agent or a partial event, and the object of the gathering is everyone named in the verse before it — those who have gone ahead and those who lag behind, the dead of every generation and the living of the present one. What is promised is a single assembly of the entire species. The sentence does not explain how bodies return or when the assembly convenes; the Qur'an treats those questions as secondary to the fact itself. What it insists on is the certainty: the One who has kept the record of all generations will bring them together to face it, and the sūrah has already told its audience that the knowledge required for such a gathering is already in place.

**Two Names That Explain the Sentence**

The verse ends with two divine names, al-Ḥakīm and al-ʿAlīm, wise and knowing, and their placement is not decorative. Wisdom answers the question of purpose: a gathering of all humanity makes sense only if human lives have a weight that outlasts death, accounts that need settling, and injuries that were never repaired in the world. Knowledge answers the question of accuracy: no case is misread, no intention is lost, no plea is misunderstood, and nothing can be omitted from a record kept by the One who knows what every person did and intended. Together the names close both escape routes a person might hope for — that the judge does not care, or that he will not know — and they close them in a single short sentence attached to the promise itself.

**The Same Assurance in Other Sūrahs**

The Book repeats the promise with the same vocabulary of certainty whenever it addresses doubt about the resurrection. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān puts it in the form of a prayer that is also a confession: *“Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt.”* (3:9). Sūrah al-Anʿām goes further and grounds it in God's own attribute: *“He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment— about which there is no doubt.”* (6:12). The gathering, in other words, is not merely something God can do; it is something He has committed Himself to, and the commitment is stated as an expression of mercy rather than of menace. The verse under commentary belongs to that family of statements, and it carries the same reassurance: the assembly is being convened because justice requires it.

**Why the Objection Was So Stubborn**

The Makkan objection to the resurrection was not a philosophical puzzle; it was a refusal that carried social consequences, since a reckoning after death would change how a person could live in Makkah. The Book records the argument in its opponents' own words elsewhere: *“And they argue with Us— forgetting they were created—saying, ‘Who will give life to decayed bones?’”* (36:78). The sūrah's answer here is subtler. It does not begin with power over dust; it begins with knowledge of persons. The men being addressed were being told that their names, families, dealings and arguments were all held by someone who had no trouble tracking generations that had never met. If the objection had been that a just God would not bother, the names at the end of the verse answer it. If the objection was that he would not know, the same two names answer that too.

**The Visible Version of the Same Claim**

The Qur'an habitually argues for the raising of the dead from the greening of the earth, and the sūrah has just spent several verses on rain falling on dry ground. Sūrah al-Rūm draws the conclusion aloud: *“See then the impact of Allah's mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same Creator˺ can raise the dead.”* (30:50), and Sūrah Fuṣṣilat says the same with an earlier stage of the process in view: *“you see the earth devoid of life, but as soon as We send down rain upon it, it begins to stir ˹to life˺ and swell.”* (41:39). A farmer watching a field come back does not regard the event as a suspension of nature; he regards it as the normal work of the One who made the field. The verse under commentary is the doctrinal statement of what the farmer has already seen.

**Gathering as the End of Division**

There is a quieter meaning in the word *gather* that the sūrah's audience would have felt. The society being addressed was split into clans, factions and rival houses, each with its own account of honour, its own grudges and its own version of events. The gathering announced here ends all of that by putting everyone in one place under one judge, with the same facts available and the same standard applied. The divisions that shaped daily life in Makkah will not survive the assembly, and the Book treats this as part of the good news: a reckoning in which the powerful cannot purchase a different verdict and the despised cannot be overlooked. The two names close the verse because wisdom and knowledge are what make such a court possible, and the sūrah's argument about provision turns out to have been an argument about justice all along.

**The Answer Given to the Decayed Bones**

Sūrah Yā Sīn reports the same objection and answers it with two arguments that belong together, and both of them are compressed into the names at the end of this verse. *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being.’”* (36:79). The first argument is the precedent of creation; the second is knowledge of what has been created, down to the last particle. The sūrah then adds an observation from ordinary life, that the same God who gives fire from green wood can surely reconstitute what He assembled once already (36:80). Sūrah al-Naḥl states the timing without hesitation: bringing about the Hour would take the blink of an eye or less, and God is capable of everything (16:77). The men asking the question were measuring a resurrection against their own difficulty, not His.
verses.26:
> Indeed, We created man from sounding clay moulded from black mud

**The Sounding Clay**

The word rendered *sounding clay* is *ṣalṣāl*, and it describes the dry, baked material that rings or rattles when struck. Sūrah al-Raḥmān makes the image explicit by comparing it to pottery: *“He created humankind from ˹sounding˺ clay like pottery”* (55:14). The choice of term is precise. Clay that has been shaped and left to dry is not mud anymore; it holds a form, it can be handled, and it makes a sound when knocked. The Qur'an is describing a formed vessel rather than a handful of earth, and the word anticipates the moment in the account when the shaping is complete and the breath is given. Everything about the phrase keeps the human being's material origin in view: durable enough to hold a shape, and ordinary enough to be found in any riverbed the audience had ever walked beside.

**Dark, Altered Mud**

The second description is *ḥamaʾ masnūn*, black mud whose smell and texture have changed through fermentation. The Arabic vocabulary here is deliberately unflattering, and the Book uses it in a passage whose whole purpose is to undermine pride. A human being who measures his worth by his ancestry is being reminded that the first of his line was moulded from the darkest, softest, least valuable substance available. The Qur'an makes the same point with other words elsewhere, but never more bluntly: the sūrah of the Fire and the Heights describes the material, and the sūrah of the Star asks the doubters to consider what they themselves were made from. The lesson is not that the body is contemptible. It is that the body's origin provides no basis for looking down on anybody.

**The Several Names the Qur'an Gives the Clay**

The Book describes this beginning in several ways, and the variation repays attention. Al-Anʿām speaks simply of clay (6:2), al-Mu'minūn of *“an extract of clay”* (23:12), al-Ṣāffāt of *“a sticky clay”* (37:11), and al-Sajdah of God originating human creation from clay before perfecting it (32:7). Some exegetes read the different terms as stages in a single process — dust, then water, then a sticky mixture, then a dried form — while others read them as aspects of the same material described from different angles. The variation also matches the Book's general habit of describing central events repeatedly, in different settings, so that each telling brings out a different implication. Here the emphasis falls on the forming and the dryness; in the sūrah's later narrative the same material will return as an argument in a dispute.

**One Origin as the Foundation of Human Equality**

If every person traces back to a lump of shaped mud, no family, tribe or nation has a claim to superior substance. The Qur'an states the consequence elsewhere in the plainest terms: *“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women.”* (4:1), and Sūrah al-Ḥujurāt draws the social conclusion: *“Indeed, We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may ˹get to˺ know one another. Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you.”* (49:13). The verse under commentary gives the material fact on which those two statements rest. In a city where lineage was currency, the reminder that the founding ancestor was clay was not a poetic flourish; it was an argument about how people should treat one another.

**From Shaped Earth to a Creature Addressed by God**

The remarkable thing about this verse is what it does not describe. Nothing is said here about the breath, the spirit or the command to the angels, and the reason is that those belong to the verses that follow. What the verse fixes is the starting point, and it fixes it with a word about crafting: the material was shaped, not merely assembled. Sūrah al-Sajdah gathers both halves of the process into one sentence, saying that God *“perfected everything He created”* and then specifying that He *“originated the creation of humankind from clay”* (32:7). Perfection in the Qur'an's usage does not mean that the material was noble; it means the workmanship was exact. The same hands that shaped a vessel from dark mud are the hands that will later address the human being as a responsible creature, capable of hearing a command, of obeying it and of refusing it.

**Why the Origin Is Repeated So Often**

The Qur'an returns to the story of human beginnings at every stage of its argument: when it answers the deniers of resurrection, when it corrects tribal arrogance, when it explains the first disobedience, and when it warns about the end. The repetition is not padding; it is the same fact applied to a different problem each time. In this sūrah the context is the refusal of a message and the pride that produced it, and the verse quietly places the proudest creatures in the story — the audience, and the rebellious spirit who will appear shortly — in front of their own origin. Whatever a person thinks he is, the record begins with dark mud that was shaped, left to dry, and then given life by a decree he could not have resisted or refused.

**The Fuller Account of How a Person Is Made**

One passage sets out the process in a sequence rather than a single image, and it is addressed precisely to people who doubted that they could be brought back: *“O humanity!
