If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then ˹know that˺ We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then ˹developed you into˺ a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then a lump of flesh —fully formed or unformed—in order to demonstrate ˹Our power˺ to you.”* (22:5). The same passage goes on to describe the settling of the embryo in the womb for an appointed term and the stages of life that follow, ending with the feeblest age, when a person knows nothing after having known much. Set beside the verse under commentary, the point is cumulative. The Book takes a being who began as dark, moulded earth and traces every stage of his formation as an act of the same will, then asks him how he supposes that will has become incapable. Sūrah al-Rūm adds the diversity of languages and colours as further evidence of a creator who is not short of means (30:22).
verses.27:
> As for the jinn, We created them earlier from smokeless fire

**A Creation That Came Before Ours**

The verse places the making of the jinn before the making of the human being, and it does so without ceremony. The Qur'an nowhere dates the event or describes the interval; it states an order and moves on. What the order establishes is that human beings are not the first conscious creatures to inhabit the world, and that the story of a proud, intelligent being refusing a command is older than humanity itself. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf states the point in the mouth of the being concerned, who argues that he was created before Adam and from a nobler material. The verse under commentary therefore prepares the ground for everything that follows in the sūrah, where a creature older than man refuses to bow to him and then asks for time to work against him.

**What the Word "Jinn" Names**

The Arabic root behind *jinn* carries the sense of concealment, which is why the word is used both for these creatures and for anything hidden from sight. The Qur'an treats the jinn as a created order with the same moral accountability as human beings: *“I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me.”* (51:56). They hear, they choose, they are addressed by revelation — Sūrah al-Jinn opens with the report that a group of them listened to the Qur'an and went back to their people as warners (72:1). Nothing in the Book supports the picture of these creatures as a class of magical servants summoned by human beings. What the Book insists on is that they are a community with obligations, and that the traffic between them and human beings was never authorised.

**Smokeless Fire**

The material is described as a flame that gives no smoke, and the Qur'an uses the same phrase in Sūrah al-Raḥmān: *“and created jinn from a ˹smokeless˺ flame of fire.”* (55:15). The description is about subtlety. A smokeless flame is the least solid form fire takes: it burns, it moves, it produces nothing you can hold in your hand. Any reader who has watched a flame dance understands why the Book chose this image for beings that see without being seen, move through the world without occupying it, and are known to human beings chiefly by their effects. The language is not offered as a physics lesson. It is offered as an intelligible way of saying that there are minds in creation whose substance is unlike anything a human being has handled.

**Fire and Clay in the Wrong Hands**

The material described in this verse becomes, a few lines later in the sūrah's narrative, the basis of an argument, and the Book has already recorded how that argument was made elsewhere: *“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (7:12; 38:76). That inference is rejected in the strongest terms, and the rejection has consequences for the way a Muslim reads this verse. Fire is not nobler than clay; both are created things, and the difference between them says nothing about the rank of a person or a spirit before God. The verse under commentary gives the material fact without endorsing any hierarchy, and the reader is expected to hold both halves of the lesson: yes, the jinn were created from fire, and no, that fact entitles them to nothing. Rank in this Book is measured by obedience and by consequence, not by composition.

**An Unseen Order and the Limits of Human Knowing**

The Qur'an mentions the jinn often enough to establish that they exist and rarely enough to leave the details alone. It does not describe their societies, their lifespans, their appearance or their numbers. The information given is always attached to a moral purpose: to show that the world is larger than human perception, to warn against consulting them for hidden knowledge, and to correct the human habit of assuming that reality ends where human senses end. A believer who takes the Book seriously receives an account of the universe with more inhabitants than he can see, and with no invitation to speculate about them. What he is told is enough for his conduct, and the Book's reticence about everything else is itself a lesson in how to handle knowledge of the unseen. The jinn themselves are shown to be ignorant of what people wrongly credited them with. Sūrah Sabaʾ reports that when Solomon died, *“nothing indicated to the ˹subjected˺ jinn that he was dead except the termites eating away his staff”*, and it draws the conclusion in their own case: *“if they had ˹really˺ known the unseen, they would not have remained in ˹such˺ humiliating servitude.”* (34:14). Sūrah al-Naml shows one of them offering Solomon a service he could perform but making no claim to hidden knowledge (27:39). Whatever power these creatures possess, the Book never grants them the one thing human beings were most eager to buy from them.

**Why the Story Needs Another Kind of Creature**

If the sūrah's readers were asked why the account of human creation needs a companion verse about the jinn, the answer lies in what follows. The scene about to unfold is a court with a command, a refusal and a sentence, and the refusal comes from a being who was not made of mud. The Book is setting out the two kinds of creature that will share the earth and the accounting: one from dark clay, shaped and breathed into, and one from a flame that leaves no ash. Both were created, both owe their existence to a word, and only one of them will decide that his origin excuses him. The verse is short, and it puts into place the last piece the narrative requires.
verses.28:
> ˹Remember, O Prophet˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to create a human being from sounding clay moulded from black mud

**A Scene Brought Forward Into the Present**

The sūrah turns from the sky, the earth and the rain to a moment that took place before any of its audience existed, and it introduces that moment with the word *when*. The Arabic formula *idh* is used throughout the Qur'an to recall an event and place it in front of the listener as though he were standing in it, and it is addressed here to the Prophet personally. He has just been mocked by men who claimed he was mad and who demanded wonders; he is now shown an assembly in which God speaks, the angels listen, and the creature he has been sent to is the subject of the announcement. The scene is not offered as information about ancient times. It is offered as a place to stand, and the man under attack is invited to see where the story he is carrying actually began.

**The Announcement Made Before the Act**

God does not create the human being first and explain afterwards. He states the intention to the angels before the act, and the Qur'an preserves the wording: I am going to create. The same pattern appears in the fuller account in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the announcement names the purpose — *“I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.”* (2:30) — and the angels respond with the question that shows they had grasped what such a creature might do: *“Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?”* (2:30). The answer given there, that God knows what they do not know, is withheld here. This telling is not concerned with the objection. It is concerned with what the human being is made of, and the announcement delivers that fact immediately.

**What the Angels Heard the Human Being Is**

Nothing in the sentence describes the creature's purpose, rank or capacity. He is named as *bashar*, a human being, a word that points to visible flesh and skin, and the material is given twice over: a clay that rings when struck, black mud that has fermented and changed. The angels, who are made of light — a description the Prophet gives in a well-known report — hear that a new creature is coming from the earth's damp floor. Everything that will follow in the sūrah, the command to bow and the refusal that shames the refuser, rests on this introduction. The Book wants its reader to know exactly what the angels were told to lower themselves before, because the objection raised against the command will be an objection about material, and the answer to it has to be anchored in what was said at the outset.

**Why the Emphasis Differs From Sūrah al-Baqarah**

The two accounts are not contradictory and are not interchangeable. In al-Baqarah the emphasis falls on the office the human being will hold and on the angels' concern about the damage he may do; here the emphasis falls on the substance he is made from and on the shaping that will precede the breath of life. Each telling serves the argument of its own sūrah. Al-Baqarah is answering a people who doubted whether a new covenant could follow an old one, so it speaks of authority and succession; al-Ḥijr is answering mockers and correcting pride, so it speaks of mud. The variation is a feature of how the Qur'an narrates, and it is one of the reasons the exegetes treat the two passages as complementary rather than repetitive. Both announce the same act; each draws out the detail its audience most needed.

**The Angels as Witnesses to Their Own Test**

The announcement puts the angels in a position they had not occupied before. Until this point in the story they have been creatures of unbroken praise and service; now they are told that something is coming which will require a decision from them about their own rank. The Book mentions their exact standing elsewhere: *“And to Allah ˹alone˺ bows down ˹in submission˺ whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of living creatures, as do the angels—who are not too proud ˹to do so˺.”* (16:49). They bow, and they are not too proud. The verse under commentary sets up the moment when that description will be put to the test, and it does so without warning or suspense, as though the reader already knows how the story ends and is being invited to watch the details.

**What the Announcement Says About Human Worth**

A creature made of dark moulded clay is announced in the divine presence before he exists. Sūrah al-Isrāʾ states the outcome of that decision in a sentence that every human being inherits: *“Indeed, We have dignified the children of Adam, carried them on land and sea, granted them good and lawful provisions, and privileged them far above many of Our creatures.”* (17:70). Nothing in that dignity comes from the material of the body or from anything the person has done. It was conferred in advance, before the first human being drew breath, in an announcement to an assembly that had already been serving its Lord without interruption. That is the shape of honour in the Qur'an: it arrives as a gift and a responsibility, and the only question the Book ever asks about it is what a person does with what he was given rather than what he was made of.

**One Material for the Whole Species**

The announcement speaks of a human being, and the material named belongs to no one in particular. Every member of the species is described in the same terms elsewhere: *“One of His signs is that He created you from dust, then—behold!—you are human beings spreading over ˹the earth˺.”* (30:20), and Sūrah Ghāfir traces the whole of a life from that dust through its stages to old age and an appointed end (40:67). The effect of the shared origin is to make the pride of lineage and the pride of nation absurd on their face. A man who boasts about his family is making a claim about the quality of mud, and the Qur'an has already told him whose mud it was. The verse under commentary establishes the material before any human being exists to take credit for it, and the equality that Muslim scholars derived from this narrative — that no people has a claim to substance over another — rests on this announcement to the angels.
verses.29:
> So when I have fashioned him and had a spirit of My Own ˹creation˺ breathed into him, fall down in prostration to him.”

**Two Acts Before the Command**

The sentence places two divine acts before it asks anything of anyone. The first is fashioning: the Arabic verb describes giving something its due proportion, so that every part is fitted to its purpose. The second is the breathing of the spirit, which turns the shaped form into a living being. Nothing in the order is accidental — the body is prepared and then animated, and only after both acts does the command go out. Sūrah al-Sajdah states the same sequence with an added phrase about the work being done properly: *“Who has perfected everything He created. And He originated the creation of humankind from clay.”* (32:7). Perfection here is a statement about craft, not about material. The same hands that shaped a vessel from the earth's dark mud made it exactly as it needed to be for what was going to be placed inside it.

**"A Spirit of My Own" — What the Phrase Does and Does Not Say**

The Arabic reads *min rūḥī*, of My spirit, and the construction is one the language uses to honour a thing by attaching it to a great person — My house, My servant, My messenger. Muslim theologians have guarded the phrase carefully, because God is not composed of parts and nothing is breathed out of Him the way breath leaves a body. The exegetes offered two readings. Some take the spirit here as a reference to God's power, meaning that the human being was animated by an act of divine command; others take it as the spirit itself, a created being, honoured by being attributed to its creator. Both readings keep the essential point: what entered the human body was created by God and given by God, and the attribution of the gift to the giver is what makes a creature of clay capable of knowing, choosing and answering.

**A Command Addressed to Those Present**

What follows the two acts is an imperative: fall down before him. The command is plural and it is issued to the assembled angels, and everything that happens in the next verses is a response to those four words. The Book states the event in five other places — al-Baqarah, al-Aʿrāf, al-Isrāʾ, al-Kahf and Ṣād — with the same outcome each time. The Qur'an does not soften the command or explain why a being made of clay should be bowed to; it reports the order and lets the response of the creatures reveal what kind of creatures they are. Sūrah al-Kahf adds a detail that widens the scene: the command went to the angels, and one among them who was of the jinn rebelled against his Lord's command (18:50). The verse under commentary gives only the order, and the order is unconditional.

**Why the Prostration Is Not Worship of a Creature**

A question arises for any reader: how can a creature be asked to bow to another creature? The classical answer is that the command came from God, which is what made the act obedience rather than idolatry, and that the bowing was directed toward Adam as a greeting or as a direction of attention, not as an act of worship. The Qur'an itself shows prostration functioning as a mark of respect among human beings in the story of Joseph, whose family fell down before him in fulfilment of his dream: *“Then he raised his parents to the throne, and they all fell down in prostration to Joseph.”* (12:100). The difference between the two kinds of prostration is the intention and the object, and the Book's own usage confirms that the same posture can carry two meanings. What made this prostration obligatory was the One who ordered it, not the one before whom it was performed.

**The Same Command Told Six Times**

The Book returns to this moment again and again: the command to bow, the general obedience, and the single refusal. Al-Baqarah records it as a covenant (2:34), al-Aʿrāf as part of the shaping of the human being (7:11), al-Isrāʾ and Ṭā Hā as a reminder to people who would rather follow the refuser, and Ṣād as a scene that begins with God's announcement of the creation (38:71-72). The repetition serves the Qur'an's habit of anchoring the human story at its beginning: every debate about obedience, every temptation, every argument about who deserves authority, leads back to the moment when a command was given to beings who could see what human beings cannot. The verse under commentary contributes the two acts that made the command reasonable — the shaping and the breathing — and then leaves the reader to watch what the angels do.

**What Is Given Cannot Be Earned or Claimed**

Everything in this verse happens before the human being has done anything at all. He has not obeyed or disobeyed, thanked or rebelled; he does not yet exist as a person who can act. The honour of being bowed to arrives entirely as an act of God's choosing, and this is the structure the Book keeps for every honour a person receives. Sūrah al-Isrāʾ lists the gifts given to the children of Adam — dignity, conveyance on land and sea, good provision, precedence over many creatures (17:70) — and none of them is presented as a reward for merit. A reader who follows the argument of the sūrah to the end will find a creature arguing from his own substance; the verse under commentary has already placed all the substance on the other side of the ledger.

**The Breath, the Trust, and the Accountability**

What the breathing of the spirit produces is not merely a living body but a responsible creature. The Qur'an states the weight of that arrangement in a verse about the trust that the rest of creation refused: *“Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they ˹all˺ declined to bear it, being fearful of it. But humanity assumed it, ˹for˺ they are truly wrongful ˹to themselves˺ and ignorant ˹of the consequences˺.”* (33:72). The passage does not say precisely which trust is meant, and the commentators debated it, but the human capacity to obey or refuse — the very capacity being tested in this scene — is the thing that makes the offer meaningful. The verses that follow in this sūrah will show what a creature does with that capacity when it turns against its maker. The angels were told to bow before the kind of being that could carry such a responsibility, and the bookkeeping of the whole story depends on the fact that the human being is not a machine. What was breathed into the form was the power to answer.
verses.30:
> So the angels prostrated all together—

**The Obedience That Needed No Discussion**

The command was given, and the verse reports the response in a single clause with no interval. Sheer obedience is all. The Book elsewhere describes the angels as creatures whose obedience is not an achievement but their condition, and the descriptions are consistent: they do not speak until God has spoken and they act only on His command (21:27), they fear their Lord and do whatever they are commanded (16:50), they never disobey whatever God orders and always do as commanded (66:6). The verse under commentary is that description in action. No question is raised, no condition attached, no delay recorded between the imperative of the previous verse and the prostration of this one. In a sūrah whose audience was arguing about signs, the contrast between an assembly that moves when told and a city that demands explanations is unmistakable.

**"All Together": the Weight of a Single Word**

The Arabic ends with *ajmaʿūn*, a word that gathers an entire group into an unbroken whole. It is not the ordinary plural for a collection of individuals; it says that the assembly went down as one body, with no exception and no gap. The Book uses this firmness deliberately, and the next verse will show why: the totality of the prostration is what gives weight to what follows. A reader who has been told that every single angel lowered himself cannot fail to notice the one who did not. The word also settles how the divine command works in a creation that contains many ranks: obedience is not negotiated between ranks, and the most honoured angels are not exempt from an order given to all. The prostration was by the whole host because the order was to the whole host.

**The Angels' Standing in the Order of Creation**

Honour belongs to the angels in the Qur'an — they are described as honoured servants (21:26) and as the nearest to God (4:172) — and the verse's point is not that they are unimpressive. It is that their standing never becomes a reason for standing apart. They are witnesses to the arrangement of the world and they carry out its business, and yet when the command comes to bow before a creature of clay, they bow. The Book records the divine rebuke to any creature that would think rank excuses obedience: *“The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah.”* (4:172). Two of the highest created stations, a prophet and the closest angels, are named in one sentence precisely because pride at the top of the order would be the most destructive kind.

**What a Prostration Physically Claims**

The posture is not incidental. To prostrate is to place the head, the seat of a person's dignity, on the ground, so that the body enacts what the heart is supposed to be saying. Every creature that bows is stating something with its form: it is not the owner of itself, and it accepts what it has been told. This is why the act became the test in this scene rather than a spoken declaration. Words can be managed; the body's admission of a lower position cannot be dressed up. The angels had no material objection available, and no speech is recorded from them. They bowed, and their prostration announced publicly that a command from God settles a matter, whether or not its reasons have been explained.

**An Identical Line in Another Sūrah**

Sūrah Ṣād contains the same scene and, at this point in the story, brings the same words over into its own account: after the announcement of the creation of a human being from clay and the breathing of the spirit, it records *“So the angels prostrated all together—”* (38:73), and then, in the following verse, the single exception. The two sūrahs run in parallel for several verses because both are retelling one event to two different audiences, and the reader who notices the overlap is meant to notice the difference in what each sūrah surrounds it with. Al-Ḥijr places the scene in the middle of a passage about signs in creation; Ṣād places it where a proud people are being reminded that the first refusal of God's command came from a creature who thought he was made of something better.

**The Silence of an Assembly That Agreed**

The verse is short and it contains no speech from the angels, which is itself a statement. They had listened to an announcement and received an order, and the record says nothing about their deliberations because there were none to report. In a Book that preserves the arguments of the mockers, the demands of the proud and the questions of doubters, the silence of this assembly is conspicuous. What the sūrah is about to describe is a refusal that produced twenty verses of speeches, and this verse shows what the alternative looks like: a single clause in which a whole creation did what it was told and said nothing about it, because the deed was enough.

**Service as the Angels' Constant State**

The prostration in this verse is one visible instance of a service that runs continuously in the Book's picture of the world. The angels carry out the decrees of God in the affairs of creation, and Sūrah al-Qadr describes their movement on the night of the decree: *“That night the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit descend, by the permission of their Lord, for every ˹decreed˺ matter.”* (97:4). Sūrah al-Nabaʾ pictures them standing in ranks on the day of reckoning, silent until given permission to speak (78:38). Everything recorded about them is obedience, ranked and disciplined, and the permission clause that recurs in these descriptions matters: even their speech waits on a grant. The scene in this sūrah is therefore not an isolated act by creatures who usually do something else. It is the standing order of their existence applied to a single moment, which is why the obedience is described in one clause without a word of explanation.
verses.31:
> but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others

**The Name and Where It Comes From**

Iblīs is the name the Qur'an gives this creature, and it appears eleven times in the Book, twice of them in this sūrah. The Arabic lexicographers did not agree on its origin. One line of explanation connected it with an Arabic root that carries the sense of despair, since he is the creature who gives up hope of God's mercy; the reported view of several early authorities is that it is not an Arabic word at all but a name taken over from another language, in which the corresponding term means the one who slanders or throws across. The Qur'an itself never explains the name and never derives it from anything, which is worth noting in a Book that regularly explains the meanings of the words it uses for the unseen. What the name points to, in either account, is a being defined by a single act: he refused, he was cast out, and the language around him is the language of a ruined relationship.

**Refusal as a Chosen Act**

The verb used here is *abā*, which means to refuse with the will, and the Book pairs it elsewhere with pride so that the reader never mistakes it for weakness of understanding: *“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, ‘Prostrate before Adam,’ so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful.”* (2:34). Sūrah al-Kahf describes the same act from the standpoint of loyalty: he *“was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord”* (18:50). Nothing in any account suggests that he misunderstood the order, doubted who gave it, or failed to hear it. He knew the command, understood it, and declined. This is why the sūrah will spend the next verses on his reasoning: the Book is not describing a mistake but a position, argued and defended, and the argument is the most dangerous thing about it.

**The Offence of Standing Apart**

The verse says that he refused to be *with* the prostrators, and the wording matters. The command had been addressed to the group, and obedience was therefore a communal matter in which every creature present had a place. His refusal did not merely decline an action; it extracted him from the assembly that performed it. In this Book, belonging to a body of worshippers is not a private preference, and the person who holds back from what the community has been commanded stands in a different line from the one who simply does not understand. The Qur'an's treatment of the hypocrites makes the same distinction: they are present in body while their refusal separates them, and the Book describes their condition in the language of standing behind rather than moving forward.

**Angel or Jinn?**

Because the command was given to the angels and Iblīs is described as the exception, some commentators took him to be an angel who sinned, and they argued that his exemption from the prostration showed he belonged to their category. Sūrah al-Kahf settles the question in a few words: *“he was one of the jinn”* (18:50). The opposite position resolves the apparent difficulty by observing that a group can be addressed by the name of its majority, or that the jinn were present in the same assembly; the classical exegetes also reported the view that the jinn were a type within the wider order of angels. The explicit statement in al-Kahf is the stronger evidence, since it names his kind directly, and the next verse of this sūrah will quote him speaking as one who distinguishes his own creation from Adam's. Whichever way a reader settles the question, the Qur'an's concern is clear: it is not describing a nature that sinned by necessity, but a creature who was free to obey and chose otherwise.

**Pride, the Root That Does Not Show**

The Book names the motive in the parallel accounts and leaves it implicit here. He refused, and he did so out of a sense of his own superiority, which is what the source of every similar refusal has always been. Sūrah al-Naḥl states God's attitude in a single sentence: *“Without a doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. He certainly does not like those who are too proud.”* (16:23). Pride in this vocabulary is not high self-regard alone; it is the belief that a creature stands above an obligation. That belief is what made a being who had spent his existence in the presence of God capable of setting his own assessment of a command over the command itself. The verse reports the act in four words, and the rest of the sūrah will show what such a belief produces.

**One Dissent in an Unbroken Assembly**

The scene is built on a contrast that cannot be missed. A whole creation bows, and one being does not, and the Book turns its attention to that one. This is not a matter of narrative proportion; it is a lesson about how the Qur'an weighs acts. The obedience of the many is recorded in a clause, and the refusal of the single creature commands the rest of the passage, because refusal in the face of clear obedience is the more consequential event for everyone who comes after. Everything that happens in the sūrah from this point — the request for time, the promise of misguidance, the war against human beings — follows from one creature's decision to hold his head up while an assembly lowered theirs into the ground.

**The Refusal That Became a Pattern**

The Book treats this refusal as the beginning of a division that runs through human history. Iblīs expected to win followers, and Sūrah Sabaʾ reports the outcome in a sentence that reads like a ledger: *“Indeed, Iblîs' assumption about them has come true, so they ˹all˺ follow him, except a group of ˹true˺ believers.”* (34:20). The exceptions receive as much attention in the Qur'an as the majority, because the whole contest is about which of them a person joins. Iblīs is also described as the one who makes wrongdoing attractive, and the Book's vocabulary for his work — whispering, promising, adorning — all proceeds from the posture he adopted in this verse. He was the first creature to decide that a command from God could be assessed rather than obeyed, and the consequences were not limited to himself. Every later refusal draws on his example, which is why the Book names him in connection with those who follow him rather than treating the scene as a private quarrel in an invisible assembly.
verses.32:
> Allah asked, “O Iblîs! What is the matter with you that you did not join others in prostration?”

**A Question From the One Who Needs No Answer**

The verse records God addressing the creature by name and asking him why he is not among those who bowed. Nothing about the question is an inquiry after information, since the Book everywhere states that God knows what is hidden and what is revealed. The interrogative is a summons. It gives the offender the floor and requires him to say aloud what he has decided, so that the position he holds is brought out of concealment and into his own words. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf uses the same method — *“What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?”* (7:12) — and Sūrah Ṣād presses it further: *“Did you ˹just˺ become proud? Or have you always been arrogant?”* (38:75). Across the three accounts, God asks, and the creature answers, and the answer is his own judgement of himself.

**The Three Versions of the Question**

The three questionings are not duplicates. The first element in Ṣād, whether his arrogance is new or long-standing, reaches a question about character that the others do not ask, and it cuts both ways: a sudden pride could be repented of, while a settled pride is a condition. Al-Aʿrāf asks about the obstacle, naming the command as the thing he failed to keep. The question in this sūrah is phrased through the community: what is the matter with you that you are not with those who prostrated. Each wording draws out a different face of the same act: the new or old pride of the one who did it, the obstacle he allowed to stand between himself and an order, and the separation from a body of worshippers that his refusal produced. Read together, the three give the reader the anatomy of a single refusal.

**Being Named in the Address**

The question opens with the name: O Iblīs. He is spoken to by the God who created him, in a direct address that uses the name he is known by, and there is no vituperation in the sentence. The Book records the exchange without adding a rebuke to the question. Whatever the outcome of the scene, the offender is not shouted at, accused, or dismissed before he can speak. This pattern is consistent with the way the Qur'an presents the divine dealings with creatures that have gone wrong: the door is held open until the creature himself closes it. Adam and Eve, later in the same story, are asked a question too, and their answer brings them forgiveness. The difference between their outcome and Iblīs's will lie entirely in what each of them says.

**The Language of Joining**

The Arabic in this verse describes him as one who failed to be *with* those who prostrated, and the phrasing treats the prostration as a company a person can either enter or stand outside. It is worth watching how the Book talks about worship as a shared act, from the rows of prayer to the ranks of the angels. Obedience that is performed alone still counts, but the command here was given to a collective and answered by a collective, and the one who held back stepped out of it. The wording also closes off a defence the reader might otherwise imagine: there was no private arrangement by which he could satisfy the order in another way. The command was not to understand the wisdom of prostration, or to feel submission inwardly, but to be among those who did it.

**A Hearing Before Any Sentence**

No punishment is announced in this verse, and none of the three accounts passes sentence before the creature has spoken. The Book's judicial manner is worth noticing here because it recurs at the final judgment, where the condemned are asked questions they cannot answer — *“Did a warner not come to you?”* (67:8) — and reply that warners did come and were rejected (67:9). Those questions do not gather information either; they make the record public in the accused's own voice. Applied to Iblīs, the method shows that his expulsion was not a hasty reaction to a wrong step. He was asked, he was heard, and he used the hearing to argue his case. The severity of what follows is the severity of a verdict that could not have been different, because the creature had stated his position and refused to revise it.

**The Chance He Did Not Take**

Everything in the scene gives room for a return. He is addressed, named, asked, and given the opportunity to speak, and the Book records no threat that would have made an honest answer costly. A creature who had understood the situation could have said that he had failed an obligation, and the record of Adam's response in the same story shows where such an answer leads: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we shall surely be among the losers.”* (7:23). The question in this verse is therefore a test of what the creature will do with a chance that he will never have again. What he does with it — an argument built on his own composition and his own superiority — becomes the template for every refusal that answers a command with self-justification.

**The Question Put to Adam and Eve**

The same manner of questioning appears later in the story, and the difference in outcome shows what the question was for. After the first couple had been misled and had covered themselves with leaves, *“their Lord called out to them, ‘Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?’”* (7:22). They were asked a question and they answered with a confession, and the Book records the result immediately: *“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.”* (2:37). Al-Ḥijr does not narrate that part of the story, but a reader who knows it can see the two answers standing side by side. The God who asks is the same in both scenes. What differs is the answer, and the Book lets the contrast speak without comment.

**A Sending That Leaves No Excuse Behind**

The pattern of asking before judging is not limited to the beginning of the story. The Book states it as a general principle of how God deals with communities: *“This ˹sending of the messengers˺ is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺.”* (6:131). The question put to Iblīs is the first instance of that principle in the sūrah's narrative: the creature knows, the creature is addressed, and the creature is given the floor. The same care that makes a warning precede a punishment shapes this interrogation. A reader who notices it will find it harder to imagine that anyone — a rebellious spirit or a mocking townsman — is judged on a matter he never had a chance to consider. The inquiry is the mercy, and the refusal is what turns it into a record.
verses.33:
> He replied, “It is not for me to prostrate to a human You created from sounding clay moulded from black mud.”

**An Answer to a Question That Was Not Asked**

He was asked why he had not joined the prostrators. He replies by explaining what he is not prepared to bow to, and the reply never touches the actual question of his obligation to obey. This is the structure of the refusal in all three accounts, and the fuller versions show what lies behind it: *“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (7:12; 38:76). The shape of the argument is a comparison between two materials, followed by a conclusion about rank. What is missing from the argument is the only premise that mattered — that a command from God settles an obligation regardless of what the creature makes of the reasoning behind it. The verse reports the answer as it was given, and the reader is expected to see that it is not an answer at all.

**The Word "Human" Spoken With Contempt**

Iblīs calls the being he was ordered to bow to *bashar*, a human, and then identifies him by the material he was made from. The word itself is neutral; it is the setting that makes it an insult. In the mouth of a creature made from a flame, naming another creature's substance is a way of stating what he thinks the other creature amounts to. The Qur'an records the contempt without endorsing it, and the sūrah has already supplied the reader with the facts the speaker wanted to leave out: the shaping, the measure, and the spirit breathed into the form by God's own command. A reader who has just come from those verses knows perfectly well that the human being is not reducible to the clay he was made from, which is what makes the sneer in this reply so blind. He is describing his rival by a stage that has already passed.

**Fire and Clay: a Syllogism With a Missing Premise**

The reasoning has the form of a syllogism: fire is nobler than clay; I was created from fire; therefore I am nobler than the one created from clay; therefore it is not for me to bow. Every step depends on a premise that the Book never grants. The superiority of one created thing to another is not something a creature can measure by inspecting its own composition, because the material of a body says nothing about the standing of the person who has been placed in it. The Qur'an's own test of rank is stated in a verse addressed to all humanity: *“Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you.”* (49:13). The argument from substance is precisely the measure that this verse abolishes, and the creature making it in the divine presence was in no position to apply a standard that had already been disowned.

**What Knowledge Has to Do With Rank**

Where the Book does compare people, it compares what they carry rather than what they were made from. *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Are those who know equal to those who do not know?’”* (39:9). The comparison in that verse is between knowledge and ignorance, both of which are things a person can acquire or neglect, and neither of which any creature is born holding as a birthright. Iblīs made the opposite move: he treated an origin he did not choose as a title he had earned. The Qur'an nowhere denies that the materials of creation differ in their properties — fire and clay behave differently, and the Book says so plainly. What it refuses is the leap from a difference in composition to a difference in worth, and the refusal is definitive: the creature who tried to make that leap was answered with expulsion rather than with an argument.

**Fire Rises and Clay Rests**

Later commentators read the two materials as pictures of the two attitudes the scene displays, and the observation is worth recording as an observation rather than a proof. Fire by nature leaps upward and consumes what surrounds it; clay by nature lies where it is put, holds water, and is shaped by its maker's hands. A creature who reasons from his own element to his own dignity has already taken the upward posture; a creature moulded from the ground has already been taught to be handled. Al-Maybudī draws the contrast in these terms, and the comparison illuminates the story without replacing its plain sense. The Book's own vocabulary does something similar when it contrasts those who are too proud to serve with the angels who are nearest to God and are not (4:172).

**The Command, Not the Reason, Was the Test**

The deepest trouble with the reply is that it substitutes analysis for obedience. He was not asked to understand why a being of clay should be bowed to; he was told to bow. The Book states the principle that his answer violated in a verse about the community of believers: *“It is not for a believing man or woman—when Allah and His Messenger decree a matter—to have any other choice in that matter.”* (33:36). Submission that waits for a satisfactory explanation is not submission but review, and review is not a posture a creature can hold toward its maker. That is the lesson the sūrah is building, and the next verses will show the length to which a creature will go once he has decided that his own assessment of a command is what counts.

**The Reply He Was Not Able to Give**

The Qur'an preserves another answer to a similar accusation, spoken by a human being who was being pressed to deny his creator. A companion in the story of the two men in the garden asks, *“Do you disbelieve in the One Who created you from dust, then ˹developed you˺ from a sperm-drop, then formed you into a man?”* (18:37). The argument is the opposite of the one Iblīs made: it reasons from the same material — dust, then a drop, then a formed human — to the goodness and power of the maker, rather than from material to personal superiority. Both speakers acknowledge where they came from. One draws humility out of the fact and the other draws a claim. The sūrah leaves the reader with the contrast, and the contrast exposes the reply in this verse for what it is: not an argument at all, but a preference for one's own reasoning over an obligation.

**The Silence in the Reply**

Nothing in the answer asks for forgiveness, admits a fault, or acknowledges the command. The Arab grammarians note that the reply is phrased as a statement of what is *not for him*, as though the obligation belonged to someone else's dignity rather than his own conduct. Every word of it is about rank, and none about duty. The Book does the reader the favour of recording it without correction, so that the shape of it can be examined: a claim about substance, an implied comparison, and no reference to the one who gave the order. When the same style of reply is used by human beings in later generations — and the Book reports many similar exchanges — it is recognisable because this one was recorded first, in an assembly of angels, from the mouth of a creature who had every advantage of knowledge and chose to use it in defence of himself.
verses.34:
> Allah commanded, “Then get out of Paradise, for you are truly cursed

**The Sentence Comes After the Refusal**

The order to leave follows directly from the answer Iblīs had just given, and the Arabic particle at the start of the command ties the two together: since that is your position, then get out. Nothing new is introduced into the case. The creature had been asked, he had answered, and the answer itself produced the verdict. This is the pattern the sūrah uses with the mockers as well, who are left to their chosen course and told to wait, and it reflects a manner of dealing with creatures that the Book never hides: a person is not usually struck down in the middle of his argument. He is allowed to state his case, and then the consequences of the case arrive. The verse is the hinge where the argument in the assembly becomes a sentence pronounced in the assembly.

**"Paradise" and What Leaving It Meant**

The place he is ordered out of is the elevated garden, the dwelling of the angels and the setting of the scene, and the loss is total. In the parallel telling, God adds a detail that makes the reason explicit: *“Then get down from Paradise! It is not for you to be arrogant here. So get out! You are truly one of the disgraced.”* (7:13). The location was not compatible with the attitude. Arrogance in a place where every creature is a servant, among angels whose service is unbroken, was a contradiction waiting to be resolved, and the resolution was his removal. The verse does not describe the regret, the looking back, or any of the small humiliations that a reader might imagine. It records the command and moves on, which gives the sentence more weight rather than less.

**The Word "Cursed" and Where It Was Used Before**

The Arabic term is *rajīm*, the same word this sūrah used eleven verses earlier when it said the sky was protected *“from every accursed devil”* (15:17). The connection is exact and probably deliberate. What was described there as a fact about the sky — that the being and his kind are excluded from the highest company — appears here as part of his sentence in the same vocabulary. The title is not a new name invented for the occasion; it is a condition already in force, now stated to his face. The Book also attaches the term to any creature that misleads, which is why a Muslim says the same word when seeking refuge before reciting: *“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed.”* (16:98). The command to leave in this verse is where that condition was declared.

**The Pride That Was the Real Cause**

The Book states the motive repeatedly, and it does not reduce it to a bad decision made in a moment. Al-Baqarah says he *“refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”* (2:34), and al-Aʿrāf records the words that show the arrogance in operation. Pride in the Qur'an is not simply a high opinion of oneself; it is the refusal to accept a command on the grounds that it does not suit one's station, and that is precisely what happened here. Sūrah al-Naḥl states God's attitude toward the condition in a sentence that any reader can carry away: *“God certainly does not like those who are too proud.”* (16:23, substance). The creature's expulsion from the garden is the outward form of an inward state that made the place impossible for him, and the sentence makes visible what had already happened inside.

**Why This Scene Matters to the Sūrah's First Audience**

The men who mocked the Prophet in Makkah measured themselves by their lineage, their wealth and their standing among the tribes of Arabia; pride was not a vice in their culture but a form of property. The sūrah's narrative places before them the most consequential act of pride in the history of creation and describes where it led. The lesson is not aimed at a hidden spirit but at the audience of the recitation, which is the pattern of the passage: creation is described, the angels bow, one creature refuses out of self-regard, and a community full of self-regard is told the story. The Book's method here is to answer a social attitude with a scene from before human history, so that the proud listener can recognise the posture he is holding by watching what happened to the first creature who held it.

**A Verdict With No Route Back in the Same Scene**

The Book records what Adam and Eve did after their mistake, and the contrast illuminates this verse. When they were confronted, *“they replied, ‘Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.’”* (7:23), and they were forgiven. Iblīs makes no equivalent move. He does not ask for pardon, confess a fault, or acknowledge the command he refused, and the sentence he receives is spoken in a scene with no route back inside it. The Book leaves the reader to draw the comparison, and the comparison is severe. The difference between the two cases is not the size of the wrong but the direction of the response, and this verse is the point at which the second possibility closes for the creature who chose the first.

**The Departure He Had Already Chosen**

A detail in the wording repays attention: the command to leave is issued after the creature had already removed himself from the company in another sense. He had declined to be *with* the prostrators; his refusal had separated him from the assembly before any sentence was passed. The expulsion from the garden makes that separation physical and permanent, but it does not create it. This is how the Book habitually speaks about punishment, as the manifestation of a state the person has chosen rather than an arbitrary infliction. The angels bowed, he did not, and everything after that — the question, the answer, the verdict, the exit — follows like a line drawn from an initial point. The sūrah records the line and lets its first audience, and every later one, work out what it is standing on.
verses.35:
> And surely upon you is condemnation until the Day of Judgment.”

**A Curse With a Fixed Horizon**

The sentence attaches the curse to a specific endpoint: until the Day of Judgment, the day of reckoning when every account is settled and every creature receives its due. The Arabic name for that day, *yawm al-dīn*, means the day of recompense, and it is the great boundary of the Qur'an's timeline, mentioned again and again as the point at which histories end and verdicts are issued. Iblīs's punishment is therefore dated. It is not described as annihilation or as the withdrawal of his existence; it is a stated condition lasting the whole span in which human beings will be alive, tested and recorded. The Book's whole narrative of temptation, from the garden to the last generation, fits inside the period covered by this one line of sentence.

**What Condemnation Means in the Qur'an**

The word rendered *condemnation* is *laʿnah*, and everywhere the Book uses it the sense is removal from mercy rather than the infliction of pain. Sūrah al-Baqarah describes those who die in rejection as *“condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity.”* (2:161), and Sūrah al-Aḥzāb states the same of those who offend God and His Messenger, adding that the condemnation continues in this world and the next (33:57). When the term is applied to Iblīs, then, the claim is that the creature has been severed from the thing he had forfeited by his own act, and the rest of what follows in his story is the working out of a condition already set. The Qur'an never describes him as weak, foolish or ignorant. What it describes is a being cut off from mercy and aware of it.

**The Hadith on Pride and the Garment It Vies For**

The Prophet is reported to have related the words of God concerning the root of this whole scene: *“Pride is My cloak and greatness My robe, and he who competes with Me in respect of either of them I shall cast into Hell-fire.”* The report is in Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4090, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī, with a parallel in Sunan Ibn Mājah 4174, and it is included as the nineteenth of the well-known Forty Hadith Qudsi. The image explains the verdict in this verse. A cloak belongs to the one wearing it, and a creature that drapes itself in greatness has taken up an attribute that has no second owner. What Iblīs asserted in the previous verses was an assessment of his own station; the report names that assertion as a rivalry, and the casting out described here is the outcome the report predicts.

**The Same Curse in the Parallel Accounts**

Sūrah Ṣād gives the sentence in nearly the same words, with the possessive added: *“And surely upon you is My condemnation until the Day of Judgment.”* (38:78). Al-Aʿrāf records the expulsion with a different emphasis, ending with the words *“You are truly one of the disgraced.”* (7:13), and adding, in the verse that reports his request for time, that the request came from a creature already under sentence. The consistency across three tellings is striking. Each one keeps the same elements: the order to leave, the condition of being outcast, and a duration that ends at the day of recompense. The variations are small, and none of them softens the sentence into a temporary lesson. The Book reports the outcome the same way every time it tells the story.

**The Day of Judgment as the Limit of His Long Life**

The creature who asked for time in the next verses received something remarkable: permission to continue existing across the entire span of human history. The verse under commentary sets the outer edge of that permission. The Book elsewhere describes the day when the trumpet is blown and all that is in the heavens and the earth is seized with terror, and it describes what happens to those on the wrong side of that day in terms that leave no room for further activity. An enemy whose window closes on that day is an enemy whose schemes are confined to the world where human beings are being tested. This is why the sūrah can move from the scene of his expulsion to the ordinary pressures on a believer's life without any sense of a cosmic threat. The threat has an expiry date, and the date is fixed.

**The Contrast With the Response of Adam**

The Book records how human beings handled their own failure, and putting the two responses side by side shows what this curse was for. Adam and his wife, once they had slipped, said *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23), and the Book reports that God turned toward them. The expelled creature never makes such a request; in the verses that follow, he asks only for time. The sentence in this verse is therefore not a sentence passed on a creature who begged and was refused. It is the outcome for one who did not beg. The Book records the sequence of both stories in the same chapter of revelation so that no reader can miss what was available and what was chosen instead.

**A Curse That Serves the Story It Tells**

There is one more observation to be made about the length of this punishment. It lasts until the very day when the purposes it serves are complete. The temptations, the warnings, the prophets, the communities that accept and reject, the patience of the righteous — the whole machinery of the human test in the Book runs inside the period covered by this one sentence. The creature was cast out with a term, and the term is the history of the human race. What the sūrah describes, then, is not an accident that befell the created order but a condition built into it, known from the beginning, with its conclusion fixed. The next verses will show the creature's response to the sentence, and the shape of that response is what the Qur'an expects its readers to recognise in their own lives.
verses.36:
> Satan appealed, “My Lord! Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.”

**The Name He Is Called by Here**

The verse introduces the speaker with a title rather than the personal name used in the previous lines: he is called *shayṭān*, the devil. In Arabic the word suggests distance and estrangement, and the Book applies it both to this being and to any creature, human or spirit, that takes up the same role. It is not a name he chose. It is a description of what he is, and the sūrah has just used its participle, accursed, for the sky's excluded intruder. The translation keeps the shift from the name Iblīs to the title, and the shift is worth noticing: the Book records the sentence under the personal name, and the plea that follows under the title that says what he has become to the world he is about to be released into.

**The Plea That Asks for Time and Not Pardon**

Of all the things a creature under sentence could request, he asks for an extension. There is no apology in the sentence, no admission of fault, no request for the removal of the curse; he asks to be kept alive. The parallel accounts keep exactly the same wording: *“He appealed, ‘Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.’”* (7:14), and *“Satan appealed, ‘My Lord! Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.’”* (38:79). What makes the absence of a plea for forgiveness so striking is that the Book has already shown what a plea looks like when it is made. His own refusal to make one, after being addressed and questioned, is the fullest demonstration of the arrogance that had just been condemned in him.

**"My Lord": the Submission He Could Not Abandon**

The appeal opens with the words *my Lord*, and the address matters. The creature who has just refused an order, argued against it, and been expelled for it still calls God his Lord. He does not claim sovereignty, deny his maker, or set himself up as an alternative deity. Sūrah al-Baqarah states plainly what his situation became when it describes him as *“becoming unfaithful”* (2:34, ending), and the Book elsewhere records his admission that God is the one who created him. His rebellion is therefore not unbelief in the ordinary sense. It is a monstrous inconsistency: a creature that fully acknowledges who owns him, refuses to obey, argues about rank instead, and then asks that owner for more life. The Qur'an records all of it, and the intelligence displayed in the asking is part of the warning.

**Why He Wanted to Live Until the Resurrection**

The request names the day of resurrection rather than the day of judgment, and the difference is deliberate. The day of resurrection is when the dead are raised and the accounting begins; a delay until that day is a delay until the last possible moment of the world as human beings know it. In the verses that follow, he explains what he intends to do with the time. The Book does not present the request as a wish for reflection, retirement or repentance. It is an application for a working life, and the work is described immediately. There is a bitter precision in the choice of date: he asks to remain in the world exactly as long as the world provides opportunities to harm the creatures who were preferred over him.

**Respite in the Qur'an's Vocabulary**

The Book has a specific word for granted delay, from a root meaning to postpone, and it uses the same root for the answer given later in this sūrah to the men demanding a sign, who are told that on the day the angels come their end will not be postponed. The vocabulary links Iblīs's request to something much wider: the fixed terms given to communities, the years granted to the prosperous, and the interval that allows a person to turn. The respite granted to this creature is one instance of a pattern that runs through creation. God grants time. Time is what makes choice meaningful, and the Book's warnings are all addressed to creatures who still have it.

**Despair Turned Into a Program**

The lexicographers connected the name Iblīs with an Arabic root that carries the sense of despair, and whether or not the etymology is accepted, the psychology fits the verses: a creature with no hope of return, still powerful, still informed, and now devoted to making sure that others join him. Sūrah Sabaʾ reports the outcome he anticipated, that most follow him and only a group of true believers hold out (34:20). The plea in this verse is the moment his grievance acquires a plan. He cannot wound the One who expelled him, so the world that was made for human beings becomes the field of his campaign. Everything the Book will say about his methods — whispering, promising, dressing wrongdoing as attractive — grows out of this short sentence asking for time.

**The Longer Version of the Same Vow**

Sūrah al-Nisāʾ records the vow with the details supplied: *“cursed by Allah—who said, ‘I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants. I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah's creation.’”* (4:118-119), and it closes with a verdict on anyone who takes him as a guardian instead of God. The addition of empty hopes is important, because it names the currency he trades in. Sūrah al-Isrāʾ puts the same list of methods in the form of an order given to him — incitement, cavalry and infantry, partnership in wealth and children, promises — and then states what the promises are worth: nothing but delusion (17:64, ending). Set beside the verse under commentary, the shorter telling loses none of its meaning. He asked for time; the fuller accounts show what he intended to do with it.
verses.37:
> Allah said, “You will be delayed

**A Request Granted in Four Words**

The answer to the plea is one clause, and it contains no rebuke, no condition, and no further discussion of the argument the creature had made about his own composition. He asked for time, and time was given. This is the same economy the sūrah shows in the parallel accounts: al-Aʿrāf records the exchange and its answer without commentary (7:14-15), and Ṣād repeats the grant in identical terms (38:80). The Book's manner here is worth attention. When the creatures of the Qur'an make large demands or large pronouncements, the response is often surprisingly short, because the response is not the argument. Here the brevity itself is a message: the request was never in dispute, and nothing about being granted it changes what the creature is or what he has done.

**The Form of the Grant**

The Arabic is an active statement of granting, and the phrase the translation gives is a single clause about his future condition. Later in the sūrah, the same exchange appears in al-Aʿrāf in the form of a sentence that enrols him among a class: you are among those granted delay (7:15). The versions differ in this small way, and the difference is instructive. One tells him that he will be postponed; the other tells him that he has become one of a group of postponed beings, a member of a category rather than the holder of a private exception. Both are accurate to what happened, and neither suggests that he has obtained a privilege. What has been given is what every living creature has: an interval that is not endless and is not the creature's to manage.

**A Grant Is Not an Approval**

Readers who wonder how a request from such a creature could be granted miss the distinction the Book keeps throughout: permission is not endorsement, and delay is not forgiveness. Sūrah al-Qalam states the principle in the context of the deniers who mistake their prosperity for a verdict: *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend.”* (68:44). The Qur'an names this drawing-on *istidrāj*, the leading of a person step by step while he believes he is being favoured. What Iblīs received is the greatest instance of it in the Book: an extension of existence for the whole duration of human history, granted to a creature who had just been sentenced, and granted in answer to his own request. He obtained a longer life, not a different standing.

**The Same Answer in Two Other Tellings**

Al-Aʿrāf and Ṣād both preserve this part of the exchange, and reading the three texts together shows how completely the Qur'an controls the material. In al-Aʿrāf the plea is put in the form of a request to be postponed to the day of resurrection, and the answer follows immediately. In Ṣād the request and answer are given in words nearly identical to those in this sūrah. The Book's habit of narrating the same event several times, each telling choosing the details its own audience needs, is one of the features that distinguishes its method of instruction: no account is offered as a complete archive, and none contradicts the others. What the reader receives across the three is a single event seen from three angles, and the angle here has to do with the fate of people who are given time.

**The Interval That the Whole Human Story Occupies**

The verses immediately before this one fixed the curse at the day of judgment. The verse before the curse fixed the entire span of human testing inside that same period. Now the interval itself becomes an arrangement with a purpose: an enemy who is present, informed and driven, and a human being who is free to choose. Sūrah al-Mulk describes the purpose of creation in a line that gives the interval its meaning: God created death and life to test which of his creatures would do best. A world without a tempter would be a world in which obedience cost nothing, and the Book presents the granting of this request as part of the design of a world in which conduct counts. The creature's victory in obtaining time is the beginning of his own exposure.

**Mercy Hidden in an Answer to an Enemy**

There is one further observation to make about the shape of this grant. Human beings were granted the same thing and more: time to live, time to change their minds, and the possibility of returning to their Lord after they have gone wrong. The creature sentenced in this verse asked for time and received it without any possibility of pardon in his case, because he never asked for pardon. The Book sets the two situations side by side and leaves the reader to see which position he occupies. What was given to Iblīs by request is given to human beings by default, and the sūrah's use of the vocabulary of respite — for the disbelievers who will not be delayed, for this creature who will — keeps the two mercies in view at once.

**The Same Verb, Two Opposite Outcomes**

The word used in this verse for being delayed comes from the same root that appears earlier in the sūrah, where the men who demanded a sign from the sky were told that when the angels come *“the disbelievers will not be delayed”* (15:8). One verse announces the end of postponement for a mocking town; this one announces its grant to a rebellious spirit. The Book uses one vocabulary for a single reality: time is granted and time is withdrawn, and the difference lies entirely with the decree of the One who sets the terms. There is no contradiction here to resolve, and the exegetes treat the two verses as parts of one doctrine. What the reader of the sūrah receives from the pairing is a sense of the scale on which delay operates: an enemy receiving a long extension, and a powerful community whose extension could end before the next harvest.
verses.38:
> until the appointed Day.”

**A Day That Is Known and Withheld**

The grant is bounded by a day the Qur'an calls appointed, and the Arabic phrase is literally the day of the known time: a moment whose occurrence is certain and whose date is fixed in a register, though it has not been disclosed to the creature who must live until it arrives. The distinction between certainty and disclosure is the whole content of the phrase. Iblīs knows the day exists and knows he must wait for it, and the Book never says he was told when it would be. The same combination — fixed beyond change, hidden from creatures — appears in the opening verses of this sūrah, where every community is said to have its term and no one can hurry or postpone it. The delay granted to this creature is not an exception to that rule. It is an instance of it.

**Which Day Is Meant**

The commentators offer two main readings of the phrase. One takes it as the day of resurrection, which is what the creature himself asked for in the previous verse, and which the Qur'an names in several places as the day when the dead are raised for the accounting. The other takes it as the end of the world as human beings know it, the first blast at which all that lives dies and the order of the present creation ends. Al-Ṭabarī reports both positions with their chains, and the second has the advantage of explaining the word *time* as a moment of transition rather than a duration. The first reading has the advantage of matching the request that was made. Whichever is intended, the two moments are adjacent in the Qur'an's timeline, and the Book's stress is always on the certainty of the appointment rather than on the identification of the hour.

**The Hidden Hour and Human Responsibility**

The Book makes a doctrine of the fact that the last hour is not announced, and it gives the reason: *“The Hour is sure to come. My Will is to keep it hidden, so that every soul may be rewarded according to their efforts.”* (20:15). A date that could be counted down would turn conduct into scheduling; a world with no date at all would have no accountability. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf asks its readers whether they have reflected on the signs of the heavens and the earth and on the possibility that their end is near (7:185), and the question only has force because the hour cannot be calculated. The creature in this scene is inside the same arrangement as every human being. He has been given a term that he knows is coming and cannot determine, which is precisely the condition the Book describes for all accountable creatures.

**Al-Aʿrāf and Ṣād on the Same Appointment**

The other two tellings of this exchange preserve the phrase and the surrounding material. Al-Aʿrāf records the plea for postponement and the answer that follows, then the creature's declaration of his intentions regarding human beings (7:14-17). Ṣād gives the request, the grant, and the reference to the appointed day, then moves to the same declaration and to God's statement about those who will be beyond his reach (38:79-83). Set beside this sūrah, the three accounts agree on every element that matters: a request, a grant, a limit, and a campaign. The Qur'an's repetition of the story across different sūrahs functions as corroboration rather than redundancy, and a reader who follows the same event through all three is in a position to see which details each passage chose to highlight.

**What the Limit Does to the Campaign**

Everything the creature is about to announce must be accomplished within the term set here. He will work through history, mislead generations, dress wrongdoing as attractive, and attempt to draw the children of Adam away from their Lord, and all of it happens inside a period whose end is already recorded. The Book's confidence in describing the enemy is built on this. When the sūrah later tells a believer to seek refuge from temptation, the refuge is offered against an adversary whose reach is known, whose methods are recorded, and whose sentence is dated. Sūrah al-Naḥl summarises the limitation in one sentence: *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.”* (16:99). The appointed day in this verse is the outer boundary of everything he has been permitted to do.

**The Interval as a Gift to Human Beings**

The delay granted in the previous verse and bounded in this one is given to an enemy, and yet the Book consistently treats the same interval as a service to the people he works against. It is the time in which a person can hear a warning, change a course, repair an injury, and return to his Lord; the Qur'an's endless appeals to reconsider depend on its existence. Sūrah al-Nūr states the response that settles the matter for a believer who is called to judgment: *“We hear and obey.”* (24:51). Between the sentence passed on the first refuser and the day appointed for its conclusion, the whole of human history is laid out as an opportunity, and the sūrah's reader is standing inside it. What the creature received as a working permit turns out to be the space in which everyone else is invited to choose.

**A Term With No Exceptions and No Extensions**

The verse closes a small unit of the sūrah that has been building from its opening lines: no community perishes before its term, nothing can move that term forward or back, and now the same rule is applied to the oldest enemy in the story. The Book consistently denies that any creature holds its own clock. This is not a counsel of passivity, since the same Book commands its readers to work, to seek provision and to prepare. It is a statement about where the boundary lies between what a creature can control and what it cannot. A delay was granted by request and limited by decree, and the two facts together describe the situation in which every human being, tempter and tempted alike, has always lived.
verses.39:
> Satan responded, “My Lord! For allowing me to stray I will surely tempt them on earth and mislead them all together

**An Accusation Dressed as a Preposition**

The Arabic phrase rendered *for allowing me to stray* is built on the preposition *bāʾ* followed by the act attributed to God, and its effect is causal: because you led me astray, I will do this. The creature who argued about his own rank and refused an order now assigns the responsibility for his own ruin to God. The Book places the two responses to divine questioning side by side, and the contrast could not be sharper. When Adam and his wife were asked about their mistake, they said *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves.”* (7:23). Iblīs says, in effect, that he has been wronged. He does not deny the act; he transfers its authorship, and with it the blame, to the only party who cannot be blamed.

**The Doctrine the Sentence Touches**

The sentence touches a real question that the Qur'an treats in several places: how are statements about God's guidance and misguidance to be understood? The Book does say that God leaves some people to stray and guides others, as in the verse about the parables that *“He leaves many to stray, and guides many”* (2:26, substance), and in the account of the condemned who admit that they never really invoked anything at all, which the Qur'an concludes by saying, *“This is how Allah leaves the disbelievers to stray.”* (40:74). The Book also explains the order of events in the case of a person who goes wrong: *“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate”* (61:5), and it shows the same pattern in Iblīs himself, whose pride came first and whose expulsion followed. The creature's preposition skips the part of the story in which he chose.

**"I Will Adorn and I Will Mislead"**

The verb behind *tempt* is the one the Qur'an uses for making something appear fair and desirable, and the Book applies it to this creature's method everywhere: he beautifies wrongdoing so that the person committing it sees it as reasonable, perhaps even as virtue. Sūrah al-Naḥl warns people not to let him dress things up as he did with those who came before, and the sūrah of the Cattle describes how the deeds of some are made to look good to them by his activity. The method tells the reader something about the enemy's estimation of human beings: he does not rely on force, because force would not work, and he does not rely on convincing arguments, because the arguments for the truth are stronger. He relies on presentation, on appetite, and on the slow adjustment of what a person is willing to call acceptable.

**The Arena Is the Earth**

His vow specifies the earth as the place where the campaign will be conducted, and the Book has already established why. It is the place human beings were sent after their mistake, *“You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”* (2:36). Their time there is short, provisional, and full of the pressures that make choice real: livelihood to be earned, families to be raised, rivals to be placated, illness and death to be absorbed. The creature who was expelled from the garden is not permitted to reach into that arrangement directly; he works from within it, using the ordinary substance of a life as his material. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf describes him lying in wait on the straight path, approaching from front, back, right and left (7:17), which is the language of a roadside ambush rather than a siege.

**The Scope of the Claim**

The declaration ends with the word the translation renders *all together*, and the ambition is total: not a faction, not a family, not a generation, but everyone. He knows the exception exists; the next verse records his own acknowledgement of it. What the wording expresses is not a prediction but an intention, an open war on the entire species rather than a quarrel with the individual who was preferred over him. Volume itself is part of his method, since a world in which the majority are on one road makes the other road look eccentric and a person judges by what he sees around him. Sūrah Sabaʾ treats the ambition as a realised fact and reports the exceptions with care: *“they ˹all˺ follow him, except a group of ˹true˺ believers.”* (34:20).

**Grievance Turned Into a Programme**

Nothing in the vow aims at the One who expelled him, since no such attack is possible, and the failure of the target explains the shape of the plan. He will strike at what God has honoured instead. The Book treats this as the defining feature of his conduct and uses it to explain the hostility that the righteous and the messengers meet from human societies: the whisperer is at work behind the mockery in the market, the jeering at the man who prays, the pressure that turns a family against its convert. The Book's method of dealing with this campaign is not to deny its reality, since the enemy has just announced it in his own words, but to describe it accurately and to name the place of safety. That description is the subject of the verse that follows.

**The Excuse That Became a Standard Argument**

The Book records the same move being made by human beings, and it treats it as a self-contradiction rather than a defence: *“Had it been Allah's Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful.”* (6:148). Sūrah al-Naḥl reports the identical argument from earlier communities and answers it with a single line about the messengers' duty: to deliver the message clearly (16:35).
