Sūrah al-Zukhruf gives the verdict on the reasoning itself: *“They have no knowledge ˹in support˺ of this ˹claim˺. They do nothing but lie.”* (43:20). What the creature says in this verse, then, is the original of a formula that has been reused by every generation that wanted to keep its conduct and blame its maker. The sūrah records it first, in the mouth of the enemy, so that a reader can recognise the sentence when it is spoken by someone he knows.
verses.40:
> except Your chosen servants among them.”

**The Exception Voluntarily Acknowledged**

The creature's own vow contains its limit. He has just claimed the whole of humanity as his field, and in the same breath he carves out a group he cannot reach: your chosen servants. Nothing forced the admission; he was not being cross-examined and no correction had been made to his statement. The exception is his own assessment of where his influence stops, and it therefore carries an authority other statements about him do not. The Book records the same limitation in other places, sometimes in God's words: *“˹Allah added,˺ ‘You will truly have no authority over My ˹faithful˺ servants.’”* (17:65), and sometimes as an outcome: the assumption he made about people came true for most of them, with a group of true believers excluded (34:20). What the enemy states here is later confirmed from above.

**The Two Readings Behind "Chosen"**

The Arabic word *al-mukhlaṣīn* has been recited and explained in two ways, and the difference is meaningful. One reading gives *al-mukhliṣīn*, those who are sincere, describing people whose devotion to God has been purified of mixed motives. The other gives *al-mukhlaṣīn*, those whom God has specially chosen and selected for Himself, making the protection an act of God rather than a quality the person achieves. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭūbī report both and their arguments; the reading with the divine choosing fits the plain contrast in the verse, because it explains why this group is out of the enemy's reach. The two senses belong together in the Qur'an's teaching: the people God selects are the people who dedicate themselves to Him, and the Book never describes one without implying the other.

**What Makes a Person Out of Reach**

Since the enemy states a limit, a reader naturally asks what puts anyone on the safe side of it, and the Book answers not with a list of achievements but with a description of the person's inner orientation. Sūrah al-Naḥl makes the criterion trust: *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.”* (16:99). The Book never suggests that those who trust are the ones who are never approached; it suggests that when they are approached, the approach fails. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf gives a practical rule for the moment of contact: *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”* (7:200), and al-Naḥl places the same instruction around recitation of the Qur'an. The protection in this verse is therefore a relationship, actively maintained, rather than a status a person holds without effort.

**The Chosen Among a Hostile Majority**

The sūrah's ear has already been tuned to numbers. Its opening verses described the prosperous deniers eating and enjoying themselves while their end approached, and the entire scene being narrated here involves an assembly in which all obeyed except one. The exception in this verse works the same way. The Book expects its reader to understand that the saved group may be the smaller party, and it prepares him for that expectation in several places, including the account of the foremost in faith and the reminder that only a group remained loyal. Sūrah al-Qalam also records the accusation the deniers made against the Prophet, that he was a madman, which is the social price of being outnumbered. A reader who measures his conduct by the behaviour around him has already accepted the enemy's most effective method.

**God's Choice Is Stated Plainly Elsewhere**

The Qur'an has no difficulty in describing God as the one who selects among people, and it says so in connection with guidance, messengership and mercy. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states it in the same chapter where guidance and misguidance are discussed: *“Nor would Allah ˹directly˺ reveal to you the unseen, but He chooses whoever He wills as a messenger.”* (3:179). Sūrah al-Shūrā describes God choosing for Himself whoever He wills among those who turn toward Him (42:13). The exception that the enemy is forced to admit is thus not a title the righteous invented for themselves; it is an arrangement the Book names from beginning to end. The creature who thought he could measure creatures by their material has learned that the designation belongs to the one who created them, and he is left to work around people he cannot move.

**The Shape of the Story's Future**

By the end of this verse, the whole of the drama that follows in human history has been laid out: an enemy with a term, a sentence, and a declared intention; a people he claims, and a group he concedes he cannot reach. The sūrah will continue with the angels who visited Abraham, the destruction of the people of Lot, the fate of the dwellers of the Stone Valley, and it will close with a command to the Prophet about how to live among the mockers. Everything afterward in the chapter is an application of this little exception. The reader is being invited to see himself in one of the two groups, and the Book's manner of offering the choice is characteristically restrained: no description of the chosen, no instructions yet, just the words of the enemy, admitting that his reach has a boundary he cannot cross.

**Servanthood as the Mark of Safety**

The group that is beyond his reach is named in this verse as servants, and the title is the whole criterion. It is the same word the Qur'an uses as a badge of honour for the highest creatures: the angels are described as honoured servants who do not speak until God has spoken (21:26-27), and elsewhere as *“servants of the Most Compassionate”* (43:19). The creature who refused to bow did so because he judged service beneath him; the ones he cannot touch are precisely those who accept it as their identity. In the Book's vocabulary, then, the word that the proud consider a humiliation is the word that marks the protected. Sūrah al-Zumar describes the same safety from the other side, telling those who avoided the worship of false gods and turned to God that they have good news in store (39:17). The verse under commentary gives the enemy's own testimony to the same fact.
verses.41:
> Allah said, “This is the Way, binding on Me

**The Answer to a Vow**

The creature had just announced what he would do to human beings. The reply is not a warning and not a correction of his plan; it is a statement about a road. The Arabic phrase is built around a preposition that literally means upon: this is a path upon Me, straight. The construction is unusual and the exegetes pause over it, because a path is not normally said to rest on anyone. The sense they give is that God has taken the guidance and the protection of this road upon Himself as an undertaking. The verse therefore answers a threat of misguidance with a guarantee, and the guarantee is stated in the first person by the One who owns the destination. What the enemy intended to do is now a matter between him and a road its maker has pledged to keep open.

**A Commitment God Takes Upon Himself**

The Qur'an uses the language of God binding Himself in a small number of places, and each one is a statement about mercy rather than obligation. Sūrah al-Anʿām says of Him: *“He has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together for the Day of Judgment— about which there is no doubt.”* (6:12, ending). The Book also describes His promise in the same way when it tells the believers that God has undertaken to grant them a reward. Nothing in this vocabulary suggests that a creature has imposed a duty on the Creator; the point is that God has announced His own commitment and that His announcement cannot fail. Understood this way, the phrase in this verse is one of the most reassuring sentences in the sūrah: the enemy's campaign is answered by a pledge made before the campaign began.

**The Straight Path in the Book's Language**

The noun is *ṣirāṭ*, and it appears in the Qur'an over and over as the road that leads to God. The opening sūrah of the Book asks for it: *“Guide us along the Straight Path, the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray.”* (1:6-7). Sūrah al-Anʿām describes it as a single road with other ways branching off it: *“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”* (6:153). Sūrahs Maryam, Yā Sīn, and al-Zukhruf all summarise the path in the same words, that God alone is Lord and should be worshipped (19:36; 36:61; 43:64). The road in this verse is therefore not an abstract moral order but the known way of the prophets, and its markers were visible to every audience that heard the sūrah.

**Who Walks It**

The Book never describes the path as a lane that carries people along; walking it is an ongoing act of a person's will. Sūrah al-Insān states the arrangement in a single line: *“We already showed them the Way, whether they ˹choose to˺ be grateful or ungrateful.”* (76:3), and Sūrah al-Muzzammil adds, *“So let whoever wills take the ˹Right˺ Way to their Lord.”* (73:19). Sūrah al-Kahf gives the same choice in the strongest terms: *“˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord. Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve.”* (18:29). The straight path is guaranteed, but it is not enforced, which is what makes the enemy's activity possible in the first place. He was permitted to call people from the roadside; he was not permitted to block the road, and the verse under commentary is the charter that says so.

**The Ambush Language of Sūrah al-Aʿrāf**

Sūrah al-Aʿrāf records the same creature describing his strategy as an ambush: he will lie in wait on the straight path and come at people from front, back, right and left (7:17). That image fits what this verse establishes. An ambush presupposes a road people are travelling, and the ambusher's whole business depends on traffic he cannot stop from passing. The Book also warns human beings against adopting the same technique in their own dealings, telling one community not to sit on every road, threatening and turning away those who believe, and not to try to make the way appear crooked (7:86). Taken together, the passages describe the road as contested but never closed. The One who laid it has undertaken that the route remains open, which leaves the traveller, not the adversary, holding the decision.

**What the Exegetes Draw From the Sentence**

Al-Rāzī reads the verse as a statement about the path of obedience and servitude by which a person escapes the enemy's suggestions, and he notes that what is guaranteed is the road, not the traveller's preference. Other commentators stress the grammatical weight of the pronoun: because the path is said to be upon God, its straightness is not a quality that can be argued away by those who travel it, and its destination is not in doubt. The practical consequence drawn by the sūrah's readers over the centuries is that a person is never required to find a road that does not exist; the invitation is to walk a way that has been maintained and to trust the one who maintains it. The enemy's announcement in the previous verses was answered before he made it, and this sentence is the answer.

**The Road as a Reply to Fear**

There is a reason this declaration sits exactly where it does. The verses that follow will describe human beings being led away in groups, other human beings entering gardens in peace, and the difference between the two companies. Before any of that, the sūrah places the sentence in which God speaks of a path as His own charge, and the effect on a reader is to move the question from the enemy's strength to his own direction. The adversary in this story has knowledge, experience and a fixed term, and the Book grants him all of it. What it does not grant him is the road. That belongs to the One who made it, who has announced in advance that it is straight, and who has bound its upkeep on Himself in a sentence that no creature has ever been able to amend.
verses.42:
> you will certainly have no authority over My servants, except the deviant who follow you

**The Word for Authority**

The Arabic term translated *authority* is *sulṭān*, and it covers power, a claim, and a warrant. Its use here is exact: the creature is denied all three. He is not given power over the servants of God, he is not granted a claim on them, and no warrant exists for what he attempts among them. Sūrah al-Isrāʾ records the statement in the very same form and attaches to it a promise of protection: *“˹Allah added,˺ ‘You will truly have no authority over My ˹faithful˺ servants.’ And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian.”* (17:65). Al-Naḥl explains what the denial means for the person on the receiving end: *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.”* (16:99). The sentence is not a description of the enemy's weakness in general — he is given room, longevity and method — but of the boundary of his reach over God's own people.

**Whom the Authority Reaches**

The same passage in al-Naḥl continues by naming the group he does control: *“His authority is only over those who take him as a patron and who—under his influence—associate ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺.”* (16:100). The relation described there is patronage chosen by the human being, which is the exact point this verse makes when it says the followers are *deviant* rather than seized. The Book never presents the followers as innocent captives. Sūrah Sabaʾ reports the outcome of the enemy's expectation in the same terms, that most followed him except a group of true believers (34:20), and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ frames the contest as two alignments, believers fighting for the cause of God and disbelievers fighting for the cause of the devil, before adding that the devil's schemes are ever weak (4:76). His authority is real, and it operates through consent.

**"My Servants": the Possessive as Protection**

The words *My servants* carry the weight of the sentence. The Arabic adds the possessive pronoun to the noun, which in this Book is a mark of honour: the angels are God's honoured servants (21:26), the Prophet is addressed as His servant in the opening of Sūrah al-Isrāʾ, and the whole human race is described as servants whose provision is guaranteed. A creature who is owned, sustained and named by God is not available to a rival as property. Sūrah al-Zumar tells the servants of God directly not to despair of His mercy, and the same possessiveness runs through the Qur'an's addresses to humanity. The protection granted in this verse is therefore not an unusual privilege reserved for an elite. It is what it means to be a servant of the One who has refused to hand over His own.

**Who Are the Deviant Who Follow?**

The Arabic word rendered *deviant* describes someone who has gone out of the way and stays there, and the phrase *who follow you* makes the relationship mutual rather than imposed. He offers; they come. Sūrah al-Anʿām describes the same configuration as a giving over: *“Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Way.”* (6:39, ending). Sūrah al-Aʿrāf describes the ones who take devils as masters instead of God, thinking they are rightly guided (7:30). In every case the Book places the choice on the human side and the invitation on the enemy's side, which is what makes the distinction in this verse so pointed. Authority over the willing is conceded to him; authority over anyone else is denied.

**The Party and Its Loss**

The Book uses a phrase for the people who follow him, and it never presents the group as a threat. Sūrah al-Mujādilah states it flatly: *“They are the party of Satan. Surely Satan's party is bound to lose.”* (58:19). The declaration is not a prediction about a battle but about a final accounting, and it is made in the same Book that reports the enemy's own confident vow of total deception. The contrast between what he expected to achieve and what his party actually obtains is drawn by the sūrah itself in the verses that follow this one, where the followers are assembled at a place of meeting. The reader is being told, in advance of the outcome, which side of the ledger holds the advantage.

**The Empty Promises**

The last element of the enemy's equipment is the one the Book names most often: what he offers does not exist. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ states it plainly — *“Satan only makes them ˹false˺ promises and deludes them with ˹empty˺ hopes. Truly Satan promises them nothing but delusion.”* (4:120), and Sūrah Ibrāhīm reports his own speech of admission at the end, when he tells his followers that he had no power over them and that what he promised was nothing but illusion (14:22, substance). The verse under commentary thus completes a picture the Book draws in three strokes: he has no authority, he has no property rights over anyone, and what he trades in is a currency that does not exist. What remains is the choice of the person who follows, and to that the Book addresses itself for the rest of the sūrah.

**What the Sentence Gives a Believer**

The immediate practical effect of this verse is relief, and its effect over a lifetime is a discipline. A Muslim reciting it is told that the enemy's most frightening claim about himself has been overruled from above: he cannot take anyone. The Book correspondingly never asks a believer to defeat the devil by force, only to refuse his invitation and seek refuge with God. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf gives the instruction for the moment of pressure — *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”* (7:200) — and Sūrah Fuṣṣilat repeats the same counsel with the promise that God will be sufficient. The boundary drawn in this verse is where prayer takes effect, and the Book's readers have used it that way from the beginning.
verses.43:
> and surely Hell is their destined place, all together

**The Appointed Meeting**

The Arabic word rendered *destined place* is a noun of appointment, the same kind of word a person would use for a fixed engagement with a time and a location. The creature who asked for a delay, obtained one, and pledged to mislead all of humanity now has an appointment entered on his own account. The Book uses this vocabulary for the final gathering throughout: Sūrah al-Qamar says of the mockers, *“Better yet, the Hour is their appointed time—and the Hour will be most catastrophic and most bitter.”* (54:46). There is a grim fitness in the arrangement. He was the one who wanted time extended; what the sentence confirms is that a date has been set for him and for everyone who joined him, and neither the date nor the destination is negotiable.

**A Destination Shared by the Tempter and the Followed**

The verse groups them. The pronoun covers the enemy and those who took his path, and the Book is explicit about that grouping in the parallel passages. Al-Aʿrāf records the sentence in the scene of expulsion: *“I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”* (7:18), and Sūrah Ṣād repeats the same words (38:85). Sūrah al-Mujādilah calls the followers the party of Satan and states the outcome of that party in a sentence built on loss (58:19). The shared destination is the Book's way of saying that a leader and his followers are judged in the same ledger when the leadership is in wrongdoing. The one who planned the misguidance and the ones who chose it have arrived at the same appointment from opposite ends of the same road.

**What the Company of the Followers Means**

The Book never suggests that followers in this sense are passive. It describes the relationship as a choice made with knowledge, and it records, on the day of accounting, the recriminations that break out between the two parties. The followers will blame those who led them, and the leaders will disown the blame. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf reports the followers asking for a double punishment for those who led them astray, and Sūrah al-Baqarah records the misled followers saying that if they had a second chance they would disown their leaders as they were disowned (2:167). That future argument is exactly what the present verse forecloses. There is no distinction available at the appointment; the destination is one, and the party arrives together.

**Justice in a Shared Sentence**

A reader may ask how one destination can be just for a rebellious spirit and for human beings whose circumstances differed across centuries. The Book's answer is that the sentence is not identical for each person within the destination, and its own texts say so: the next verse describes gates and a portion assigned to each group, and other passages describe degrees of punishment. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf states the principle at the scale of individuals: whoever brings a good deed will be rewarded tenfold, and whoever brings a bad deed will be punished only for one (6:160, first half), while Sūrah al-Zalzalah says that every atom's weight of good and of evil will be seen. The shared place in this verse is therefore not a flattening of responsibility but the common end of a shared road.

**The Vow Returned Upon Its Author**

Everything the creature said in the previous verses is now answered in the currency he chose. He promised to mislead all together; the sentence places him with all those he misled. He asked for time; he received a term. He claimed a rank by his material; the destination is assigned by conduct. The Book's style here is not rhetorical flourishes but precise return, and the pattern appears wherever it deals with the arrogant. Sūrah al-Naḥl states it as a rule when it warns people not to let the enemy dress up wrongdoing as he did with those before them, and the narrative of the sūrahs shows the rule applied to the proud of every generation. The verse is the beginning of the account of what his campaign actually won him.

**Who Was Listening When It Was Recited**

The first audience of this sūrah was composed of the men whose mockery is recorded in its opening verses, and they were being told that the destination of unbelief has been set since before human history began. The Book does not narrow the category to the ancient nations; it speaks to the people who were mocking a living prophet. Sūrah al-Zumar warns the same audience directly, addressing the servants of God who had gone to excess against their own souls and telling them not to despair of mercy (39:53), and the sūrah's readers receive both sentences in the same Book: an appointed place for those who follow, and an open door for anyone who turns back before the appointment arrives.

**A Place That Is Not Described Here**

The verse names the destination and stops. No fire, no torment, no duration is described, and the restraint is characteristic of the way this sūrah handles the subject. The details come elsewhere in the Book, and the sūrah will add one detail of its own in the next verse concerning the gates. What this verse supplies is the fact of a meeting that nobody escapes: an enemy with an appointment, a party with an appointment, and a date that the One who made every term in the sūrah's earlier verses has already entered on the register. The vocabulary of appointment, which the sūrah has used for towns, generations and souls, now applies to the last destination any creature will reach, and the sentence is written the way the others were: certain, dated, and unalterable.
verses.44:
> It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated.”

**Seven Gates and What the Commentators Understood by Them**

The classical exegetes generally read the seven gates as the levels of the fire, each one a separate station with its own degree of severity. Al-Baghawī, al-Zamakhsharī and al-Kalabī are among those who take the number this way, and the reading fits the second half of the verse, which assigns a separate portion of the company to every gate. Other explanations were also offered: that the gates are the kinds of entry by which people arrive at their punishment, corresponding to the classes of their deeds; or that the number signifies completeness and multiplicity rather than a count to be pressed. What the verse does not do is invite speculation about the shape of the architecture. The detail is given in a scene whose purpose is to establish that nothing about the end is improvised, and the assignment of a place to every group is the part of the sentence that carries the weight.

**A Portion Designated for Each Gate**

The second clause says that each gate has its allotted share of the company, and the Arabic verb suggests something written down and apportioned. The followers of the enemy are not poured into one undifferentiated mass; they arrive in groups, and each group is directed to its own entrance. The sūrah has already used this vocabulary of appointment and measure in its earlier verses, where every community has a written term and provision comes down in precise quantity. The same careful administration governs the last destination. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf supplies the corresponding principle for individuals when it says that a good deed is rewarded tenfold while a bad deed brings only its equivalent, and that no one will be wronged (6:160, second half). The gates in this verse are where that principle becomes visible.

**Gates as Openings and as Barriers**

The Book uses gates for both mercy and severity, and the two uses illuminate each other. The arrogant are refused entry at the gates of heaven: *“the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.”* (7:40). The righteous arrive at gates already open, and the keepers greet them with peace and the command to enter and remain (39:73), while Sūrah Ṣād describes the gardens of eternity with their gates standing open for their people (38:50). At the end of the world, the sky itself becomes gates as it splits (78:19). A gate in this vocabulary is a boundary with an authority behind it. Whoever enters does so by permission, and the number of openings in this verse tells the condemned that their arrival, too, has been arranged rather than merely permitted.

**The Grading of Punishment**

The verse presupposes that wrongdoers will not all be treated identically, and the Book states the principle in several places. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ says that the hypocrites will occupy the lowest depth of the fire, and it distinguishes between those who wronged themselves and those who did good in the same passage. Sūrah al-Aḥzāb places different groups at different stations of recompense. Sūrah al-Anʿām already quoted establishes that the penalty is measured to the deed rather than exceeded by it. What is described in this verse is therefore not an arbitrary sorting but a distribution by the record, and the record is kept by the One who knows every intention. A reader who grasps that the exits are graded will not be able to comfort himself with the thought that being wrong is a single condition with a single price.

**Faith in What No Eye Has Seen**

Everything described in this verse lies beyond human observation, and the Book presents such reports as a matter of belief rather than of verification. Sūrah al-Sajdah states the counterpart for the righteous in a verse that makes the same point from the other direction: *“No soul can imagine what delights are kept in store for them as a reward for what they used to do.”* (32:17). The Qur'an gives the unseen world in the detail that conduct requires and withholds the detail that curiosity wants. Muslims have read these verses for their warning and their encouragement, and the tradition has consistently discouraged attempts to map the other world as though it were a place one could survey. The seven gates are named because the people who are assigned to them need to know that their destination is prepared.

**A Register That Assigns Every Place**

The second half of the verse speaks of groups designated to their gate, and the vocabulary of designation belongs to the Book's wider account of a record in which nothing living is left unaccounted for. Sūrah Hūd states the principle at the scale of the smallest creatures: *“There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah. And He knows where it lives and where it is laid to rest. All is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.”* (11:6). The register that notes where a creature lives and where it is buried is the same register that decides where a person arrives at the end of the road. The assembly of the condemned in this verse is therefore not a crowd pouring through one opening; it is an ordering, and the ordering is the visible form of a record kept for each member of the company. Nothing about the destination is casual, and nothing about the arrival is left to chance.

**Why the Detail Is Given to a Mocking Audience**

The men of Makkah who heard this sūrah recited were living in a city where the visible world seemed entirely in the hands of its powerful families. They had no reason to expect that their conduct would be examined, and the deniers among them treated warnings as material for jokes. The sūrah answers with an architecture of judgment that is as carefully organised as any settlement they knew, with entrances and assigned quarters, and with a company already gathered in every one of them. The verse does not say what the fire is like. It says that the arrangements have been made and that the assignment has been recorded. For an audience that measured the seriousness of a matter by its planning, that is a more effective warning than any description of flames.
verses.45:
> Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and springs

**A Sentence That Turns the Sūrah Around**

After the gates of punishment, the verse declares what awaits the God-fearing, and it does so in a line whose structure mirrors the sentences about the enemy's party. There is a destination, a company and a place described by what grows in it. The Arabic word for the righteous here is the same noun used throughout the Qur'an for those who guard themselves against wrongdoing, and it is the word that opens the second sūrah of the Book: *“This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺.”* (2:2). The term names a practice rather than a status. The gardens and springs are given to people described by what they did with the warning they received, and the sūrah has just shown its audience two roads whose ends are now named in consecutive verses.

**Gardens and Springs as a Pair**

The pairing recurs verbatim elsewhere. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt opens its description of the reward with the same words, then adds what the people of the gardens are doing there: *“Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and springs, ˹joyfully˺ receiving what their Lord will grant them. Before this ˹reward˺ they were truly good-doers ˹in the world˺.”* (51:15-16). The Book's description of the gardens keeps returning to water, and the reason is not difficult to see. Its first audience lived in a landscape where water was the difference between life and death, and where a spring meant a settlement. Sūrah Muḥammad describes rivers of water that never changes, milk that never turns, wine that gives delight, and purified honey, then adds fruit of every kind and forgiveness from their Lord (47:15). The point is abundance without the decay that marks every good thing in this world.

**The World That Made the Image Necessary**

In the Arabian Peninsula, gardens were not scenery; they were engineering. Water had to be lifted, channels maintained, palms protected from the wind, and a single failed spring could empty a valley. The men being addressed knew exactly what a garden represented: sustained effort against a hostile climate, and a future secured for one's family. When the Qur'an describes the reward as gardens with running water beneath them, it is speaking in the most desirable terms available to its listeners, and it is also correcting them. The gardens of this world need labour to survive and will pass to other hands. The gardens promised here are described as a gift granted by the Lord of the person receiving it, an inheritance that does not depend on maintenance.

**What "Amid" Says About the Life of the Garden**

The Arabic places them *in* the gardens and springs, not merely at them or beside them. The construction suggests a condition rather than a location: they are surrounded by the two things that made life good in their own experience, with no wall of danger and nothing to defend. The Book's descriptions of the rewarded state consistently emphasise this quality of being enveloped: in gardens under which rivers flow, in shade that does not shift, in a peace that is not interrupted. Sūrah al-Naḥl summarises the state by saying that they will have whatever they desire in gardens of eternity (16:31). Taken with the previous verses, the sūrah is not promising a holiday; it is describing the removal of everything that made the world a place of strain.

**Who the Righteous Were in Practice**

The Book defines the term by description rather than by label, and the descriptions are concrete. Sūrah al-Baqarah names the people the Book guides: *“who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (2:3), and continues with belief in what was revealed and in the hereafter. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān invites its readers to hasten toward a garden prepared for those mindful of God, and then describes them as people who give in ease and hardship and who restrain their anger. The word rendered *righteous* in the verse under commentary is the quality that runs through all of these: a person who takes the warnings seriously enough to adjust his conduct. What the gardens reward is therefore not an emotional state or a family name but a way of living that the sūrah's own audience had been invited to begin.

**The Return to What Was Lost**

The Book's account of human beginnings ends with an expulsion from a garden, and its account of human destiny ends with an entry into one. The two scenes are deliberately matched: what was lost through disobedience is restored, and the account of the restoration includes one detail that makes the correspondence exact, since the people who enter will never be asked to leave. The verse under commentary names the destination in language that would have reminded every listener of the first home of the species. It does not explain how a person gets from the two roads to the two gates. That explanation has been spread through the sūrah from its first lines, in the vocabulary of guidance, warning, respite and choice.

**The Order of Mercy and Threat**

The sūrah answers the enemy's vow with a statement about the straight path, denies him authority over God's servants, names the destination of his party, and then, before anything else, names the destination of the righteous. The order places hope after warning, and the Book repeats this arrangement as a matter of principle. Sūrah al-Ḥijr itself will devote the next verses to the details of the reward: peace, the removal of old grudges, surroundings that never wear a person out. Readers who stop at the gates of punishment have read only half the passage. The sentence about gardens and springs exists to make sure that the road described in verse 41 is not merely a way of escape from something but a way to somewhere, and the somewhere is described in the terms its first audience found most desirable.
verses.46:
> ˹It will be said to them,˺ “Enter in peace and security.”

**A Sentence Spoken Over Them**

The line is phrased in the passive, and the commentators discussed who says it. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī report that the greeting is spoken by God, while others, including al-Shawkānī, understand the angels as the speakers, since the Book elsewhere describes the keepers of the garden receiving its people at the gates with peace and the invitation to enter and remain (39:73). The ambiguity is not a defect in the verse; it removes the speakers from attention and leaves the words themselves in the foreground. What matters to the listener is that the command to enter comes from outside himself, that it is spoken as a welcome rather than a verdict, and that the person receiving it does nothing to earn the sentence at the moment he hears it. The promise is announced; he is invited across his own threshold.

**"Peace" as the First Word of the New Life**

*Salām* is the greeting of the next world in the Qur'an, and the Book repeats the fact often enough for it to function as a definition of the place. The people of the garden pray with the words glory and praise, exchange a greeting of peace, and close with praise of the Lord of all worlds (10:10). Believers are told that they will be greeted with peace where they dwell (14:23), that their greeting on the day they meet Him will be peace (33:44), and that peace will be their greeting from the Most Merciful (36:58). Even the name of the destination is built on the word: God invites to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to the straight path (10:25). The first thing done to a person entering the garden is to be given the word that names the absence of every harm.

**"Security" as the Second Half of the Blessing**

The Arabic term for the second word describes safety from fear, and the pairing with peace covers the two ways life in this world goes wrong: conflict with others and the dread of loss. Sūrah Sabaʾ records the same double blessing spoken by the people of the garden themselves, that they have been settled in an everlasting home where they are touched by neither fatigue nor weariness (35:35). The Book's earlier narrative supplies the contrast directly, since human beings were told after their mistake that they would find in the earth a residence and provision for an appointed stay, and that they would be enemies to one another (2:36). What the verse under commentary announces is the settled end of that arrangement: no more enmity, no more eviction, and no further sentence pending.

**A Welcome That Reverses the First Sentence**

Everything in this short line is the mirror image of the expulsion that opens the human story. There a command was given to leave, and the creature receiving it was called cursed; here a command is given to enter, and the people receiving it are wished peace. The words used in the two scenes are opposite in a way that cannot be accidental, and the sūrah's structure makes the comparison available, since it has just narrated the expulsion of the enemy and is now describing the entry of the righteous. The garden in the Book is not merely the place where good people go. It is the original dwelling of the species, the place from which the first human beings were sent into a testing world, and the arrival described in this verse is the completion of a return that the whole revelation has been arranging.

**The Greeting Believers Practice Now**

The same word has been carried by Muslims into their daily dealings, and the Book treats the practice as an extension of the heavenly greeting rather than a mere courtesy. Sūrah al-Nūr, in a long passage about households and social obligations, instructs believers to greet one another with a blessed and goodly greeting, and the Qur'an's own summary of a Muslim community includes the mutual greeting as one of its habits. Children are taught the phrase before they understand the doctrine. When the Book says that peace is the word spoken over the people entering the garden, it is describing the completion of something practiced in fragments in this world, and the men of Makkah who heard it early were being told that the courtesy they already knew between the believers was a rehearsal for the words that would open their final home.

**What the Greeting Assumes About the Person**

The people being addressed have just come from the two roads described earlier in the sūrah, and their arrival is not described as an achievement at the door. What the Book has said about them is that they were mindful of God, and that their conduct followed from that mindfulness. The greeting itself says nothing about performance. It welcomes them and gives them peace, and the sentence is spoken by someone else entirely. This is the pattern the Book keeps for the reward: it is described as a grant, a gift, a mercy, and an inheritance, in language that leaves no room for the idea that a person purchases his way inside. What a person brings to the door is a life directed toward his Lord; what he receives there is spoken over him by another.

**The Voice That Will Be Heard**

The sūrah has been filled with speech: the mockers mocking, the enemy arguing, God answering, the Prophet being addressed. The last word of this verse belongs to the same economy of speech, and it is spoken in a register the sūrah has not used before. Nothing is being denied, corrected or judged. The voice simply welcomes and reassures, and then the next verses describe an assembly in which the guests recline, face one another, and have every trace of old bitterness removed. For an audience that measured its days by arguments, the promise of a place where the only address a person hears at the threshold is a greeting of peace is a complete description of rest.
verses.47:
> We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. In a friendly manner, they will be on thrones, facing one another

**The Removal Is Done to Them, Not by Them**

The sentence is spoken in the first person plural: we will remove. The people being described do not clean their own hearts of the resentment they carried; the removal is performed for them, and this points to something the Book assumes about bitterness, which is that it does not usually yield to a person's own determination. What is being described is not the forgiveness of a wrong, since the wrongs in question occurred among believers themselves, during a life in which loyalties shifted, families divided and quarrels were left unresolved. The verse states that the last trace of all of it will be taken away before the group settles into its home. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf records the same act in the same words when it describes the people of the garden and adds a detail: rivers flow beneath them as the removal happens.

**Bitterness and What Produces It**

The Arabic term covers rancour, the sour residue of an injury that has not healed, and the Book treats it as a serious fault rather than a reaction. It recommends no such thing as a good grievance. In the sūrah of deeds and their consequences, the prayer taught to the believers includes a plea that bitterness not be allowed into their hearts toward those who believe: *“Our Lord! Forgive us and our fellow believers who preceded us in faith, and do not allow bitterness into our hearts towards those who believe.”* (59:10), and the Qur'an names the envier's envy as one of the things a person must seek protection from (113:5). When the verse under commentary describes the removal of bitterness, it is describing the cure of a disease that the Book spends considerable effort preventing in this world.

**The Worldly Quarrels That Are Being Healed**

The Book does not pretend that its community was composed of people who had always agreed. Its own narratives record disputes over the leadership of the community, quarrels about distribution, accusations, defections and settlements that ended badly. The people promised these gardens were exactly those believers, with the grudges their circumstances had produced. The verse's wording therefore does not reward a community that had never suffered friction; it describes the removal of the friction itself. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf supplies the response that accompanies the healing, when the people of the garden praise the One who guided them, add that they would never have found the way except by His guidance, and confirm that the messengers had brought the truth. Gratitude replaces grievance, and the change is credited to God.

**Brothers and Companions Facing One Another**

The Arabic word rendered *in a friendly manner* has the sense of brothers or close companions, and the point is the reciprocal orientation: they sit facing one another, which in the culture of the Book's audience was the posture of presence, attention and settled company. A person who is sulking does not face his neighbour. The seating therefore dramatises the removal described in the first clause. The couch of the scene is mentioned in several passages, and the Book returns to the detail that the people of the garden are arrayed upon them, reclining, face to face. The image is of a gathering in which nothing needs to be concealed and no one has turned away. Al-Rāzī reads it as a description of souls purified and able to receive light from one another without the friction of bodily impulse.

**No Hierarchy in the Seating**

The Book's descriptions of the garden do not mention ranks, and this verse's arrangement is flat and reciprocal. Each of the people seated faces an equal; there is no arrangement of those who are served and those who serve, no host and no guests with unequal standing. The sūrah has just described the party of the enemy as a group allotted to gates, sorted and portioned, and the contrast is deliberate. What the Book offers its people is a gathering of equals whose differences were settled by the guidance they all accepted. Readers from societies organised around precedence and patronage could not have missed the strangeness of the picture, and the Book repeats it in passages about believers being brothers and the honour of a person being measured by his conduct alone.

**The Companion You Fought With**

The most affecting aspect of this promise is what it demands of the reader in this world. The people who will face one another as companions are the ones whose conflicts were real. The generation that received the sūrah first knew former enemies who had become brothers in the same community, families split by the message and later reconciled, and men whose disagreements about leadership would eventually produce grief. The Book tells them that the bitterness left over from all of that will be removed, not celebrated or relived. The instruction that goes with the promise is given elsewhere and takes the form of a command to forgive and to repair, since a person who refuses to lay down a grievance now is asking for a place whose first act is to take grievances away.

**What the Removal Says About the Garden**

The Book describes paradise in terms of what is not there at least as often as in terms of what is: no idle talk, no hardship, no fear, no fatigue, no expulsion, no resentment. The pattern suggests that the reward is defined by the absence of everything that damaged human life in the testing world, and the removal of bitterness heads the list after the greeting of peace. There is a logic to the order. Wrongs committed between people are the deepest marks a life carries, and the final dwelling cannot be a place of rest while those marks remain. This is why the sūrah announces the removal as an act of God before it describes the couches, the garden or the springs: the community must first be made fit for the company it will keep.
verses.48:
> No fatigue will touch them there, nor will they ever be asked to leave

**The End of Exhaustion**

The word rendered fatigue describes the weariness that follows exertion, the state in which a body has spent what it has and demands rest. The Book applies to the people of the garden a promise that this will never happen again, and it is a greater claim than it may appear to a reader who has not lived by labour. The Book's own picture of the world it is describing as finished includes sweat, effort and toll: the Qur'an tells human beings that they will find in the earth a residence and provision, which means work; it describes the journey of life in stages from infancy to old age and the weakness of the last stage. Sūrah Fāṭir records the people of the everlasting home stating the same blessing about themselves in almost identical words (35:35), and the two verses together make the promise a fixed feature of the reward rather than an incidental detail.

**The End of Expulsion**

The second clause answers a different fear. Human beings in the Book have already been expelled from a garden once, and their descendants live in a world of moves, evictions, exiles, displaced families and journeys that cannot be undone. To be told that no one will ever be asked to leave is to be promised permanence in a place one has come to love, and the Arabic phrasing describes an order to depart rather than a suggestion or a removal by force. The Book uses the same language elsewhere for the permanence of the reward, adding that the people of the garden will not be removed from it and will remain as long as the heavens and the earth endure, unless God wills otherwise, when it speaks of the eternal abode. What the verse excludes is the whole category of loss by relocation.

**The Pairing of the Two Negations**

The two halves of the sentence cover the two ways that a good condition can fail: it can become burdensome, or it can be taken away. A person's life in this world may be good and still exhausting, and it may be pleasant and still precarious. The Book's description of the final rest denies both possibilities in a single line, and this method of describing the reward by negation runs through the Qur'an. Sūrah al-Ghāshiyah describes a garden in which no idle talk is heard (88:11). Sūrah al-Naḥl says its people will have whatever they desire (16:31). Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt mentions that they will not be subject there to death other than the first, nor to torment. Each negation removes one of the anxieties the reader brings with him from his own life, and this verse removes the two that are hardest to shake.

**The Terror That the Verse Answers**

The audience of this sūrah was a trading people whose security could vanish with a caravan, and whose dwellings could be abandoned in a season of drought or feuding. The poor among the early believers had lost homes and property; the emigrants would later leave everything behind and arrive in a city where they owned nothing. When the Book tells them that there will be no fatigue and no eviction, it is addressing the two experiences that had shaped their fears most sharply, and it does so without offering a political remedy in this world. The promise is not that hardship will be abolished on earth; it is that the condition it produces is terminal and the destination that follows is not. The Book repeatedly tells its readers that their stay here is appointed and provisional, which is what makes the permanence of the next dwelling a message rather than a fantasy.

**The Chain From Gardens to Permanence**

The four verses from 45 to 48 form one complete description, and each line removes a source of unease: gardens and springs answer need; the greeting of peace answers conflict; the removal of bitterness answers the injuries left from the past; and this verse answers the fear of losing the whole thing. The sequence ends with permanence, which is what makes the earlier promises meaningful. A beautiful house that a person must leave is a source of sorrow, and the Book's audiences knew it. The sūrah therefore closes the description with the one quality that turns a gift into a home, and it states it as a decree about the future: they will never be asked to leave. Nothing in the account depends on the residents' performance, and nothing threatens to remove them from what they have been given.

**What the Verse Says About the Other Destination**

The Book describes the fire with the opposite pair of details, and the comparison is instructive rather than decorative. Sūrah Ṭā Hā says of the evildoer in the fire that he can neither live nor die (20:74), and Sūrah Fāṭir says of the disbelievers in the fire that death will not be decreed for them so that they might die, nor will its torment be lightened for them (35:36). Exhaustion without respite, permanence without relief: the two destinations are described with matching vocabulary and opposite outcomes, which is the Book's normal practice wherever it sets the two ends of human life side by side. A reader who has followed the sūrah from its opening verses about appointed terms and delays will see the logic. Everything in this world, including the punishment of the guilty, has a term; the world to come does not.

**The Word They Were Waiting For**

The verse's final word in Arabic covers being kept in a place and made to remain there, and it is used in the Book for the permanence of reward. Its force for the first listeners lay in what it replaced. They had been told, in the same sūrah, about communities whose terms ran out, about the mocked messenger who was told to leave the mockers alone for a while, and about a creature sentenced to wait until an appointed day. Everything around them was measured, temporary, and liable to end. The description of the garden ends with the cancellation of that whole arrangement. There is no term to count, no appointment to wait for, and no announcement of departure. What the Book gives its people in this verse is the one thing they could never have in the world: a place to stay.
verses.49:
> Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A Command to Deliver a Message About God**

The verse is an instruction to the Prophet, and its content is a statement God makes about Himself: tell them that I am the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. The Book contains many commands of this kind, but this one is placed immediately after a description of the gardens promised to the righteous, which is why the commentators read it as an address to the people who had failed to earn them. Al-Qushayrī's summary of the arrangement is exact: if God is generous and accepting toward those who obeyed Him, He is forgiving and merciful toward those who sinned. The sentence closes a door on despair before any reader can open it himself. Nothing in the verse asks whether the person deserves the news; it is delivered because the One who sent it decided to have it delivered.

**The Difference Between the Two Names**

The two titles at the end of the sentence are not duplicates. The first, *al-Ghafūr*, describes forgiveness as the covering and removal of a wrong; the second, *al-Raḥīm*, describes mercy as the giving of good after the wrong has been dealt with. A person who is forgiven is cleared of a debt; a person who is shown mercy is treated as though the debt had never existed, and is given more. The Qur'an often pairs the two when it speaks of accepting those who turn back, as in the command to the believers to say to those who come to them, peace be upon you, for *“Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. Whoever among you commits evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repents afterwards and mends their ways, then Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”* (6:54). The verse under commentary supplies the same two names as a general announcement, with no conditions attached to the announcement itself.

**Who Are the Servants Being Addressed**

The possessive in the words *My servants* is a mark of honour in the Book, and its use here is deliberate. The men and women being told about forgiveness are the same people whose failures had been recorded in the previous verses and who knew what they had done. Sūrah al-Zumar speaks to exactly this audience in words that could be read as an expansion of this verse: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”* (39:53). The Qur'an never treats the news of mercy as a reward for the spiritually accomplished. It is broadcast to the people most in need of it, and the reason is that the alternative, despair, is described elsewhere in the same Book as an accomplice to further failure.

**Mercy in the Qur'an's Account of God**

The Book speaks about God's mercy more often and more expansively than about any other relationship between Him and human beings. In the dialogue at Mount Sinai, God says of Himself, *“My mercy encompasses everything.”* (7:156), a claim the Qur'an does not make for any other attribute in the same wording. Sūrah al-Anʿām has God taking mercy upon Himself as a commitment, announcing that He will gather all people for the Day of Judgment in the same breath (6:12). Sūrah Ghāfir names Him *“the Forgiver of sin and Accepter of repentance”* (40:3), and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ provides the simple equation for anyone who has wronged himself, that he should seek forgiveness and will find God All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:110). The verse under commentary belongs to this body of statements, and it is the one the Prophet was told to carry to the servants themselves.

**The Hadith on the Precedence of Mercy**

The Prophet is reported to have related what God wrote concerning this subject: *“When Allah completed the creation, He wrote in His book with Him upon the Throne: Verily, My mercy prevails over My wrath.”* The report is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3194 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2751, agreed upon by both collectors, with the wording of the record written and kept above the Throne. The image is of a decision made at the beginning of creation and preserved where the creation cannot touch it. Whatever a person's fear of judgment may be, the Book and the reports that accompany it consistently present mercy as the attribute God has given precedence, and the sūrah's own sequence performs the same act: a description of punishment, followed immediately by the announcement that God is forgiving and merciful.

**Forgiveness and the Turning That Follows**

The Book never describes forgiveness as an amnesty that leaves a person as he was. Sūrah al-Anʿām's verse about the merciful Lord attaches two conditions to the person seeking it, repentance afterwards and mending one's ways, and Sūrah al-Nūr states the same combination when it tells believers to repent and follow the straight path. Forgiveness in this vocabulary is the reception of a person who has turned, which is why the announcement in this verse is not permission to sin but an invitation to return. The servant who reads it while carrying a heavy record is being told that the record is not the final word about him. Sūrah al-Furqān promises the same, that God will replace the evil deeds of the repentant with good ones, and the verse under commentary is the announcement that makes such a return thinkable.

**News That Had to Be Carried by a Man**

The command at the start of the verse specifies the messenger: tell them, O Prophet. The news is revealed but it is conveyed by a human being who spoke to human beings in their own language and who knew from his own experience what it meant to need forgiveness. The Prophet's own reported teaching included a prayer he is said to have used repeatedly, asking God, who loves forgiveness, to forgive. The verse's force in this sūrah is therefore double: it tells its audience something about God that no one can discover by reasoning, and it does so through a man standing in front of them, which is the whole structure of revelation in the Qur'an. What the servant receives from the verse is a sentence he could not have known to write about his own case.
verses.50:
> and that My torment is indeed the most painful

**A Sentence That Completes the One Before It**

The Book states the two names in verse 49 and, in the next breath, states the punishment, and the grammatical linkage makes them a single message. The Qur'an uses the same pairing elsewhere in words that are close to this passage: *“Know that Allah is severe in punishment and that He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”* (5:98). Sūrah Ghāfir lists the titles of God in a row, including the forgiver of sin, the accepter of repentance and the severe in punishment (40:3). Readers are not offered the mercy without the warning, and they are not left with the warning alone. What a person does with the two facts together, in the Book's teaching, determines whether the mercy reaches him, and the sentence about punishment exists to make sure the announcement of mercy is understood as a summons to turn rather than as a licence to continue.

**Why the Book Keeps Fear Alive**

A religion that spoke only of mercy would tell its followers exactly what they wanted to hear, and the Qur'an never takes that route. It describes people who mistook delay and prosperity for approval in its own earlier verses, and it treats the mistake as fatal. The Book therefore keeps the other pole in view, sometimes in a single verse, as in the warning that no one can be sure of escaping God's plan: *“Did they feel secure against Allah's planning? None would feel secure from Allah's planning except the losers.”* (7:99). The sūrah's reader has just been shown the destination of a creature who reasoned himself into rebellion, and the sentence about torment is placed where no one can skim past it. Fear in the Qur'an is not a psychological weapon; it is one half of the information a person needs in order to act.

**The Emphatic Construction of the Sentence**

The Arabic builds the meaning with emphasis upon emphasis: the pronoun intensifies the attribution, the noun carries the definite article, and the adjective is one of the words for pain. A literal rendering would read something like: and that My punishment, it is the painful punishment. The construction cannot be reduced to a mild statement about consequences. It is the Book's own voice, in the first person, naming the outcome of persistence in a way no commentator has ever managed to soften, and it is issued by the same speaker who used the words All-Forgiving and Most Merciful one line earlier. The Qur'an's presentation of the two attributes in a single breath means that they must be held together, and the fact that both are spoken by God about Himself is what makes the combination stable.

**Whom the Punishment Reaches**

The Book is consistent about whom the warning concerns, and it names them without ambiguity. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt states that those who disbelieve in God's signs and in the meeting with Him are the ones with no hope in His mercy, and that they are the ones who will suffer a painful punishment (29:23). Sūrah Ghāfir's list of divine titles ends with the reminder that to Him is the final return (40:3). The warning is not addressed to someone who has sinned and turned back; the Book's own stories include murderers, adulterers and persecutors who returned and were received. The torment described in this verse is what awaits the person who dies in his position rather than the person who fails and rises again, and the Qur'an's many invitations to return exist precisely because the second possibility remains open for as long as life lasts.

**Mercy Precedes, and Justice Remains**

The two verses cannot be read as though one cancelled the other, and the reports that accompany them hold the balance. The Prophet related that God wrote concerning Himself, that His mercy prevails over His wrath, in a report found in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3194 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2751. The precedence described there is a statement about the divine disposition, not a decree that judgment will not be executed; the same Book whose mercy encompasses everything also warns that God is severe in punishment, in a verse quoted above, and that the wrongdoers will not escape. What the precedence means in practice is that no one is punished before mercy has had its full opportunity with him: a warning is sent, a term is granted, a lifetime is given, and the door of return stays open until it closes for reasons the person himself supplies.

**The Plainness of the Book's Language About Pain**

The Qur'an does not shelter its audience from the subject. It uses the vocabulary of pain and punishment without abstraction, without euphemism and without embarrassment, and the same Book that describes paradise in terms of gardens and springs describes the fire in terms of what a body and a soul will endure. Sūrah Ṭā Hā describes its inhabitants as neither living nor dying there (20:74), and Sūrah Fāṭir adds that their torment will not be lightened (35:36). The purpose of such plainness is not cruelty but accuracy. A person who has been given a clear account of what awaits persistence can no longer claim that the warning was vague, and the Book's own summary of the matter leaves the responsibility with the reader rather than with the messenger.

**Two Verses as One Lesson**

Taken as a unit, these two verses give a complete account of the relationship the sūrah asks its reader to hold with his Lord: a mercy that is announced without conditions on God's side, and a consequence that is described without softening on the other. Communities that lose one half of the lesson are recognisable in the Book's own pages. The people who depend on mercy alone slide into the complacency the sūrah has already described, eating and enjoying themselves and being diverted by hope. The people who see only the punishment arrive at the despair that Abraham is warned against later in the same sequence of verses. The verses are placed side by side because they are meant to be recited side by side, and the reader who holds both is the reader the Book is addressing.
verses.51:
> And inform them ˹O Prophet˺ about Abraham’s guests

**The Second Command to Inform**

The verse repeats the formula of verse 49, tell them, and turns from doctrine to narrative. The Qur'an's method here is worth noticing: instead of adding a further statement about God's attributes, it hands the Prophet a story and tells him to carry that to his people. The listeners in Makkah knew Abraham's name and claimed him as an ancestor; the Book uses that familiarity to place a scene from his life before them. The two instructions sit next to each other in the passage, and they cover the two things a messenger is asked to deliver: what God says about Himself, and what happened to the people who trusted Him. The story that follows is one of several in this sūrah, and it is introduced with the same authority as the announcement about mercy.

**Who Abraham Was in the Book's Account**

The Qur'an names Abraham in dozens of places and describes him in terms that no other figure receives. He is called a model of excellence, devoted to God and perfectly upright (16:120), and utterly grateful for the favours he received, so that God chose him and guided him to the straight path (16:121). Sūrah al-Nisāʾ states the distinction directly: *“And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend.”* (4:125). He is the figure in whom the Book anchors the religion of submission, the father of the line that produced the prophets of Israel, and the builder, with his son, of the sanctuary at Makkah. For an audience that took pride in descent, the choice of his story was exact.

**The Word for Guests**

The Arabic word is *ḍayf*, and it means guests in the most concrete sense: people who come to a person's home and are owed hospitality by the custom of the land. The same root appears elsewhere in the Book for the honour of being a guest and for the obligations that follow. The desert cultures of Arabia treated the arrival of a stranger as a test of the household, and the Qur'an's other telling of this story describes the visitors as *“Abraham's honoured guests”* (51:24), with the adjective supplied on the sūrah's own initiative. When the Book uses a word from the daily life of its audience, it is not decorating the narrative. It is placing a story about the unseen world in the frame of the most familiar human obligation, and asking the listener to judge the scene by the manners he already practised.

**The Guests Were Messengers**

The visitors were angels, and the same passage that calls them guests names them as messengers: *“And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺. They greeted ˹him with˺, ‘Peace!’ And he replied, ‘Peace be upon you!’ Then it was not long before he brought ˹them˺ a ˹fat,˺ roasted calf.”* (11:69). They arrived in human form, and the Book does not describe the form in any detail, which has been the general practice of Muslim exegetes when handling such scenes. What the narrative stresses is the action: they came with a message, they were received as guests, and the occasion turned out to be an announcement about the future of Abraham's line and the fate of a city. Two worlds meet at a tent door, and the Book tells the encounter as a domestic story.

**The Other Tellings of the Visit**

The Qur'an narrates this visit in several places, and the details differ in ways that suit each context. Sūrah Hūd describes the greeting, the calf, Abraham's alarm when the guests did not eat, the good news of Isaac and the plea he made for the people of Lot (11:69-76). Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt gives the scene in a few swift lines and then moves to the destruction of the cities (51:24-34). Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt introduces the same angels with the news before they reach Lot (29:31-32). Each telling selects the elements its sūrah requires, and none contradicts another. The passage under commentary chooses to introduce the guests without describing them at all, which obliges the reader to continue into the verses that follow to learn why they came.

**What the Story Adds to the Sūrah's Argument**

The sūrah has just described two destinations and the people assigned to them, and it has announced the mercy of God and the severity of His punishment. The narrative that begins here supplies the human form of the same themes. Abraham receives strangers and serves them; the strangers are the bearers of good news he had long ceased to expect; the same visitors are on their way to a people whose destruction has been decreed. Belief and denial, hospitality and hostility, mercy and judgment all appear in one scene, told in the vocabulary of an ordinary evening. The Book's habit of teaching doctrine through narrative is at its most deliberate here, where the abstract announcements of the preceding verses are given faces and a house.

**A Story the Prophet Was Told to Carry**

The command at the start of the verse places the story in the Prophet's hands. He was being mocked in the streets of his own town by men who called him a madman and demanded angels from the sky; he is told, in effect, to tell them about a man who received angels at his own table. The parallel is not spelled out, and the Book rarely spells out such parallels, but the audience is capable of drawing it, and later in the sūrah the Prophet's own consolation is stated directly. What the verse delivers is a story about a household where the arrival of the unseen world was met with food and a greeting of peace, which is exactly the posture the messengers had been offering Makkah and not receiving.
verses.52:
> who entered upon him and greeted ˹him with˺, “Peace!” He ˹later˺ said, “Surely we are afraid of you.”

**The Greeting That Opens the Story**

The visitors begin with peace, and this detail is preserved in every telling of the scene. Sūrah Hūd gives the exchange in full, including Abraham's reply in kind: *“And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺. They greeted ˹him with˺, ‘Peace!’ And he replied, ‘Peace be upon you!’”* (11:69). The Book records the courtesy of two parties who do not yet know each other, and it records it approvingly, since the same Book commands its readers to greet one another and instructs them to answer a greeting with something better or at least equal to it (4:86). The scene begins with the smallest and most ordinary act in the culture of the audience, and everything that follows in the passage, an announcement of the impossible and a sentence of destruction, unfolds from a doorway opened to strangers.

**Why Abraham Was Afraid**

The fear that Abraham expresses in this verse has an explanation in the parallel account, and it is a culture's explanation rather than a psychological one. Sūrah Hūd says of the guests, *“And when he saw that their hands did not reach for the food, he became suspicious and fearful of them.”* (11:70). In the society of the sūrah's first hearers, a guest who refused the food he was offered was declaring hostility or bringing danger into the house. Abraham had prepared a meal, as the other account details, and the guests did not eat. His alarm is therefore not the dread of a timid man; it is the correct reading of a social signal, and it tells the reader how completely the visitors had entered the world of human custom while remaining outside it.

**Hospitality as an Act of Faith**

The Book's account of that evening is, among other things, a portrait of how a believer treats strangers. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt records what Abraham did: *“Then he slipped off to his family and brought a fat ˹roasted˺ calf, and placed it before them, asking, ‘Will you not eat?’”* (51:26-27). The phrasing is quick and practical, the behaviour of a man who does not debate whether the visitors deserve his attention. His character is described elsewhere in words that fit the action: *“utters gratitude for Allah's favours. ˹So˺ He chose him and guided him to the Straight Path.”* (16:121). The hospitality practised in this verse is the visible form of the gratitude the Book attributes to him, and the fact that the guests turned out to be angels is not what made the welcome correct.

**The Prophet's Own Fear When Guests Arrived**

Fear at the arrival of an unknown visitor was not limited to Abraham's story. Sūrah al-Kahf and other passages show the prophets reacting to the appearance of the unseen world when it came to them in disguise, and the Book records their alarm without criticism. The Qur'an's prophets are consistently portrayed as human beings who experienced what their hearers experienced: hunger, illness, laughter, grief, fear. When the Book's opponents demanded a messenger who was not a man, the answer given was that the messengers sent were men, eating in markets and walking the streets (25:7). The verse under commentary contributes to that picture. The friend of God stands at his own door, uncertain whether the strangers are a threat, and the record preserves the moment.

**When the Unseen Crosses a Threshold**

The scene's drama comes from the fact that the two worlds meet at ordinary ground level. The Qur'an does not present the unseen as a distant subject for speculation; it presents it arriving at a house, greeting its owner, and accepting a meal that it then does not eat. The result is a genuine confusion on the human side, and the Book lets the confusion stand for several verses before resolving it. The visitors are not described in any physical detail, and the reader is never told what Abraham saw when he looked at them. What is given is the sequence of events and the emotions they produced, and that is enough for the story to convey its lesson about a world whose boundaries are thinner than the audience assumed.

**"We Are Afraid of You": a Sentence That Makes the Story Honest**

The Book could have presented Abraham as untroubled throughout, greeting angels as though he knew all along who they were. It does the opposite. He is recorded as afraid, and the fear is not a flaw that the story later corrects; it is the reason the visitors must begin their message with reassurance. This small admission does more for the narrative's credibility than any description of angelic splendour could, and it fits the sūrah's audience precisely. The men of Makkah were being told that the man they considered the father of their religious heritage had once stood at his own door suspecting his guests of ill intent. The scene has the texture of a real evening, and the Book's account of revelation rests on such textures.

**Peace Given and Peace Returned**

The AbrahAmic scene begins and ends with the same word on both sides, and the pattern was later made into a rule for the community. The greeting is given; the greeting is returned; hostility is disarmed before it can be assumed, and the guest who might be an enemy is met with a claim of safety. The Book instructs believers to greet one another, to return a greeting with one better or equal (4:86), and to enter each other's houses with a greeting of blessing. When the verse under commentary shows the two parties exchanging peace before anything was known about one another, it is showing the community the practice in the home of the man whose way of faith it was told to follow. The angel who had come with news of a son and a sentence on a city was first received as a guest with peace.
verses.53:
> They reassured ˹him˺, “Do not be afraid! Surely we give you good news of a knowledgeable son.”

**The Reassurance Comes First**

Before the message, the angels calm their host. The Book's arrangement of the sentence is deliberate: the instruction not to fear precedes the announcement, and the announcement is introduced as the reason for it. Sūrah Hūd records the same order of events with the visitors explaining their mission at once: *“They reassured ˹him˺, ‘Do not be afraid! We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.’”* (11:70). A guest who has already alarmed his host owes him an account of himself, and the visitors give it. In a single verse they identify their nature, remove the cause of the fear and then deliver the news they came with. The sūrah's reader is being shown, in the space of two lines, how quickly the unseen world can move from threatening to gracious.

**Good News of a Son**

The promise is the central content of the verse and the reason the visitors were described in the sūrah at all. The child is not named here, and the omission has the effect of putting the emphasis on the wonder rather than on the individual. Other passages supply the name: Sūrah Hūd tells of the good news of Isaac and, after him, Jacob (11:71), Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt says that Abraham was given the news of a forbearing son (37:101) and later of Isaac, a prophet, and one of the righteous (37:112), and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt describes him blessed with Isaac and Jacob, with prophethood and revelation reserved for his descendants (29:27). The sūrah holds the name back and gives the attribute instead, which is a habit of this Book: the reader is told what the gift was like before he is told what it was called.

**Why the Son Is Described as Knowing**

The Arabic adjective describes knowledge, and its use here carries more than a compliment. The child promised to an elderly man and a barren woman is described by a quality that belongs to the prophetic line rather than by strength, beauty or wealth, and the same adjective appears in the other telling of the same moment (51:28). The Book's own summary of what Abraham's descendants received makes the connection: prophethood and revelation were reserved for his line (29:27).
