A son is a future, and the verse defines the future in terms of knowing rather than of inheriting. For an audience that measured a family's worth by its numbers and its herds, the description quietly moves the measure to what a person carries inside him.

**A Promise That Exceeds Nature**

The announcement is impossible by the arithmetic of the couple's age, and the Book does not evade the fact; it records Abraham's astonishment and his wife's laughter in the parallel accounts. What the verses stress is the authority behind the promise. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt gives the angels' reply to the couple's surprise: *“They replied, ‘Such has your Lord decreed. He is truly the All-Wise, All-Knowing.’”* (51:30). Sūrah Hūd puts the same point in the mouth of the visitors when Sarah exclaims in wonder: *“Are you astonished by Allah's decree? May Allah's mercy and blessings be upon you, O people of this house.”* (11:73). The promise to Abraham belongs to the same family of announcements as the births of John and of Jesus, each of them impossible by ordinary reckoning and each of them reported as an act of God.

**The Two Announced Sons in the Book's Pattern**

The Qur'an tells the story of a promised child several times, and the details are arranged for comparison. Zachariah receives news of John in old age and asks how it can be, and the answer is that God does what He wills (3:40). Mary receives news of a son with no father at all. Abraham receives news of a son when both he and his wife are past the age of childbearing, and the Book records the reaction of each recipient. The pattern is consistent: the messenger asks, is answered, and the answer attributes the outcome to God's decision rather than to any cause. Read beside the announcements of mercy in the verses just before the story, the promise to Abraham is one more instance of a God who gives what nature does not supply.

**What the Good News Meant to a Man With No Heir**

Abraham's concern for offspring appears elsewhere in the Book, in his prayer for the city and in his request that his descendants be included in the covenant made with him (2:124). For a man of his culture, a son meant the survival of his name, the continuation of his household, and the future of the mission he had been given. The announcement in this verse answers a need he had carried for decades, and the Book makes clear that the answer arrived without his arranging it. The visitors do not ask him to prepare, work or wait in a particular posture. They tell him what God has decided and leave him with the news, and the sequence of astonishment, explanation and reassurance that follows in the sūrah is the human side of receiving something that cannot be earned.

**The Voice That Interrupts Fear**

The sentence's structure places two acts in one breath: fear is dismissed and good news is given. The Book's readers have been told a few verses earlier that God's mercy is announced to His servants and that His punishment is severe, and here the two truths appear in a single scene as comfort to a frightened host and as a sentence awaiting a doomed city. The angels in this verse are the same visitors who will shortly tell Abraham about the people of Lot, and the message they carry to him is that the impossibility in his own life has been overruled in his favour. What the verse gives the sūrah's first audience is a picture of the unseen world arriving at a believer's door and, before anything else, taking away his fear.
verses.54:
> He wondered, “Do you give me good news despite my old age? What unlikely news!”

**The Astonishment of a Human Being**

The verse records Abraham's reaction, and the reaction is surprise rather than doubt. The Book does not present the friend of God as a man who receives an announcement about his own household with composure; it presents him asking how such news can apply to him. The parallel account gives the fuller form of the question, in which he asks whether the visitors bring news of a son when old age has befallen him, and the Book preserves the exact wording of his incredulity. Prophets in the Qur'an are consistently written this way, as men who lived inside the conditions of the human body. Their faith is not displayed as the absence of ordinary feeling but as conduct maintained in the middle of it.

**Age and the Arithmetic of the Household**

Abraham's objection is not theological but biological. He is old, and the other account makes the situation plainer by recording his wife's age as well: she laughs when she hears the announcement, and later exclaims at the thought of bearing a child when both she and her husband are past the years for it (11:71-72). The Book deliberately places this arithmetic in the foreground. If the promise could be fulfilled by ordinary means, it would have been a calculation rather than a gift; the marriage had spent a lifetime proving that the ordinary means had failed. The reader is being shown the human estimate before the divine answer arrives, and the sūrah's narrative depends on the estimate being as hopeless as it appears.

**The Rhetorical Question and Its Force**

The two clauses of the verse are both questions, and the second is closer to an exclamation than an inquiry: what unlikely news. The Arabic constructs the sentence with a particle of astonishment, and the effect is to convey a man standing in his own doorway unable to fit what he has heard into anything he knows about the world. This is a different register from the flat refusal of a denier, and the Book's later verses will make the distinction explicit when Abraham clarifies that he is not despairing. His question is the ordinary reaction of a person being told that a boundary he had accepted as final has been moved, and the Book finds the reaction worth recording.

**The Book's Other Impossible Births**

The same pattern appears wherever the Qur'an describes a child promised against nature. Zachariah, told that he will have a son in his old age and that his wife is barren, exclaims, *“My Lord! How can I have a son when I am very old and my wife is barren?”* and receives the answer, *“So will it be. Allah does what He wills.”* (3:40). Mary asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her. The Book reports each question without embarrassment and answers each with an act of God. Read together, the accounts establish a single principle: the announcement of a child in impossible circumstances is one of the recurring signs of the prophetic story, and the astonishment it produces is part of the sign rather than a defect in the recipient.

**Why the Narratives Keep the Details of Family Life**

The Qur'an could have reported simply that Abraham received good news. Instead it gives the meal, the alarm at guests who did not eat, the wife's laughter, the old age of both partners and the words they spoke in their surprise. The Book's method of teaching through narrative depends on these details, because the abstraction that God gives to the old would make no impression on a listener, while the scene of an elderly couple hearing impossible news does. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt adds the physical gesture of Sarah striking her forehead in wonder (51:29), an ordinary human movement that no revelation needed to record and that the Book records anyway. The reader is not being given a thesis about divine power; he is being shown a household in a moment of upheaval.

**Not Despair but Amazement**

The distinction the sūrah draws between the two reactions will occupy the verses that follow, and its shape is already visible in this one. The words Abraham uses concern the unlikelihood of the event, not the poverty of God's ability. He is measuring the announcement against his own enfeebled body, which is a very different act from measuring it against the mercy of his Lord, and the exegetes who commented on the passage took care to say so. The Book keeps the two apart deliberately. A person who asks how something can happen is standing on the edge of belief, while a person who concludes that God cannot or will not act has already crossed the line, and the sūrah's placement of both attitudes within a few verses sharpens the contrast.

**A Question the Audience Would Have Asked**

The first hearers of this sūrah lived by the rules of cause and effect, and they had demanded signs from the sky on the assumption that the ordinary order of nature could not be interrupted. The story of Abraham's household makes the same assumption visible in the mouth of a prophet and then removes it without argument. Nothing in the account proposes that the world works differently in general; it reports one household in which a decree of God altered what the couple's bodies had settled. The fact that the news arrived through guests who did not eat, to a man who was old, concerning a wife who was barren, is the sūrah's way of telling its audience that their estimate of what is possible was smaller than the world they lived in.
verses.55:
> They responded, “We give you good news in all truth, so do not be one of those who despair.”

**The Reply to a Question About Possibility**

The visitors answer the astonishment directly, and their answer does not attempt to satisfy the arithmetic. They do not tell Abraham that the calculation is wrong, or that the years are fewer than he thinks, or that some physical change has occurred in him. They state the standing of the news itself: it is given in truth, which in this context means that it is certain, decided and beyond reversal. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt gives the same reply in the words of the angels when Sarah expresses her wonder, that such has the Lord decreed and that He is truly the All-Wise, All-Knowing (51:30). The answer to a question about how is therefore an answer about who, and the visitors let the how remain in the hands of the One who decreed it.

**"In All Truth": the Guarantee Behind the Promise**

The Arabic expression rendered *in all truth* carries the sense of something firmly established, and the Book uses its root for the realities that do not fail. The Qur'an applies the same word to the revelation itself, to the promises of God, and to the meeting with Him, and in each case the meaning is that what has been said will occur. The Book elsewhere states the general principle that God does not break His promises, and the visitors' sentence applies it to a particular household on a particular evening. The force of the reply is therefore that Abraham's difficulty is not being disputed; it is being placed beside a truth that outranks it. The promise is not conditional on his capacity to imagine its fulfilment, and the visitors do not require him to.

**The Command Not to Despair**

The second half of the verse carries an instruction, and it is stated in the negative form the sūrah has already used for Iblīs: do not be among a group. The Arabic warns him against joining a category of people rather than against a single act, and the Book keeps that distinction because despair is not a moment but a condition. The Qur'an treats it as a serious fault on the human side rather than a reasonable response to difficulty. Sūrah Yūsuf phrases the rule for Jacob's sons in words that leave no ambiguity — *“do not lose hope in the mercy of Allah, for no one loses hope in Allah's mercy except those with no faith”* (12:87) — and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt attaches the same condition to those who reject God's signs and the meeting with Him (29:23).

**Despair in the Book's Vocabulary**

The Qur'an's word for despair describes the cutting off of expectation, and the Book applies it almost exclusively to the person who has lost confidence in God's capacity or willingness to give. Sūrah al-Rūm observes the pattern in human behaviour at large, where a taste of mercy produces pride and a touch of hardship produces immediate despair (30:36). Sūrah al-Zumar sets out the correct understanding of the matter in the address to the servants who have exceeded all limits, telling them not to lose hope in God's mercy, since He forgives all sins (39:53). The two attitudes the Book rejects are therefore extreme on either side of the middle, the presumption that treats mercy as a guarantee of impunity and the despair that treats the record as final.

**Why Despair Is Treated as a Danger**

The seriousness the sūrah gives to the matter lies in what despair does to a person's capacity to act. A man who believes that his case is closed has no reason to change his conduct, seek forgiveness or return to his Lord, and the Book's entire message of repentance depends on hope remaining available. Sūrah al-Zumar's invitation is addressed to the people with the worst records precisely because they are the ones most likely to conclude that there is nothing left for them. The warning in this verse is therefore a rescue as much as a correction. Abraham is told not to join the company of the hopeless at the very moment when his own God is standing at his door with an announcement, which makes the instruction a description of what the news deserves.

**Hope as a Discipline to Be Practised**

The instruction in this verse is given to a man of profound faith, which means the Book treats hope as something that requires maintenance rather than something that comes naturally to a believer. The Qur'an characterises the people of the garden as those who abandon their beds to invoke their Lord with hope and fear (32:16), placing the two attitudes together in the practice of prayer. The same pairing of the two names, forgiving and severe in punishment, which the sūrah announced a few verses earlier, is at work here: the believer fears what he deserves and hopes for what God has promised, and he holds both in his worship. The visitors' command not to despair is addressed to a man who was surely not despairing, which is the point, and it fixes the position each of them is to occupy.

**What the Exchange Teaches the Sūrah's Audience**

The men being addressed in Makkah were living under pressure, mocked for a message they were being invited to accept, and the Book's own account of their situation shows how easily a person in that position can slide into defeat. The story they are hearing about Abraham is placed before them as a picture of what waiting looks like when the promise has not arrived yet. He had been given the covenant decades earlier and was still without an heir; the visitors arrive and tell him not to be among the hopeless. The message the sūrah delivers through this scene is that the delay of a promise is not the failure of the promise, and that the category of the despairing is not one a servant of God is permitted to enter while the mercy of his Lord remains the subject of the announcement.
verses.56:
> He exclaimed, “Who would despair of the mercy of their Lord except the misguided?”

**A Clarification Rather Than a Correction**

Abraham's answer is not a dispute with his visitors but an explanation of what his surprise meant. The exegetes read his question in the previous verse as wonder at the news and not as doubt about God's power, and this sentence confirms the reading: he is not one of the people who has given up on the mercy of his Lord. He says it as a general truth rather than as a personal defence, and the phrasing turns the accusation of despair around so that it belongs to a category he does not occupy. A man who had been given a covenant decades earlier and was still waiting for its fruit could have been forgiven for losing confidence. His answer is the statement of a person who had not.

**Who the Misguided Are**

The Arabic word rendered *misguided* describes someone who has left the road and is wandering, and the Book uses it for the people whose error has become a condition rather than an accident. Sūrah Yūsuf makes the connection between despair and unbelief explicit, when Jacob warns his sons not to lose hope in the mercy of God, since no one does so except people without faith (12:87). Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt states the reverse with equal clarity, that those who reject God's signs and the meeting with Him are the ones with no hope in His mercy, and that they will suffer a painful punishment (29:23). The equation in Abraham's sentence is therefore the Book's own: the despair of God's mercy is not a mood to be pitied but a symptom of lost direction.

**The Mercy No One Should Doubt**

The sūrah has already declared, in God's own voice, that He is the All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, and it has been careful to state that mercy alongside the warning of punishment. Abraham's statement applies the same doctrine to his own situation before the promised gift has arrived. Elsewhere the Book describes the scope of that mercy in terms that make despair unreasonable on any account: God tells Moses that His mercy encompasses everything (7:156), takes mercy upon Himself as a commitment (6:12), and addresses the servants who have exceeded all limits against their own souls with the instruction not to lose hope, since He forgives all sins (39:53). A person who measures God's mercy by the size of his own record has made himself the standard rather than his Lord.

**The Two Errors the Book Corrects**

The sūrah has set the two names side by side, and the correction it applies is symmetrical. Presumption is the error that treats forgiveness as a certainty that requires nothing, and the Book warns against it in the sharpest terms: *“Did they feel secure against Allah's planning? None would feel secure from Allah's planning except the losers.”* (7:99). Despair is the error that treats the record as a verdict already issued, and the verse under commentary names it as the mark of the misguided. A believer is meant to live between the two, fearing the punishment the sūrah has described and hoping in the mercy it announced, and the practice of that balance is what the Book calls worship. The teaching is stated plainly because the two errors are so easy to fall into and so comfortable once entered.

**Why Abraham Was the Right Person to Say It**

The Book's portrait of Abraham makes this sentence consistent with everything else said about him. He is described as a model of excellence, devoted and upright, utterly grateful for the favours of his Lord, chosen and guided to the straight path (16:120-121). He is the man God took as a close friend (4:125). He had asked for offspring and had been given a covenant whose fulfilment he had waited for across most of a lifetime. When the Book puts the sentence about despair in his mouth, it is letting the reader hear the position of a man whose own history had put the mercy of God to the test, and the answer is that the test had not moved him from it.

**Hope as the Mark of a Direction**

What distinguishes Abraham's position in this verse is not that he expected a child against all probability but that he never doubted the mercy of the Lord who had promised one. The expectation is specific; the hope is general, and it rests on who God is rather than on what the circumstances permit. A person holding that position can be astonished by what he hears without abandoning it, which is exactly what the sūrah shows: the wonder and the faith appear in consecutive verses without tension between them. The Book's readers have received the same structure through the announcement of mercy and the warning of punishment that preceded this story, and the passage teaches them, through one man's answer to his guests, how to hold the two together.

**The Balance the Sūrah Leaves With Its Reader**

By the end of this exchange, the sūrah has shown its audience the full range of the human response to God: a creature refusing an order out of pride, a group allotting itself to gates, a household receiving strangers, an elderly man astonished by news, a wife laughing at an announcement, and a prophet insisting that despair has no place among the faithful. The detail is domestic and the doctrine is severe, and the Book keeps them in the same passage on purpose. What the reader is meant to carry away is not the story's wonders but its posture: a person who has heard both the announcement of mercy and the warning of punishment, and who lives in the world expecting his Lord to be what He has said He is.
verses.57:
> He ˹then˺ added, “What is your mission, O messenger-angels?”

**The Question That Follows the Good News**

Once the visitors have identified themselves and delivered their message, Abraham asks what they have come for. The order of the exchange is worth noticing: the greeting, the meal, the alarm, the reassurance, the announcement about his son, and only then the question about their errand. He does not interrogate his guests at the door. He feeds them first, the Book records their own words of reassurance, and he waits until they have finished their business with him before asking about the rest of their journey. The question is the natural closing move of a host who has done his duty and now wants to know whether his visitors need anything further, and the Book uses that ordinary courtesy as the hinge into a new scene.

**A Host's Right to Know His Guests' Business**

The culture in which the sūrah was revealed treated the guest as a person under the host's protection, and a host who knew nothing of his visitors' purposes could not know what sheltering them involved. Abraham's question is therefore practical as well as polite. The same concern appears in the story's next scene, where Lot stands between his guests and a hostile city and calls them his own, with all the obligation that word carried. When the Qur'an commands its readers to be careful in their dealings and to guard what has been entrusted to them, it is building on a social world in which hospitality created real duties. The verse under commentary preserves the etiquette of that world inside the narrative of revelation.

**The Term "Messenger-Angels"**

The translation renders the word of address as *messenger-angels*, and the compound reflects the Book's usage. The visitors are not wanderers who happened to appear; they are envoys with a commission. Sūrah Hūd introduces the same group with the same title: *“And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺.”* (11:69), and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt uses it again when the same angels reach Lot (29:31). The Book describes angelic movement as commissioned and purposive, subject to command and dispatched for decreed matters, a point stated directly in the sūrah of the Night of Decree: *“That night the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit descend, by the permission of their Lord, for every ˹decreed˺ matter.”* (97:4). The phrase in this verse places the men at Abraham's table inside that system of government.

**The Same Question in Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt**

The parallel account uses closely similar words: *“˹Later,˺ Abraham asked, ‘What is your mission, O messengers?’”* (51:31), and the sūrah then supplies the answer in detail, that the visitors have been sent to a wicked people to rain down stones of baked clay marked by the Lord for the transgressors (51:32-34). The telling in al-Ḥijr follows a different order and reserves the reason for the following verses. Reading the two passages together shows the sūrahs' method of telling one story twice: each fixes on the moment its own argument requires and trusts the reader to gather the rest elsewhere in the Book. In both cases the question is answered plainly, which is the difference between this scene and the exchanges the sūrah recorded earlier with the men who demanded signs and rejected every answer.

**A Prophet Asking a Question and Receiving an Answer**

The Qur'an records a number of occasions on which messengers and righteous people ask their Lord a question. Zachariah asks how he can have a son when he is old and his wife barren, and receives the answer that God does what He wills (3:40). Abraham asks for the mission of the visitors at his table and receives it. The Book's treatment of questions is divided by the asker's disposition: a question asked in order to learn has an answer, and a question asked in order to escape an obligation is met with a description of what is coming. The prophets of the Qur'an are shown asking, waiting and being answered, and the sūrah's first audience is placed in front of those scenes after being shown what happened to men who treated the message as a joke.

**Hospitality Given Before Identity Was Known**

Abraham had no idea who his visitors were when the meal was prepared. The Book makes that clear by the sequence of events, since his fear begins only after the food is refused (11:70). His generosity was therefore offered to strangers without any assurance about their standing, and the sūrah places that fact in front of a community whose own welcome of the Prophet and his companions was, at that stage, thin. What the Book chooses to remember about the friend of God is not the size of his herds or the strength of his household but the calf he set before unknown guests and the question he asked them afterwards. Readers who follow the sūrah's sequence from its warnings about mockery to this scene are being shown the conduct that the mockers themselves were not practising.

**The Hinge Into the Next Scene**

The question in this verse turns the story toward the city. Everything before it belonged to a household: news of a son, a promise for the future, a blessing for a family. What the visitors answer in the verses that follow concerns a people who have exhausted their term, and the same envoys carry both messages. The Book does not separate its messengers of mercy from its messengers of judgment, and this verse is the joint between the two halves of the passage. A few lines later the narrative will leave Abraham's tent entirely and follow the angels to the gates of a doomed town, and the reader is given a moment to notice that the road to both destinations ran past the same door.
verses.58:
> They replied, “We have actually been sent to a wicked people

**The Same Word the Sūrah Used Before**

The Arabic word rendered *wicked* comes from a root that covers crime and the cutting off of bonds, and the sūrah has already used it earlier in its own account of the men who mocked the Prophet, where their disbelief is said to steep into the hearts of the wicked (15:12). The visitors' answer therefore connects the town they are travelling to with the audience hearing the story. The Book's vocabulary is chosen to make that connection unavoidable: the same description that covers the people of Sodom covers the mockers of Makkah, not because their offences are identical but because both are committed against the same warning. A community reading these verses is being told that it recognises itself in the story's second half or it does not, and the recognition is left to the reader.

**Who the People Were and What They Had Done**

The Qur'an names the crime of the cities plainly and without euphemism. Lot rebukes his people: *“Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before? You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”* (7:80-81), and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt adds further details in his rebuke, including the abuse of travellers and openness in their gatherings, to which his people's reply was to demand that the punishment be brought upon them if he spoke the truth (29:29). Sūrah al-Naml records the same exchange, and Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ has Lot ask his people why they lust after men and leave the spouses their Lord created for them (26:165-166). The Book's account of the city is therefore not vague about what happened there; it is explicit about the practices and about the arrogance that accompanied them.

**A Mission to Destroy, Not to Preach**

The angels' errand differs from the mission of every prophet in the Book. Lot had been sent to his people to call them to God, and he had preached, warned and been threatened with expulsion for it (26:167). The visitors sent in this passage arrive after that effort has failed, and their task is execution rather than invitation. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt states the mission in terms of hardware: the messengers are sent to a wicked people in order to rain upon them stones of baked clay marked by their Lord for the transgressors (51:33-34). The distinction matters for the way the sūrah's audience understands its own situation. The warning they were hearing was the time of preaching, and the fate of the city illustrates what follows when that time runs out.

**The Stones and the Marks**

The detail that the stones were marked by God for particular men appears in both accounts of what fell on the cities, and it is a detail a reader of this passage should register. Sūrah Hūd describes the command arriving and the cities being turned upside down, with stones of baked clay rained upon them, marked by the Lord (11:82-83). Nothing about the punishment in the Book happens at random. The same care that assigned each community its term in the sūrah's opening verses is visible in the assignment of the projectiles, and the final line of that passage in Hūd adds a warning addressed to the audience of the revelation, that these stones are not far from the wrongdoers. The sentence in the verse under commentary is the announcement of that entire operation, delivered by envoys to a man who had no idea of the scale of what was coming.

**Envoys Who Carry Decrees**

The verse's opening places the visitors in a chain of command: we have been sent. The Book's picture of the angels is consistently bureaucratic in the older sense of the word, with assigned duties, permissions and decrees. They descend by permission of their Lord for every decreed matter (97:4), and they do not act on their own initiative. In another scene, when the Prophet is asked by Gabriel about the timing of a certain matter, the answer given is that the angels descend only by the command of their Lord (19:64). The visitors in this verse therefore speak as officers of an administration rather than as spirits with their own agendas, and the sentence they deliver to Abraham is a report of the office they hold rather than an expression of opinion about the town.

**The Crime That Was Called New**

The Book's own account of the cities stresses that the practice there had no precedent: Lot tells them that no man had done such a thing before them (7:80). The statement is not a piece of archaeology; it is part of the charge. A community had taken something that human societies had judged wrong and adopted it as public behaviour, defended it with threats against the man who objected, and met the warning of punishment with a challenge. The Book's description of that escalation, from private conduct to public practice to a demand for the penalty, is a study of what happens when a people lose the sentiment that measures shame. The angels' answer in this verse is the sentence that concludes the process.

**What the Answer Told Abraham**

The friend of God had asked his guests what their business was, and the reply told him that a people were about to be destroyed. His response, recorded elsewhere in the Book, is to plead for them (11:74-76), and he is told that the decree has already come and cannot be averted. The answer in this verse therefore does more than introduce a new scene. It puts a righteous man in possession of information about a coming judgment in time to try to stop it, and the Book shows him using that time to intercede. The result was fixed before he spoke, but the Book records the pleading, and Abraham's character is on display as a man who hears of a punishment and argues for the condemned.
verses.59:
> As for the family of Lot, we will certainly deliver them all

**A Rescue Announced Before a Ruin**

The sentence is part of the report the visitors give to Abraham, and its timing matters. The same envoys who are on their way to destroy a people state in advance that one household in that people will be spared. The Book's practice here is consistent throughout its narratives of punishment: the destruction is never described without the survival of those who had taken the warning seriously. Noah's Ark, the escape of Moses across the sea, the deliverance of the believers before the destruction of a city, all follow the same order. The reader is being taught the shape of judgment before the story reaches its climax, so that he understands that the ruin about to be narrated was aimed at conduct rather than at geography.

**The Word "Family" and What It Covered**

The Arabic word for family carries the sense of a person's dependants, the household that gathers around him and bears his name. In Lot's case the unit was small, and the Book says elsewhere that there was only one family in the city that had submitted, which is the Book's own way of measuring the success of his mission (51:36). For a tribal audience, the household was the fundamental unit of loyalty and protection, and a promise of rescue given in these terms would be understood as a rescue of everything connected to him. The verse therefore announces not a lucky escape for an individual but the preservation of the one unit in the city that belonged to the one man who had remained upright.

**"All Together": the Totality of the Deliverance**

The final element of the sentence emphasises completeness, which is the same emphasis the Book uses when it describes the angels prostrating as a body earlier in the sūrah. When the time of destruction arrives, the rescue is not partial. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt records the operation from God's side with the same insistence on totality: the believers were evacuated from the city before the torment (51:35). There is no account in the Book of a faithful man in these cities left behind because the destruction was arranged by district, and none of a household rescued except in fragments. What the visitors announce is a complete removal of everything the decree permits to survive, and one exception, which the next verse names.

**One Family Found in a City**

The Book's honesty about numbers appears in the same context as the promise of rescue. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt says that only one family was found there that had submitted (51:36). The statement follows a description of destruction, and its position makes it a lesson about how few the people who accept a prophet's message can be, even after years of effort by a superior man. The sūrah's own audience in Makkah was small and under pressure, and the story of Lot's household is placed before them as evidence that the worth of a community is not measured by its size. What is being rescued in this verse is a single family, and the destruction that follows is a whole society.

**Why the Righteous Are Never Swept Away**

The Book presents the preservation of the righteous in these narratives as a matter of principle rather than of sentiment. When Abraham raises the case of the cities with his visitors, asking whether the righteous will be destroyed with the wicked, the angels give an answer that settles the point: *“He said, ‘But Lot is there!’ They responded, ‘We know best who is there. We will certainly save him and his family—except his wife, who is one of the doomed.’”* (29:32). The exchange is the Book's own statement of the principle: judgment is by person, and the presence of a righteous man in a doomed city is answered with a rescue, not with an exemption for everyone else. The destruction of the wicked is not a natural disaster with indiscriminate effects; it is an operation with a passenger list.

**Abraham's Pleading and the Decree Already Issued**

The most telling detail in the whole sequence is what Abraham does after hearing this news. Sūrah Hūd says that he began to plead for the people of the city, and that he was told to plead no more, since the decree had already come and the punishment could not be averted (11:74-76). The Book describes him at that moment as forbearing, tender-hearted and ever turning to his Lord. Nowhere does it fault him for the pleading, and nowhere does it suggest that the request had a chance. What the passage shows is a man made of the same mercy as his Lord's own announcement in this sūrah, standing between a doomed people and a settled sentence and saying what his character required him to say.

**The Ruins That Remain as Evidence**

The rescue announced in this verse is completed in the verses that follow, and the Book attaches a consequence to the whole episode that survives to this day. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt closes its account of the cities with the words, *“And We did leave ˹some of˺ its ruins as a clear lesson for people of understanding.”* (29:35). The sūrah's own narrative of the Stone Valley, which it will reach later in the same chapter, leaves the same kind of trace in the landscape. The deliverance of one household and the destruction of a society are not written in the Qur'an as local history. They are placed on a route the sūrah's own audience travelled, along the road where the ruins of the Stone Valley also lay, and the Book turns them into an argument that the reader is expected to walk past and consider.
verses.60:
> except his wife. We have determined that she will be one of the doomed.”

**An Exception Inside the Promise**

The promise of rescue was stated as complete, and this verse reopens it to remove a single person. The placement is deliberate and painful: the exception arrives after the household has been gathered in the reader's mind as a unit, so that the loss is felt as a subtraction rather than a qualification. The Book keeps the same detail in every account it gives of the story, in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf (7:83), Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:171), Sūrah al-Naml (27:57) and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt (29:32), and the consistency is itself the message. A reader who wants to know whether family membership secures salvation is given the answer four times, in the same words, in the same narrative.

**Who She Was and What She Did**

The Qur'an names her offense in a passage that leaves no room for ambiguity. Concerning two women, it says: *“the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. Each was married to one of Our righteous servants, yet betrayed them. So their husbands were of no benefit to them against Allah whatsoever. Both were told, ‘Enter the Fire, along with the others.’”* (66:10). The betrayal described is not stated in detail in the Book, and the exegetes explained it in terms of the wife of Lot's cooperation with his enemies and her failure to keep faith with his mission. What the verse establishes is the principle the Book draws from the two cases: a marriage to a prophet carries no guarantee, and a household tie cannot substitute for a person's own loyalty to God.

**"One of Those Who Lagged Behind"**

The phrase appears in several tellings, with variations that the Book does not conceal. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf says she was one of the doomed, Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ describes her as an old woman who remained, and Sūrah al-Naml says she was destined to be one of the doomed. The wording in each case places her with the group that stayed rather than with the group that left, and the sūrah's own account of the night journey makes the point explicit when the angels instruct Lot not to let any of his household look back, with one exception, and warn that she will suffer the fate of the others (11:81). She is not described as an opponent of the message in so many words. She is described as someone who remained where she was.

**Kinship and the Limits of Rescue**

The story of Lot's wife is one of several in the Qur'an that sever the assumption that a family relationship carries a person into safety. Noah's son is refused the same rescue on the ark, and the Book records God's words to Noah when he appeals for him: *“O Noah! He is certainly not of your family—he was entirely of unrighteous conduct.”* (11:46). Abraham's father is left outside the covenant he was given, and the Book states plainly that his intercession for him did not stand. In each case the relationship is real and the refusal is real, and the Book records both. The verse under commentary belongs to that pattern, and its place in a sūrah whose first audience counted its standing by lineage is not accidental.

**The Instruction Not to Look Back**

The night of the escape is described in Sūrah Hūd, and the instruction given to Lot is precise: travel with your family in the dark, follow closely behind them, and let none of you look back, with the exception of your wife, whose fate is with the others (11:81). The Book uses the backward glance here as the outward sign of an inward attachment: the family were to leave decisively, and she was not going to. The scene illustrates something the sūrah has been teaching since its opening verses, that a person's location in the world matters far less than the direction he is facing when the door opens, and the wife of Lot is placed in the story to make that truth visible in a household.

**A Decree Determined Before the Night Journey**

The visitors describe her fate with a verb of determination: we have determined. The Book elsewhere speaks of the writing of decrees before they occur, and Sūrah al-Naml uses the same expression when it says that God had destined her to be one of the doomed (27:57). The language is the same vocabulary the sūrah used about the fixed terms of the earlier nations, and its presence here tells the reader that the escapes and the destructions in this story were not improvised on the evening they happened. The Book's account of the world keeps judgement and decree close to one another, and the verse gives the reader a single person's fate as an instance of the arrangement described in the sūrah's opening verses.

**The Household as a Place of Testing**

There is one more implication to be drawn from this verse, and the Book draws it in the same chapter where it names the two wives. The household of a righteous man is not a refuge from responsibility; it is a place where responsibility is exercised. Lot's family were carried out of the city by a decree of God, and one of them was not, and the difference was not in their address but in their loyalty. The sūrah's reader, reciting this passage, is meant to notice that the household formed around a messenger is the first place where a person's response to that message is tested. The verse refuses the reader any comfort drawn from proximity to the righteous, while leaving the mercy of God available to anyone who faces the direction the family of Lot faced on the night they left.
verses.61:
> So when the messengers came to the family of Lot

**The Scene Moves From Tent to City**

The narrative leaves Abraham's household and follows the visitors to the town, and the verse marks the transition with the plainest possible words. Nothing is said about the journey or about how the angels reached the place; the Book cuts to the arrival, which is its usual practice when a story has more than one location. The reader who has just heard the promise of a son and the announcement of a doomed people now arrives with the envoys at the door of the second household. The speed of the transition is part of the effect. Within a few lines of recitation, the same company that was seated at one man's table has arrived at the gate of a city that is about to be erased.

**Lot's Place in the Prophetic Family**

The Book identifies Lot as a messenger in his own right and places him in the same line as the patriarchs: *“And Lot was indeed one of the messengers.”* (37:133). His relationship to Abraham is described in the Book's narratives as a nephew who left with him and settled in a different land, since God says that Abraham was delivered along with Lot to the land that was blessed for all people (21:71). The two households in this sūrah are therefore connected by blood and by faith, and the verse's mention of Lot's family continues the theme of the household that has run through the preceding verses. The reader is being shown two houses in the same family, one receiving good news and one about to be rescued by the narrowest of margins.

**What His Arrival Cost Him**

The arrival of the visitors was not a pleasant surprise for Lot, and the parallel accounts say so. Sūrah Hūd reports that when the angels came to him he was distressed and worried by their arrival, and that he said, this is a terrible day (11:77). Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt uses the same words for his state (29:33). The Book is describing a man who understood his city well enough to know what the appearance of unknown male guests would set off, and who had no means of protecting them. His distress is the response of a person who has been placed in a situation whose outcome he cannot control, and the Book records it before it records anything he did about it.

**Who the Visitors Appeared To Be**

The angels had come in human form, and the Book's narratives show the city's reaction as evidence of how they looked. Sūrah Hūd describes the men of the city rushing toward Lot and his guests, and Lot's plea that they are his guests and must not be humiliated (11:78; 15:68). Nothing in the Qur'an describes the visitors' physical appearance directly, and the exegetical tradition understood from the story's circumstances that they came as young men whose looks drew the attention of a people with that reputation. What the Book gives the reader is not a portrait but a consequence: the text shows what a town did when strangers arrived, and the reader infers what those strangers looked like.

**The Reputation of the City**

The crimes of the place are given in the Book in Lot's own rebukes, and one of them is directly relevant to the scene. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt records him asking his people whether they lust after men, abuse travellers, and practise immorality openly in their gatherings, and the answer he received was a challenge to bring on the punishment if he were telling the truth (29:29). The abuse of travellers is named among their offences, so the arrival of any guest in that city was a matter that put the host in danger. The visitors in this verse walked into a place whose reputation preceded them, and the narrative's tension is set up before they have finished their first sentence.

**The Household as the Address of the Rescue**

The detail that the messengers came to the family rather than to the man alone matches the announcement made in the previous verses, where the household was named as the unit to be delivered. The rescue is arranged around the same grouping that the decree on the city was going to destroy. The Book's practice in these scenes is consistent: the punishment is announced for a place, and the preservation is announced for a household, and the two decrees meet at the same address. When the visitors arrive at Lot's door in this verse, both operations are now standing in the same street, and the reader knows what the city does not.

**The Book's Pace Through a Disaster**

The sūrah will narrate the city's end in a handful of verses, and it devotes a similar handful to its arrival. The compression is deliberate; the Book never lingers on the mechanics of destruction, and it never entertains its readers with the details of the crime. Everything superfluous is stripped away, and what remains is a sequence of actions: the visitors arrive, Lot is troubled, the city comes, the visitors state their errand, the family leaves, the decree falls. The verse under commentary is the first beat of that sequence, and its brevity is the Book's way of telling the reader that the matter had already been decided before anyone in the town knew that strangers were coming. Nor does the sūrah name the town, though other passages make its identity clear by describing the cities turned upside down and the stones rained upon them (11:82). What matters for the recitation is not the map reference but the pattern: a messenger, a household, a city, and a decree that arrives at night.
verses.62:
> he said, “You are surely an unfamiliar people!”

**A Host Reading His Guests**

The sentence is Lot's first recorded reaction, and it says nothing about danger or welcome. He tells his visitors that they are unknown to him, and the observation carries everything that follows in the scene. A small town knows its own people, and strangers stand out at once; the arrival of guests whose faces nobody recognised was a public event in a place with the reputation of Sodom. The Book's account of his words is shorter than the accounts in the parallel sūrahs, which describe him as distressed and worried by their arrival and as calling the day a terrible one (11:77). The version here gives the reason before it gives the emotion, and the reason is simply that he cannot place them.

**What He Feared for Them**

The Book makes the danger explicit in the fuller account. Sūrah Hūd says that when the angels came to Lot he was distressed and worried by their arrival, and that he said, this is a terrible day (11:77). Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt uses the same description of his state (29:33). His anxiety was not about his own safety. It concerned what his townspeople would do to guests under his roof, and the narratives show that his fear was accurate, since the men of the city were already on their way to him when the conversation resumed. The Book frequently presents righteous people as people who read their surroundings accurately, and Lot's unease is presented as understanding rather than cowardice.

**The Duties of a Host in That World**

In the society addressed by the Qur'an, the arrival of a guest placed the host under an obligation that outranked his own comfort and even his own safety. Lot's language in the verses that follow shows the weight he attached to it: he calls the visitors his guests and pleads with his people not to humiliate him, then begs them to fear God and not to disgrace him (15:68-69). When the situation deteriorates further he says that he wishes he had the strength to resist them or could rely on a strong supporter (11:80). The Book records that admission without criticism, and the whole scene turns on the fact that hospitality, once accepted, could not simply be withdrawn when it became dangerous.

**A Host Who Cannot Protect His Guests**

The verse under commentary is the moment before a host's duties exceed his capacity. Lot stood alone in a city whose men were united in their practices and who had already threatened him with expulsion when he objected: *“They threatened, ‘If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.’”* (26:167). The Book's account says that in the whole city only one household had submitted (51:36), which means he had no party to call on for protection. His visitors were twice his number, unknown to him, and evidently unaware of the danger, and the narrative places him in the position of a man who must defend strangers against a town with nothing but his own standing.

**The Book's Portraits of the Righteous Alone**

The Qur'an does not present its righteous figures only in their victories. It shows Noah mocked for centuries, Abraham thrown into a fire, Moses facing Pharaoh, the Prophet driven from his town, and Lot standing at a door at night with his reputation as the last barrier between his guests and a mob. The pattern is deliberate, and the Book's summary of the enemies of the prophets includes the observation that they were met with mockery and threats rather than with argument. What a reader takes from the scene is not the failure of Lot's position but the ordinary shape of the contest between a messenger and his people: one man, a handful of supporters, and a society that has decided what it intends to do.

**The Parallel Account's Naming of the Day**

Sūrah Hūd gives Lot words that this sūrah omits, and their absence here is worth noting. In the fuller account he says, this is a terrible day, and the Book then describes the men of the city rushing at him. The telling in al-Ḥijr reserves the description of the day for the verses that follow and keeps Lot's first line restrained. The effect is to leave the reader with a plain sentence about strangers and a sense that its speaker knows more about his town than he can express to the men standing in front of him. The narrative does not need to explain the danger to an audience that has already heard the angels describe the city as wicked; the host's unease does that work.

**What the Sentence Reveals About the City**

Lot's remark identifies his visitors as outsiders, and the city's response to outsiders is the crime that the Book names against it. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt records his rebuke to his people listing the abuse of travellers among their offences, and the account in al-Ḥijr shows how quickly the town acted on the news that unknown men had arrived. The sentence in this verse is therefore a hinge in the story. It marks the moment at which the city's characteristic behaviour becomes the trigger for its own destruction, and it does so through the words of the one man in the place who was trying to protect the strangers. From here the narrative has only to describe what the town did and what God had already determined. The Book will not let the reader imagine that the city's crime was a private matter between consenting adults; the men came as a crowd, in daylight or by night, to a guest's door. What the verse records is the moment a town's public behaviour turned a stranger into a target, and the town itself into the object of a decree.
verses.63:
> They responded, “We have come to you with that ˹torment˺ which they have doubted

**The Particle That Corrects Him**

The visitors answer with a word that sets aside what has just been said and replaces it with something more important: they are not merely strangers whose business is unknown. The Arabic particle used at the start of their reply is the same corrective device the sūrah used when it reported the mockers insisting that they were bewitched rather than dazzled, and it functions here to move the conversation from the subject of their identity to the subject of their errand. Lot had said that he could not place them; they tell him what he needs to know about why they are there. The exchange takes one line, and in that line the visit of guests becomes the arrival of the decree they had been sent to execute.

**The Warning His People Had Doubted**

The thing the visitors have come with is the punishment Lot had been warning his people about, and the Book's account of that warning is preserved in his rebukes. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt records him asking his people whether they practised their shameful deeds openly and being answered with a challenge: *“Bring Allah's punishment upon us, if what you say is true.”* (29:29). The Book's narration of the exchange shows both halves of the situation: a messenger stating what would come, and a people doubting him and demanding it be produced. The angels' reply in this verse uses their own position against them; what they had refused to believe was already on its way and standing in the street.

**Doubt as a Response to Warning**

The Qur'an treats doubt of this kind as a decision rather than an intellectual state. The people of Lot did not examine his claim and find it wanting; they challenged him, mocked him and threatened him with expulsion. Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ records the same reaction to Lot's preaching as it does to the other prophets, and it closes the passage by saying that the people denied the truth and will soon face the consequences of their ridicule (26:6). The sūrah's own opening verses described a group of mockers who asked for signs they would not have accepted, and the parallel is precise. The doubt in this verse was a settled posture, and the visitors' words convey that it had run out of time.

**When Ridicule Meets Its Object**

The Book has a consistent way of describing what happens to people who laughed at warnings, and it uses the same verb in several places: they are overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule. Sūrah al-Naḥl states it plainly, that the evil consequences of their deeds overtook them and they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule (16:34). The Book's own words for the fate of the earlier nations use exactly this formulation, and the arrival of the angels at Lot's door is one of the earliest instances of the pattern in the prophetic story. The verses surrounding this one will apply it in full detail, since the punishment reaches the city at dawn.

**Faith That Arrives Too Late**

The Qur'an records how communities behave when the warning descends upon them, and it states the rule without ambiguity. Sūrah Ghāfir describes a people crying out when they saw the punishment, declaring belief in God alone and rejecting what they had associated with Him, and the next verse gives the verdict: *“But their faith was of no benefit to them when they saw Our torment. This has ˹always˺ been Allah's way ˹of dealing˺ with His ˹wicked˺ servants. Then and there the disbelievers were in ˹total˺ loss.”* (40:84-85). The men of Sodom had asked for the punishment to be produced; when the visitors standing in Lot's house tell him what they have brought, the window for the answer they were hoping to avoid has already closed.

**The Question They Asked the Prophet**

The same challenge reappears in the Book as a question put to the Prophet by his own people, and the answer given to him is a sentence worth remembering beside this verse: *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺, ‘Is this true?’ Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord! Most certainly it is true! And you will have no escape.’”* (10:53). The sūrah's readers in Makkah were being shown a community that had made that demand and received a reply, and the visitors' words in this verse are the reply. The Book does not present the punishment as a remote doctrine that may or may not arrive. It presents it as a matter of fact already in the hands of envoys, who tell a frightened host what they are carrying because the time for argument has passed.

**What the Answer Meant for Lot**

For the man standing at the door, the sentence ends a long and unsuccessful mission. He had called his people, warned them, been mocked and threatened, and now the warning had returned to him in the form of guests. The Book records no complaint from him and no request for a delay; the verses that follow record him attempting, one last time, to shield his visitors from the town. The angels' reply in this verse is spoken to a man who had already done everything a messenger could do, and it converts the failure of his preaching into the fulfilment of his message. What his people had doubted stood in his house, and he was about to be taken out of the city before it fell. The Book's readers have seen the same sequence in the sūrah's earliest verses, where the men who asked for angels were told that on the day they arrived no further delay would be granted. Here the delay has run out for a town that spent it in mockery.
verses.64:
> We come to you with the truth, and we are certainly truthful

**The Doubled Language of Truth**

The sentence repeats its key word twice in one line. The visitors first say that they have come with the truth, then that they are truthful, and the repetition is not padding. The Book uses a doubled construction when a claim is likely to be doubted, and these words are addressed to a man whose message had been dismissed by his own people for years. Lot stood in a town that had ruled his warnings to be lies, and the envoys sent to deliver the sentence therefore give him the one assurance that mattered to him: what he had been saying was true, and the men saying it now were telling the truth. The sentence reads as vindication before it reads as a threat.

**Truth as the Event, Not Only the Statement**

In the Qur'an's usage, a thing is called true when it happens as described. The Book attaches the same word to the punishment of the earlier nations, to the resurrection, and to the promises made to the messengers, and in each case the meaning is that the event will certainly occur. Sūrah Yūnus gives the Prophet's answer to the men of Makkah who asked whether the warning was true: *“Say, ‘Yes, by my Lord! Most certainly it is true! And you will have no escape.’”* (10:53). The truth the visitors bring to Lot in this verse is therefore the arrival of something already decreed, and the second clause of the sentence confirms the authority of the messengers who carry it. What they say about the future is not a forecast; it is a report.

**The Assurance Given to a Vindicated Messenger**

The Book is careful with the morale of the men it sends. It records God telling the Prophet that he is not a madman, that every messenger before him was mocked, and that the mockers were overtaken by what they ridiculed. It records the angels reassuring Abraham twice, first about his fear and then about his astonishment. In this verse the reassurance is given to a man whose entire mission had been rejected, and the visitors confirm that the message he carried was the truth and that they themselves are truthful. Nothing in the account says the confirmation comforted him; the Book leaves the reader to understand what such words would mean to a man who had been called a liar by his whole town.

**A Lone Warner in a Hostile City**

The Book's own summary of the city's population is stark: only one household there had submitted (51:36). Lot had preached to a people who answered him with threats of expulsion (26:167) and who demanded that he produce the punishment if he was telling the truth (29:29). The verse under commentary arrives at the end of that history. The envoys do not ask him to keep preaching or to try again; they state what they have brought and what they are. In a story full of reversals, this is the one the sūrah's audience was meant to notice: a man who spent his life unheeded received the confirmation of his message through the destruction of his audience.

**The Words of Every Party Are Recorded**

The sūrah preserves the speech of everyone in these scenes: the mockers, the proud, the assembled angels, Abraham, Sarah, the visitors, and now the men of Sodom in the verses that follow. The Book's practice of quoting its characters serves a purpose beyond narrative colour, since the words recorded are cited in the judgement itself. Sūrah Ghāfir's account of the condemned closes with a statement about God's practice in dealing with wicked servants, and the Qur'an's habit is to let each side be heard before the record is closed. What the reader of this sūrah receives is a complete transcript of a confrontation that was lost by one party and won by another, and the sentence in this verse is one of its shortest entries.

**The Shape of a Warning That Was Never False**

The men who doubted Lot had accused him of lying. The verse answers that accusation with a claim about the visitors themselves, and the answer given to them arrives in the following verses in the form of events. Throughout the Book, the truth of a prophet's warning is confirmed by what happens after the warnings end, and this is one of the clearest instances. The sūrah's own reader is addressed by the same structure, since the warning he receives is the same kind of warning, delivered by an unarmed man to a society that finds it inconvenient. The visitors' two clauses about truth therefore do more than settle Lot's case; they set the standard by which the audience of the recitation is asked to measure its own situation.

**The End of the Preaching and the Beginning of the Decree**

Everything in this short sentence belongs to the moment when argument ceases and execution begins. The visitors state what they carry, confirm its truth and confirm themselves, and after this there is nothing left in the story but the actions of the city and the departure of the family. The sūrah gives a whole section of Abraham's story to hospitality, wonder and reassurance, and then moves to the punishment with this one line of certification. The effect is a clean division between the age of warning and the age of judgement, and the reader is reminded of the sūrah's warning about the men whose towns were destroyed only after the messenger had been sent to them. Lot's message had been delivered; this verse is the point at which the account closes.
verses.65:
> So travel with your family in the dark of night, and follow ˹closely˺ behind them. Do not let any of you look back, and go where you are commanded.”

**The Command to Leave Under Cover of Night**

The angels do not tell Lot to defend his house or to summon help; they tell him to leave, and to leave in the dark. The choice of hour is practical. A family walking out of a city in daylight would have been seen, questioned and stopped, and the instruction removes that risk before it can arise. The Book's narratives of rescue are often framed in this concrete way: Noah is commanded to build and load, Moses to strike the sea and cross, the Prophet to migrate by night from a city that had resolved to kill him. The rescue in each case is performed by God but it is carried out through the actions of the people involved, and the sūrah's reader is shown a decree of deliverance that arrives together with an instruction for the person being delivered.

**The Order of the March**

The Arabic instructs Lot to walk behind his household, and the commentators offered two readings of the arrangement. On one, he was to be the last in the line, guarding the rear and watching for pursuit; on the other, he was to urge the family ahead of him so that none of them straggled and got left behind. Both readings accept the plain sense, which is that the group was to move as an organised party with a person at its back rather than as a crowd scattering in panic. The detail is small and it is characteristic of the Book's way of telling these stories: the escape of a household from a doomed city is described with the practical arrangements a caravan leader would recognise.

**"Do Not Look Back"**

The instruction not to look back is the sentence that carries the scene's moral weight. The Book does not explain why the glance was forbidden, and the reason has been understood in two ways that fit together: looking back would delay the departure, and it would express an attachment to the place that was being judged. The family were being separated from a city by a decree, and the decree concerned conduct in which the city had persisted. A person who turns for one more view of a condemned place is still standing with it in his heart. Sūrah Hūd preserves the same command with one exception, and the wife who is excepted there is the woman whose fate the previous verses have already described.

**The Biblical Account of the Same Detail**

The story of the cities is told in the Bible as well, and the account in Genesis relates that Lot's wife looked back as they fled and became a pillar of salt. The Qur'an's telling preserves the prohibition and never describes the transformation, and Muslim exegetes discussed her fate by way of the destruction that the verses of this sūrah declare. The comparison is useful for a reader who wants to see how the Qur'an handles a shared narrative: it keeps the moral core, the warning and the escape, and it declines to supply the kind of detail that would turn the event into a spectacle. What remains in the Islamic telling is the instruction that the Book puts in the angels' mouths and the lesson a reader draws from a family that was told not to look.

**"Go Where You Are Commanded"**

The last clause leaves the destination unnamed, and the omission is deliberate. The family are not told that they are going to a particular town or to a particular relative's house; they are told to walk and to keep walking where the command places them. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ reports the outcome of that journey, saying that God delivered Abraham, along with Lot, to the land He had showered with blessings for all people (21:71). The instruction in this verse therefore trains its hearers in the posture the Book keeps asking them to hold: obedience to a command whose full design is not displayed in advance. A household walking through the night out of a city it had lived in for years is a picture of submission in its plainest form.

**Leaving a Place That Has Been Judged**

The verse treats departure as an obligation rather than a matter of preference. A person who recognises that a society has exhausted its term is not meant to stay and watch the ending; the Book's counsel in a different context makes the general principle explicit, asking those who claimed to be oppressed why they did not move to a land wide enough to live in (4:97). The point is not that people should abandon every difficult place, since the Book's own prophets stayed in theirs for decades. It is that the moment of a decree is not a moment for lingering, and the angels' instructions to Lot arrange exactly that: a timetable, a formation and a direction, with no provision for a farewell.

**A Rescue Carried Out in Obedience**

Everything in this verse is instruction, and the next verse records the revelation of the decree behind it. The two verses together give the reader the full structure of a divine deliverance: a decision made by God, and a set of steps for the person being saved. The sūrah's account of Lot's rescue in another chapter puts both halves in a single line, describing those who were delivered before dawn as a blessing from God, and adding that this is how God rewards whoever gives thanks (54:34-35). What the household did on that night was walk, keep together and not turn around. The Book records no other contribution from them, and it credits their escape to a mercy they did not earn on the road.
verses.66:
> We revealed to him this decree: “Those ˹sinners˺ will be uprooted in the morning.”

**A Decree, Not a Prediction**

The verse says that God revealed the matter to Lot, and the Arabic word used for it belongs to the vocabulary of decisive judgment. The same root appears throughout the Book for the settling of a case, the carrying out of a sentence and the completion of an affair, and its use here tells the reader that what is coming has already been resolved rather than merely foreseen. The Book maintains this distinction carefully: prophecy in its pages is not a forecast that could turn out differently, and the decrees given to messengers are reports of decisions already taken. The command to leave the city in the previous verse and the decree announced in this one are therefore two halves of a single act, and the household's departure is a consequence of the judgment rather than a hope of avoiding it.

**The Word for the Destruction**

The translation renders the fate of the city's people with a term of uprooting, and the image is of something cut off at its base and removed whole. The Book's accounts of the destruction use a range of such words: the cities turned upside down, a rain of baked clay, a blast, a storm of stones. Sūrah Hūd describes the event in the language of command arriving and the settlements being overturned (11:82), and Sūrah al-Qamar records a storm of stones unleashed upon them while the family of Lot were delivered before dawn (54:34). The vocabulary of uprooting in this verse emphasises totality: not a punishment that would leave the society able to continue in some reduced form, but the removal of the thing from the ground it stood on.

**The Timing: "In the Morning"**

The Book fixes the hour, and the parallel account supplies the exchange in which the angels tell Lot that the appointed time is the morning, asking him whether the morning is not near (11:81). A specific hour is given to a man who has just been told to travel through the night, and the connection between the two instructions is exact: the family needed the hours of darkness to get clear of the place. Sūrah al-Qamar describes the same morning, saying that by the early dawn the people were overwhelmed by an unrelenting torment (54:38). The Book's habit of dating the destruction of communities gives its warnings a quality that general talk of consequences does not have: a day, an hour, a term that arrives.

**Why Judgments Are Given Times in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an's narratives of punishment are never vague about occasion. The flood comes at a set time, the drowning of Pharaoh happens at a certain moment of the pursuit, the blast overtakes the cities at sunrise. The dating serves the same purpose in every case: it shows that the events were administered rather than accidental, and it removes the excuse that the warning was a general threat with no deadline. The sūrah's opening verses established the principle in the abstract, that every community has a term that cannot be moved in either direction, and the story of Lot supplies a concrete instance in which the term is announced to a prophet in advance. The reader is being taught to hear the abstract statement with this story in mind.

**What the Decree Meant for the Household**

The sentence in this verse reveals what Lot was told while he was still standing in his house with guests whose identity he had only just learned. Everything in the night's events is now arranged in the reader's mind: the guests arrived, the family was warned, the household was given its route and its orders, and the city was given a date. What the townspeople were preparing to do to the visitors in the hours that followed was happening inside a schedule they could not see. The Book does not comment on the irony directly. It simply states the decree in the middle of the story, so that a reader who has heard it looks at the city's behaviour in the next verses with knowledge that the revellers did not possess.

**The Difference Between Hearing and Believing**

Lot had preached to the city for years with no result. The decree revealed to him personally in the previous verses is the answer to his preaching, and it arrives in a form that leaves no room for doubt. The Book's pattern in such scenes is consistent: the messenger receives the certainty of his message, and the people receive the event. Sūrah al-Qamar notes that the warning had already been given and that the people disputed it (54:36). So the sequence in the sūrah is a summary of the whole history of the mission: a lone warner, an audience that argued, a decree from God, and a departure under cover of night while the town celebrated in the dark.

**The Morning as the End of a Term**

The Book's readers have already encountered the language of appointed times in the first verses of this sūrah, where no community perishes before its term and nothing can advance or delay it. The decree in this verse performs that principle on a small scale and in front of witnesses, since one man was informed of the day and hour and was still able to walk out of the city before it fell. Everything about the arrangement testifies to the same conclusion: the world is administered, the timing is set, and the warnings that arrive before the deadline are the mercy that makes escape possible. The next verses will show the city spending its last hours in the pursuit of what it wanted.
verses.67:
> And there came the men of the city, rejoicing

**An Arrival Set Against a Decree**

The verse places the city's men in the same night as the decree announced in the line before it, and the juxtaposition does the work of the passage. On one side stands a sentence about the morning; on the other, a crowd of men hurrying through the streets with something to celebrate. The Book does not need to comment. It has been telling its readers since the sūrah's opening verses that no community perishes before its term, and here it shows what a community looks like while the last hours of its term are running out. The men in this verse are not worried, informed, or sober; their arrival is recorded in two words, and the reader supplies the rest from everything that has already been said.

**The Word "Rejoicing"**

The Arabic describes pleasure and cheerfulness, and the Book uses the word elsewhere for joy of a proper kind, which makes its appearance here the sharper. The exegetes explained the cheer as satisfaction at the news of the guests' arrival, since the men of the city were hoping to use them as they had used other travellers. Sūrah Hūd gives the same moment in different language, describing the men of the city, who were used to shameful deeds, coming to Lot rushing (11:78). The two accounts agree that the approach was eager, and that eagerness was the sound of a society that had turned the abuse of travellers into an occasion for pleasure rather than shame, which is the specific accusation levelled against the city by its own messenger.

**How the News Reached Them**

The question of how the city learned of the guests occupied the commentators, and the reports indicate that Lot's wife was the one who informed them. The detail, whether or not it is pressed, fits the story's own arrangement, since the wife is the member of the household whose fate has been separated from the others in the verses just before. A community learns quickly what someone in the house is willing to tell, and the fate of a family member who gave the city what it wanted is one of the story's more terrible small notes. The Book preserves no account of her action and leaves it to the exegetical tradition; what it preserves is her separation from the rescue.

**The Behaviour of a City Without Shame**

The Book's descriptions of the cities of Lot are consistently about public conduct rather than private weakness. Lot's rebuke in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt lists openness in their gatherings among their offences (29:29), and Sūrah al-Naml records the same scene in which the town's response to his preaching was to threaten to expel the one household that wanted to remain chaste (27:56). Nothing in the account describes secret wrongdoing that a community tolerated; what it describes is wrongdoing conducted as community business and defended when challenged. The crowd arriving at Lot's door in this verse is the outcome of that state of affairs, and it is presented as the normal operation of the town rather than an exceptional outbreak.

**The Guests Within, Unaware of Nothing**

The scene's tension depends on an asymmetry the reader holds and the crowd does not. The men approaching the house know there are handsome strangers inside and intend to take them. They have no idea that the strangers are messengers with a decree, or that the ground under their city has been spoken about in a sentence from which there is no appeal. The Book's narrative lets the reader stand above the moment and watch both parties without warning either, which is the same structure the sūrah used when it described men demanding a sign from the sky while standing beneath a sky already furnished with evidence. What makes the passage instructive rather than merely dramatic is that the reader of the recitation is standing where the men of the city stood.

**A Warning Already Disputed**

The Book records that the city's end had been preceded by years in which Lot warned them, and that their response was argument and mockery rather than attention. Sūrah al-Qamar states the matter in one line: he had already warned them of the blow, and they disputed the warnings (54:36). The arrival of the crowd in this verse is therefore not the cause of the punishment but the last episode in a history of refusal, and the rejoicing in the street is part of the evidence against them. The sūrah's readers in Makkah were hearing this story recited to men who had been treating the Prophet as a subject for jokes, and the parallel would not have needed stating.

**The Night the City Spent Its Last Hours**
