The verse is short and the Book keeps it so, but everything that follows in the sūrah's account of the night flows from this arrival. A family was leaving under cover of darkness while the men of the town were gathering at the house they had just left. What the crowd took for an evening of amusement was the final hour of their settlement, and the Book lets the reader see the whole of it: the decree, the departure, the arrival and the rejoicing, all inside a few verses. There is no commentary attached to the scene in the sūrah. The reader is simply shown the last hours of a people who had decided long before what they were willing to hear.

**Rejoicing Just Before the Seizure**

The Book connects joy of this kind with the moment of judgment in more than one place. Sūrah al-Anʿām describes a people who became oblivious to the warnings that came to them, were given everything they wanted, grew proud of what they had received, and were then seized by surprise so that their cheer turned to despair (6:44). The men of the city in this verse are in exactly that position: satisfied, unalarmed and busy with the thing they had long desired, on the night before a decree fell. The sūrah does not have to gloss the scene, because its readers have been taught by other passages how the Book treats a community that is enjoying itself at the wrong hour.

**The Road the City Sat On**

Cities of this kind in the Book are not hidden in the desert; they are placed on routes that people travel, which is part of what makes their ruin instructive. A later section of this sūrah states that their remains lie along a known road (15:76), and another passage tells the Prophet's own contemporaries that they pass by the town that was rained upon, and asks whether they have never seen its ruins (25:40). The town in this verse, with its men pouring into the street, was for years a destination and a stopover for traders and travellers. The Book's judgement falls on a settlement whose habits were public knowledge to everyone who passed through its gates.
verses.68:
> Lot pleaded, “Indeed, these are my guests, so do not embarrass me

**The Claim a Host Makes in His Own House**

Lot's first words are about hospitality, and the Arabic places the guests before everything else: these are my guests. In the society the Book addresses, the declaration was not a courtesy but a claim of protection. By naming the visitors as his guests, Lot was telling the crowd that any harm done to them would be his own humiliation and that his standing in the town was bound up with their safety. The Book's records of his words in the parallel passage use the same language and add a challenge: he pleads with his people not to humiliate him by disrespecting his guests and asks whether there is not even one right-minded man among them (11:78). He is negotiating with the last currency he has.

**The Vocabulary of Shame**

The word translated as embarrassment belongs to a family of terms about disgrace and public humiliation, and the Book uses it for the exposure a person suffers when his honour is damaged in front of others. Lot was not primarily appealing to his people's conscience about their crime; he was appealing to their sense of shame about harming a host. The choice of argument tells the reader what he was working with. In a city that had lost the capacity to be ashamed of its own conduct, the one sentiment that might still have force was the idea of disgracing a neighbour, and Lot used it. The Book's later verses record how little it moved them.

**What the Appeal Revealed About the Man**

The verse shows Lot doing what a righteous man does when he is overwhelmed: he uses the tools available to him, in order, without abandoning the people he is trying to protect. He had already tried preaching, and he had been threatened with expulsion for it. He had been left, by the Book's own reckoning, with one household in the city that had submitted (51:36). Now he stands at his door trying to buy time with an appeal to honour, and the sūrah records him doing it without any suggestion that his effort was misdirected or his position shameful. The Book's prophets are shown using the means at hand: Noah builds, Moses argues, the Prophet negotiates with the tribes, and Lot pleads with a mob.

**Hospitality in the Book's Moral Order**

The Qur'an treats the protection of guests as part of the conduct expected of a believer, and the Book's list of those who deserve a person's kindness includes the near neighbour, the distant neighbour, the companion by the road and the needy traveller (4:36). Abraham's evening with unknown visitors, described earlier in this sūrah, is the positive image of the same obligation, and Lot's night is its negative one. The contrast between the two households is deliberately sharp: in one, a stranger is fed and then asked his business; in the other, a town comes to take a stranger by force. The Book places both inside a single sūrah so that its readers can see how much of a society's health is contained in the way it treats a person it does not know.

**The Guest as a Trust Placed in a Host's Hands**

The Arabic phrase Lot uses presents the visitors as something handed to him: they are his guests, which means they have entered his protection by accepting his hospitality. The Book uses language of this kind elsewhere for the obligations that arrangements create, and the fact that the guests were angels rather than ordinary travellers does not figure in his appeal at all. Lot had no idea who they were, and the obligation he was discharging was owed to them as guests, not as heavenly messengers. That is the point of the scene the sūrah presents: the duty held whether or not the visitors deserved it, whether or not the host could manage it, and whether or not fulfilling it cost him anything.

**The Escalation to God's Name**

This verse and the one that follows it form a single speech with two movements, and the second movement appeals to God. A reader is meant to notice the order. The host begins with the code of his town and ends with the fear of the Lord of the worlds, and the crowd's answer in the following verse ignores both. The Book's narratives show this progression repeatedly: a messenger tries the argument that is closest to his hearers' habits, and when it fails, he names the authority that stands above them. What remains in the text is the record of a man who tried every appeal available to him on a night when a decree had already been issued and the sentence had a date.

**Guests Whose Identity the Host Never Learned**

Lot did not know who had come to him. The Book records that the visitors were angels, and that he only learned their errand later in the night, when they told him that they had been sent against his people. Abraham's encounter with the same party shows how far the obligation runs ahead of knowledge: he received them, greeted them, noticed that they seemed unfamiliar, and hastened to bring a roasted calf, standing over them and urging them to eat, and only then discovered that his hands had been serving messengers (51:24-27). When the visitors did not reach for the food, the Book records his alarm and their reassurance that they were angels sent to the people of Lot (11:70). Hospitality in these narratives is owed to the guest as he arrives, and the household that honours a stranger may be entertaining more than it can see.
verses.69:
> Fear Allah and do not humiliate me.”

**The Appeal Moves From Honour to God**

Having invoked the claim of a host, Lot turns to the authority of the One who made them. The two sentences are short and they are run together in the text, which fits the way a man speaks when he has only a moment to say what matters. The first appeal was to the sentiment of a town; the second is to its religion. The men he was addressing believed in God, whatever their conduct, and the sūrah has already shown that Makkan audiences who lived carelessly still believed in powers above them and assigned to God daughters and partners. Lot's plea took that belief and made it the ground of his request, asking them to fear the Lord they acknowledged rather than to be shamed before a neighbour.

**The Word for God-Fearing in the Sūrah's Own Vocabulary**

The term Lot uses is formed from the same root as the word the sūrah employed a few lines earlier for the people it promised gardens and springs, the ones mindful of God (15:45). The Book's vocabulary of guarding oneself appears in both places, and the connection is exact: what Lot was asking of the crowd at his door was that they become, for one night, what the sūrah has just described as the condition of the blessed. The same word stands at the head of Sūrah al-Baqarah's description of the people the Book guides, those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer and give from what they have been provided (2:3). The sūrah therefore places the two uses of the term within a few verses, one in a description of the reward and the other on the lips of a prophet barring a doorway.

**Why a Prophet Argues From Conscience**

The Qur'an's messengers consistently address their people in the terms the people already accept. Noah speaks to a nation that fears no reckoning and points to God; Shuʿayb appeals to fair dealing in the marketplace; Hūd appeals to the gratitude owed for the strength and prosperity his people enjoyed. Lot's audience acknowledged God, and his appeal to that acknowledgement is not a tactic. It is the same message the messaging was always about, put in the form the moment required. What the Book will show in the next verse is that the crowd's answer to this appeal was a claim of permission, which reveals how far a people can travel from a belief they still profess.

**The Two Pleas Held Together**

Read as a unit, the two requests in verses 68 and 69 cover the two available frames of authority: the honour of a household and the command of God. A reader of the Book is meant to notice that the prophet did not rest with either. He did not treat the town's custom as sufficient, nor did he limit himself to the convention of hospitality; he repeated his request with God named in it, twice, while the crowd stood in his street. The sūrah records no concession, no bargain, and no moment in which Lot considers handing the visitors over. The sequence is a model of steadfastness under pressure, and it is preserved in the same Book that records the failure of an entire city.

**The Threat the Sūrah Has Already Described**

The Book's readers know what was at stake in the confrontation at the door, and they know that the city's end had been decreed before the crowd arrived. Lot's plea for his guests therefore carries a weight he himself could not have understood: he was defending men who had been sent with a sentence, and the town that ignored his appeal was spending the last night of its existence. The sūrah gives no indication that he was aware of the danger to the town at that hour, although the decree had been revealed to him earlier in the night. What the text emphasises is his conduct rather than his knowledge, and his conduct was that of a man who protects what has been entrusted to him.

**Disgrace, Fear, and the Order of a Prophet's Priorities**

The word applied to himself in both requests is the key to understanding how lightly Lot held his own position in the town. He frames his appeal around his own humiliation and asks repeatedly not to be disgraced, and yet everything he had done in that city had already cost him his standing: his people had threatened him with expulsion, mocked him, and rejected his warnings. He was not a man protecting a reputation. He was a man protecting a trust, and he named disgrace because that was the argument with the best chance of being heard. When the appeal failed, he moved, in the verses that follow, to an offer he hoped would divert the crowd, which means he was still looking for a way to keep the guests in his house.

**A Doorway as the Measure of a Society**

The scene the sūrah constructs is simple enough to be remembered by a child, and it carries that much weight. A man stands in the door of his own house, with strangers inside and a mob in the street, and he says two sentences. The crowd's reply, the offer he makes, the blindness the next verses describe, and the morning that closes the passage all follow from that exchange. The Book's method of teaching by narrative reaches one of its clearest examples here: no explanation is added, no moral is drawn, and the reader is left with the picture of a society that had reached the point where a prophet's last arguments were hospitality, shame and the fear of God, and none of the three was honoured in the street.
verses.70:
> They responded, “Have we not forbidden you from protecting anyone?”

**An Answer That Answers Nothing**

The crowd does not deny what they intend to do, and they do not engage with the two appeals Lot has just made. They reply with a reminder of an arrangement they claim was already settled: they had told him, on some previous occasion, to stay out of their way in a matter they regarded as their own. The form of the question is confrontational, and its effect is to move the discussion from what is right to what was agreed. The sūrah records the sentence in full because it shows precisely what a community does when a prophet's argument cannot be answered: it changes the subject from the deed to the jurisdiction.

**The Two Readings of the Prohibition**

Al-Qurṭubī reports two explanations among the exegetes. On one, the city's men had forbidden Lot from interfering in their practices, having warned him previously not to approach them or try to dissuade them when they took a man to satisfy their desires. On the other, and this reading is attributed to al-Kalabī and others, the prohibition had been against his hosting guests at all, on the grounds that hosting travellers obliged him to protect them and set him against the town's habits. The second reading fits the immediate context more closely, since it is his guests he is asking them to spare. Either way, the crowd is asserting a prior right to police his conduct in a matter he considered a duty.

**A Crime Made Into Policy**

What the verse exposes is the transition from wrongdoing to legislation. A people may commit an offence and feel ashamed of it; a people may commit it openly and joke about it; a people may go further and defend it as a right, which is when the shame disappears altogether and the offender begins to police those who object. The Book's account of the city places it at the last of these stages. The crowd standing in the street not only intends to commit the act; it treats Lot's objection as a violation of an established boundary. The sūrah's brief narrative gives the reader the anatomy of a society that has moved from one stage to the next without noticing.

**Where the Men of the City Stood in the Book's Own Scale**

The Qur'an measures societies by their responses to messengers, and it records these responses with a set of recurring phrases: they rejected, they mocked, they demanded a punishment, they threatened expulsion, they disputed the warnings. This verse belongs to that vocabulary. The town's answer to its prophet is not an argument but a claim of authority: they had forbidden him, and the question they ask assumes he should have obeyed. Sūrah al-Naml records the same city's response in almost exactly the same spirit, when its people's only answer to Lot's rebuke was to demand that his followers be expelled from the land for wanting to remain chaste (27:56). In both texts the town's final argument is its right to decide who belongs.

**What They Did Not Know About the Visitors**

The crowd's confidence rests on a complete misreading of the situation, and the Book has given its readers the information they lack. The visitors are not defenceless travellers. They are envoys with a decree; they have already been told of the town's end, and their errand includes its destruction. The sūrah's scene therefore has a structure that recurs throughout its narratives of judgment: a powerful group asserting itself against a small number of people who appear to have no protection, while a decree that has already been issued stands between them. The men in this verse are speaking about the limits of Lot's authority to people who have authority over the morning.

**The Failure of a Prophet's Last Appeal**

By the end of this verse, every argument available to Lot has been refused. He has appealed to hospitality and been told that he had no right to protect anyone; he has appealed to the fear of God and been answered with a claim about a previous prohibition. The Book does not present his position as pathetic, and it does not present the crowd as persuasive. It simply records that the exchange ended where the sūrah has already told the reader it would end, since the decree was announced before the crowd arrived. A reader who has followed the passage from the trumpeting of the angels' mission to this sentence sees the whole machinery of a judgment in operation.

**What the Sentence Reveals About Authority**

The question the men ask is about jurisdiction, and the Book is interested in that question throughout. The sūrah's opening verses describe a God who owns the appointed term of every community; the middle passages describe a creature who claimed a rank over another creature's worth; the story of the cities shows a town that claimed the right to decide what happened in a prophet's house. Each claim is answered in its own scene, and the answers are not arguments but events. The question in this verse is therefore more than a piece of dialogue. It is the exact form of the error that the sūrah has been tracking from its first verses, and the morning that follows in the narrative is the reply.

**The Prohibition Every Warmer Is Given**

The claim made in this verse has a familiar shape in the Book's stories. The peoples who rejected their messengers rarely argued the point; they issued a boundary. Shuʿayb's townspeople threatened to drive him and his followers out of the land unless they returned to the local faith, and he answered by asking whether they would do so even against his will (7:88). In Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ the response to that same man was a demand that he stop or face expulsion (26:167), and the people of another messenger told him they saw him as a bad omen and would stone him if he did not desist (36:18). Lot's crowd speaks the same language, and it is the language of communities that have nothing to say to a prophet except where the borders of his activity lie.
verses.71:
> He said, “O my people! Here are my daughters ˹so marry them˺ if you wish to do so.”

**The Last Offer a Host Can Make**

Having been told that he had no right to protect anyone, Lot makes an offer that places the decision back in his people's hands: his daughters are before them. The Book records the same proposal in Sūrah Hūd with the reasoning attached, where he presents them as pure for his people and asks them to fear God and not humiliate him by disrespecting his guests (11:78). The offer is the extremity of a man who has exhausted argument and is now trying to divert a crowd with something he has the authority to give. The text reports it without approving it, and the Book's readers have long debated what exactly the offer entailed.

**How the Commentators Read the Offer**

The exegetes discussed the sentence at length, since a prophet offering his daughters to men in the street raises obvious difficulties. Two broad readings were given. One holds that the daughters were offered in lawful marriage, which is how a number of scholars took it, and this reading fits the clause translated as a condition of doing something lawful. The other holds that the daughters in question were the young women of his people rather than his own children, as prophets are described in the Book as fathers to their communities. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī all record the discussion and the differences, and the agreement among them is on the conduct of the crowd rather than the details of the proposal. What the verse establishes for the reader is that Lot held nothing back in the defence of his guests.

**Marriage as the Answer to the Crowd's Use of the Body**

The offer is significant because of what it answers. The city's offence was the use of other people's bodies without any bond, and Lot's proposal substitutes a union the Book regards as the proper setting for desire. He does not ask them to become ascetics and he does not pretend that the urges they came out with were imaginary; he asks them to redirect those urges into a form that would give the women a place in their households and the men a share in responsibilities. The sūrah's readers would understand how far the offer's frame sat from the town's habits. The Book elsewhere treats the bond it names as the home of tranquility between spouses, with compassion and mercy placed between them (30:21), and the city's customs had made that arrangement irrelevant.

**The Failure of the Offer**

The next verse in Sūrah Hūd records the crowd's answer, in which they insist that he knows they have no need for his daughters and that he knows what they want (11:79). Their reply is the moment the scene's logic closes. They are not interested in lawful partnerships, households or the standing of the women in question; they want the visitors, and they say so without apology. The sūrah's account keeps the exchange short, and the reader is meant to see what a community loses when it reaches that point: not only the sense that a crime should be hidden, but the sense that any other arrangement for their desire was worth considering.

**What a Prophet's Helplessness Teaches**

The Book records Lot's plea for strength that same night, when he wishes he had the power to resist his people or a strong supporter to rely on (11:80). That sentence, spoken by a messenger in the middle of a confrontation, is one of the most human moments in the Qur'an's prophetic narratives, and it is meant to be understood alongside the offer in this verse. The Book does not present the prophets as figures who never reach the end of their resources. It presents them as people who exhaust every lawful means, ask for help when they have none left, and are rescued by God beyond anything they could arrange. The daughters offered in this verse are the last item in that list of means.

**The Moral Distance the Sūrah Maintains**

At no point in this scene does the Book invite the reader to admire the city or to sympathise with its desires, and at no point does it offer a portrait of the prophet as compromised. It reports an offer made under extreme duress, records its rejection in another chapter, and moves on to the judgment. The sūrah's handling of the whole episode is instructive in how little commentary it supplies. A reader who wants a judgement receives one from the events themselves, since within hours the town that could not be diverted by hospitality or marriage was on the ground, and the prophet who had offered his own household to protect his guests walked out under God's protection.

**The Command of God Over a Household**

The verse places Lot in a position where the two obligations he owed could not both be met in an obvious way: the protection of guests who were under his roof and the welfare of his own children. The Book's later legislation about the family and the household belongs to a community in which such situations are regulated in advance, with the consent of the parties involved and the rights of women established, and the contrast with the naked emergency in the streets of the city is part of what the story shows. A society that keeps faith with its rules does not arrive at the point where its prophet has to choose between the safety of a guest and the future of his daughters. That choice is the measure of the distance the town had travelled, and the next verses describe the ends of that journey.
verses.72:
> By your life ˹O Prophet˺, they certainly wandered blindly, intoxicated ˹by lust˺

**An Oath Sworn by the Life of a Man**

The Book swears by many things in the course of its addresses: by the sun and its brightness, by the fig and the olive, by the pen and what the scribes write, by the morning light. Here it swears by a human life, and commentators took the address as nothing less than the life of Muḥammad. The exegetes record the report from Ibn ʿAbbās that God never created or formed a soul dearer to Him than Muḥammad's, and that this is the only life the Book swears by. The oath is not decoration. It fixes the attention of the recitation on a single point in the story and makes the judgement about the city's men the content of the line that follows it.

**The Other Reading of the Phrase**

Some commentators read the phrase as the speech of the angels, swearing by the life of Lot, since the surrounding lines carry the speech of Lot and the crowd. The reading has a logic of its own: an oath placed on the lips of the visitors, affirming that the town had lost its reason, fits the role the angels play in the scene. The more widely followed reading keeps the oath as God's own, and the printed translation reflects it by addressing the Prophet directly. Either way, the sentence in this verse is a divine verdict on the men in the street rather than a piece of dialogue, and the sūrah's narrative pauses only long enough to deliver it before the morning arrives.

**Intoxication Without Wine**

The word for intoxication in this verse belongs to the Arabic vocabulary of drink, and it is used in the Book for the state produced by wine. Sūrah al-Naḥl mentions the intoxicant obtained from the fruit of the palm and the vine alongside wholesome provision (16:67), and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ forbids approaching prayer while intoxicated until the speaker knows what he is saying (4:43), a verse that belongs to the stages by which drink was finally prohibited. The men of the city were not drunk. The Book applies the word to them because the condition it names is not the drink but what the drink does: it covers the judgement and hands the person over to whatever appetite has his attention. The town's appetite had done that work for it.

**Blindness That Was Not in the Eyes**

The sūrah pairs the intoxication with a word for blind wandering, and its readers would know that the Book uses blindness for the loss of understanding more often than for the loss of sight. A verse elsewhere states that it is not the eyes that grow blind but the hearts within the chests (22:46). The crowd at Lot's door could see its visitors clearly, and it could see the man pleading with it; what it could not do was see the situation it was in, or the guests for what they were, or the hour in which all of this was happening. The Book's account of the scene therefore uses two metaphors that describe the same ruin from different sides: the judgement was covered, and the sight was gone.

**Why the Verse Comes After the Offer**

The oath is placed after Lot's offer of his daughters, and its position is part of its meaning. The crowd had just refused a lawful arrangement for the desire that had brought them out, insisting on what they wanted instead (11:79). Their refusal is the evidence for the verdict in this verse: a preference that could not be argued for and would not be traded was not a decision, it was a condition. The Book's verdict on societies that behave in this way is not that they chose an evil and could have chosen better, though the sūrah's readers were invited to choose better; it is that the choosing faculty had been taken out of their hands by the practice of the thing itself.

**The Prophet's Vindication in a Sentence**

The oath by the Prophet's life sits in the middle of a story about Lot, and the parallel between the two men is assembled by position rather than argument. The Prophet was being mocked in Makkah by men who had demanded signs, called him possessed, and asked why angels were not sent (15:6-7). The verse swears by his life in a passage that ends with a mockery-blind city being wiped out at dawn. Sūrah al-Qamar's account of the same narrative notes that the warnings had been disputed (54:36), which is the exact description of the Prophet's experience in his own city. The oath in this verse therefore does two things at once: it pronounces on Sodom and it answers Makkah.

**Swearing by What God Chooses**

The Book's oaths raised a question for theologians, since the Prophet forbade his followers from swearing by anything other than God. The scholars resolved it by distinguishing the Creator's prerogative from the creature's: God swears by whatever He wills among the things He has made, because He disposes of them, whereas a human being may not swear by anything less than God. The sūrah's use of a created life in an oath is therefore not a licence for its hearers, and the classical commentators were careful to say so. What the reader takes from it is a claim about the man whose life was chosen: God made the life of His Prophet the standard by which the state of a whole city is measured in the record.

**The Beautiful Reports the Commentators Preserved**

The commentaries on this verse gathered material the Book does not contain, including lines of Persian verse from the Sufi tradition in which the phrase became a doorway. The commentaries preserve the couplet attributed to Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār in which the crown of the oath is placed upon the Prophet's head and the mountain becomes like a hill at his threshold. The reports are testimony to what generations of readers heard in the verse, and the sūrah's own words remain the firmer ground: an oath by the life of God's messenger, and beneath it a city of men walking blind with their desire while a decree stands over their streets.
verses.73:
> So the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise

**One Sound as the Instrument of Judgment**

The verse names the means of the city's destruction with a single word: a blast, a shout, a cry that no wall could keep out and no arrangement could answer. The Book uses the same word for the ruin of several communities. It says that the blast overtook the wrongdoers so that they fell lifeless in their homes, and it says the same of the people of the thicket after Shuʿayb had warned them (11:67; 11:94). For the Thamud the Book speaks of one blast that left them like the twigs a fence-builder gathers, and Sūrah al-Ḥijr will use the very same word again for the people of the stone valley (54:31; 15:83). The vocabulary is deliberately repetitious. A reader of the Book learns that God has no shortage of instruments and no need for elaborate ones.

**The Whole Town Overtaken at Once**

The word translated as overtook carries the sense of a thing coming upon a people before they could stand against it. The men of the city were scattered through the streets, some at Lot's door and others in their houses, and none of them was in a position to meet what arrived. That is the characteristic of this kind of punishment in the Book: it is addressed to a community rather than to individuals, and it closes the account of that community in a single stroke. The narrations of the earlier prophets end in the same way, whether the instrument is water, wind, or a sound. What the Book records is not a siege or a battle but a termination.

**Sunrise: The Hour Promised to Lot**

By naming the sunrise, the verse closes a schedule that the reader has been following for several verses. The angels told Lot that the appointed time was the morning (11:81), the decree revealed to him said the city's people would be uprooted in the morning, and now the blast falls at the rising of the sun. The Book's narratives of judgment are frequently this exact about time. Noah's flood has its beginning, the drowning of the pursuers has its moment, and the towns of Lot have their hour. The precision serves a purpose beyond vividness: it demonstrates that the event was administered, and it means that a reader who has followed the sequence has watched a warning move from speech to date to outcome without a single step being missed.

**The Last Night of a City**

Everything the reader knows about this night has been told in a handful of lines. The visitors came, the family was warned, the route was given, the decree was announced, the men of the town gathered at the door rejoicing, and their prophet's last appeals were refused with a claim about their rights over him. Sunrise is the first moment after that sequence, and the Book treats it as the natural end of the story rather than as an interruption. A daybreak is the least dramatic hour available, and the ruin of the cities happens at the moment when ordinary life would have resumed: shops opening, water drawn, the market setting out its goods. The Book has already said of another people that they were seized in the middle of the enjoyment of what they had been given (6:44).

**The Cry and the Command Behind It**

The creation narratives of the Book make the connection between God's speech and the existence of things direct. Sūrah Yā-Sīn states that when God wills a thing to be, He simply says to it, "Be," and it is (36:82). The blast that overtook the towns is the same kind of utterance: a word with effects, spoken over a place that had been warned for years. This is why the Book's punishment scenes are so often wordless from the human side. There is no weapon described, no attacker, no army to resist. A sound arrives, and the city is no longer there. A reader who has absorbed the sūrah's earlier verses about the creation of the human being from clay and the guarding of the heavens has already been told what kind of world this is.

**Overtaken While Looking On**

The Book preserves another description of the destruction of the towns that places the people inside the event as spectators. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt records that a blast overtook a people while they were looking on (51:44), and the words are the same family as those used here. The detail matters because it removes every possibility of interpretation after the fact. The generation that was destroyed had watched its own end arrive, which is the opposite of the position of the sūrah's readers, who see the ruins of these towns on the road and have the whole account preserved for them. The punishment of the people was completed in a moment; the warning to those who came after them continues indefinitely.

**A Sound No Defence Could Meet**

The towns that were ruined in the Book's narratives are repeatedly described in terms of their strength: fortresses, lofty palaces, carved mountains, wells, and irrigation. The sūrah will shortly describe the people of the stone valley carving their homes out of the rock, in full confidence that such dwellings would be safe (15:82). None of that appears in this verse. The instrument of judgment was not something the city could have built against, purchased protection from, or negotiated with, and the men who had just been asserting their authority over a prophet's household had no authority over the noise that took them. The contrast is the point, and the Book does not labour it.

**What the Morning Left Behind**

The verse ends with the city gone rather than with the city described. The Book's readers learn what remained from the lines that follow, where the towns are said to have been turned over and rained upon, and where the sites are described as ruins along a route that people still travelled. Nothing was preserved except the trace, which the sūrah will call a sign for those who contemplate. The same pattern holds for the other communities the Book reports, and it is the reason the Qur'an can point to geography as evidence. A settlement that had refused every warning became, in the end, a lesson that its own ruins carried into later generations of travellers.
verses.74:
> And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay

**The Ground Turned Into a Roof**

The verse reports two actions in one sentence: the settlements were inverted, and stones were poured down on them. Sūrah Hūd gives the same account in nearly the same words, saying that when the command came the cities were turned upside down and a rain of clustered stones of baked clay was sent upon them (11:82). The image is stark and the Book states it without ornament. A place whose streets and roofs had been arranged by its inhabitants in a settled order had that order reversed, and the destruction is described from the outside, as an operation performed on the whole settlement at once rather than on individual buildings.

**A Deed and Its Counterpart**

Readers of the Book have long noticed how often the punishment of a community is described in terms that answer what the community did. The point is not that the Book always explains the correspondence, since in this passage it does not, but the pairing of an inverted city with a people whose offence was a reversal of the natural arrangement for desire has struck commentators and ordinary readers alike for centuries. The same instinct runs through the Book's treatment of other crimes: the warning that those who devour the property of orphans unjustly will have fire in their bellies, the promise that the stingy will have what they withheld hung about their necks. The order of the world that the townspeople had spent years overturning was overturned over their heads, and the text lets the reader draw the line.

**Stones of Baked Clay**

The material named in the verse is not loose rock but clay that has been hardened by fire, and the Arabic term for it is rare enough to have occupied the lexicographers. Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt records the same material in the angels' own description of their errand, where they tell Abraham that they have been sent against a people to send upon them stones of baked clay, marked by their Lord for the transgressors (51:33-34). Sūrah Hūd adds the qualification that these stones were marked by the Lord of the Prophet and that they were not far from the wrongdoers of that later generation (11:83). The detail turns a natural disaster into an addressed sentence. The stones were not debris; they were a delivery.

**Rain, and What Rain Normally Means in the Book**

The Book frequently uses rain for mercy. It describes winds sent as good tidings ahead of God's grace, driving heavy clouds to a dead land so that water comes down and every kind of fruit is brought out (7:57). The towns of Lot receive a rain as well, and it is the exact inverse of that picture: water that revives, replaced by clay that destroys. The Book's earlier account of the same event calls down a dreadful rain upon the city, and the sūrah's own line about the ruins lying along a known route depends on the reader knowing what kind of shower fell there (25:40; 15:76). The same element of creation that brings a dead earth to life is turned against a living community.

**An Overturning Witnessed by Nobody Nearby**

The towns had visitors the night before, and by sunrise those visitors had gone, walking through the dark with instructions not to look back. The Book preserves the outcome of the household's departure, saying that God delivered Lot's family before dawn as a blessing, and adds that only one family in the city had submitted (54:34; 51:36). The judgement therefore fell on an emptied place apart from the one woman whose fate has been separated from the rest. There was no audience for the event except the angels who reported it and the prophet who had been told to leave. The Book's insistence that these things happened to whole societies does not diminish the isolation in which the sentence was carried out.

**The Architecture That Could Not Help**

The Book's descriptions of destroyed communities frequently list what the people had built or controlled. Sūrah al-Ḥajj joins ruined settlements with abandoned wells and lofty palaces in a single line, and describes societies destroyed for persisting in wrongdoing, living on in total ruin (22:45). The stone valley's people will be shown carving their dwellings out of the mountains, confident in what they had cut into the rock (15:82). The towns of Lot may not have had such fortifications, but the sentence in this verse contains its own answer to every form of security: the ground on which a city stands is itself one of the things its inhabitants cannot defend.

**The Cities and the Guests Sent Against Them**

The Book's account of the night joins the visitors' errand to the sentence that followed them. When Abraham saw that his guests did not reach for the food he had brought, he grew uneasy, and they told him not to fear, adding that they had been sent only against the people of Lot (11:70). The same day they walked into the doomed town and were received by a man who did not know what they were. By evening the household had been given a route and an hour, and by sunrise the place of these events was under its own rubble. The verse's opening word, "And We," keeps the acts in the hand of God even though the Book has shown three travellers walking into town the previous afternoon.

**A Ruin Left Standing as a Lesson**

The Book does not treat the destruction of the towns as a closed file. It says of the same site that a clear lesson for people of understanding was left behind (29:35), and it addresses later generations who pass those ruins and are asked whether they will not think (37:137-138). A reader who comes to these verses with the ruins already in mind is standing where the sūrah's first audience stood: on ground that had been told about, with the evidence of the warning lying at the side of a road. The verse's two actions, the overturning and the rain of clay, are the last that the city's people ever performed anything about, and the recorder of those actions is the God whose command they had ignored.
verses.75:
> Surely in this are signs for those who contemplate

**The Aftermath Turned Into Instruction**

The verse steps out of the narrative and addresses the reader, which is one of the sūrah's recurring habits. Having described the family's departure, the decree's date, the crowd's arrival, the refusal of every appeal and the ruin of the cities, the text pauses to tell an audience what it has just received. What the account contains is not a story about the distant past but evidence directed at whoever is listening, and the Book says so in a single closing line. The pattern appears again a few lines later with slightly different wording, and again at the end of the sūrah's next case study. The repetitions form a refrain, and the refrain is addressed to people rather than to places.

**Who the Contemplative Are**

The Arabic term in this verse describes people who look at a thing and see through to what it means, and the exegetes glossed it with the idea of recognising the reality behind outward forms. The root concerns marks and features, the traces by which something is identified, so the word carries the sense of reading what is in front of you accurately. The sūrah's use of it here is precise. The ruins of the cities were available to anybody who walked that road; the men of the Book's audience who profited from them were the ones who understood what they were looking at. Insight in this vocabulary is not a superior intelligence but a superior attentiveness, and the Book treats it as a moral quality rather than an intellectual one.

**The Faculty the Book Keeps Asking Its Readers to Use**

The command to consider, reflect, reason and remember runs through the entire Book, and the sūrah's refrain belongs to that larger campaign. Elsewhere the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are called signs for people of understanding (3:190), and a passage in Sūrah Qāf states that in the account of the destroyed peoples there is a reminder for whoever has a mindful heart and lends an attentive ear (50:37). Sūrah al-Baqarah puts the matter differently when it reports the demand of those who wanted a sign they had chosen, and answers that the signs have been made clear for people of sure faith (2:118). The Book's call is never to suspend reason; it is to use the faculties of observation and judgement on material that is already in front of the reader.

**The Sūrah's Refrain and Why It Repeats**

Within a handful of verses the sūrah will say that in this there is a sign for the believers, and that the ruins of the two peoples lie on a well-known road, and then that the stone valley's people denied the messengers. The closing formulas repeat because the lesson does. The Book's practice in these narratives is to tell a compact story, refuse to supply a curtain for the ending, and then hand the material to the audience with a sentence about what it is for. Anybody who reads the sūrah straight through notices the drumbeat: account, account, account, each followed by a line asserting that the record is meant to be used. The result is a chapter that reads less like a collection of history and more like a series of exhibits with a caption on each.

**The Difference Between Knowing a Story and Being Addressed by It**

A reader of the Book knows these events already from other sūrahs, and the sūrah's customers had heard the account of Lot's people repeatedly. The verse therefore distinguishes two kinds of acquaintance. One is familiarity with a narrative about a nation that ended badly. The other is the posture of a person who takes the account as something said to him, weighing his own conduct against the pattern displayed. The Book calls the second of these contemplation, and it makes the difference the subject of the verse. In Sūrah al-Ḥijr the heedless attitude is described at the beginning, where the mockers are told to eat, enjoy themselves and be diverted by false hopes, and are promised that they will come to know (15:3). The line in this verse stands at the opposite end of that same concern.

**The Ruins Were in Front of the First Listeners**

The people who heard this sūrah recited had advantages that no later readership possesses. Their caravans travelled north through the territories where these events were said to have happened, and the Book addresses them on the assumption that they had seen the ground. That makes the verse's claim about contemplation unusually concrete. The signs in question were not deductions from an argument but objects on a route, and the men of Makkah who passed the sites on business could compare the Book's account with what was lying beside the road. The sūrah's audience is being told that the evidence had been placed where they could not avoid it.

**A Caption for Everything That Follows**

The verse's position matters as much as its content. It arrives before the sūrah's third case, the people of the stone valley, and it will be repeated in a variant after that case closes. Placed this way, it functions like a heading over the remaining material: what comes next is to be read with the same attention, and the same verdict is available to anyone who does. The Book's habit of returning to the reader after each narrative is a reminder that these accounts are not there to satisfy curiosity about the past. They are set down for people who are expected to do something with them, and the verse names the activity it has in mind.
verses.76:
> Their ruins still lie along a known route

**A Road That Outlived Its Cities**

The verse tells the reader where the evidence sits. What remains of the settlements is not hidden in an untravelled place or preserved in a temple archive; it lies beside a route that people used, which means the destruction of the towns was visible to anyone making the journey. The Book's habit when it reports these events is to give them a location that its hearers could reach. Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt addresses the Prophet's own townspeople with the observation that they pass by the ruins of these cities day and night and asks whether they will not then understand (37:137-138). The line in this verse supplies the same information more briefly, and its effect is to close off the option of treating the account as legend.

**The Word Translated "Route"**

The Arabic word rendered here as a known route is one that ordinarily means a leader or a model to be followed, and the lexicographers recorded that in the usage of the Arabs it also names a road that is travelled and kept. The same sūrah uses a different expression when it says of the dwellers of the forest and the towns of Lot that the ruins of both nations lie on a well-known road (15:79). Between them, the two verses insist on the public accessibility of the sites rather than on their beauty or their significance as monuments. The Book is not inviting its audience to imagine; it is pointing to a track on a map and telling them that they have been on it.

**Geography as a Standing Witness**

The Book's ruined peoples are usually placed in lands that its first audiences knew, and the reason is that a ruin does not require an argument. Sūrah al-Ḥajj describes destroyed settlements lying in total ruin, alongside abandoned wells and lofty palaces, and credits none of them with mystery (22:45). A traveller who came upon heaps of masonry where a town had been could hold both facts in his hands: the Book's warning and the empty space. The sūrah's readers are being asked to notice that their world contained such places, and that the account of what happened there and the shape of what remained agreed with each other.

**What the Caravans Carried Besides Goods**

Makkah's economy depended on journeys to the north, and those journeys took the traders through territory where the Book locates several of its destroyed nations. A merchant who set out with goods for trade returned with news and with the memory of the route, and the communities along the way had their own traditions about the empty sites. The Book's rhetorical use of that traffic is direct: it tells the Meccans that they travel through the lands of peoples who were stronger than they were, cultivated more, and were destroyed for denying their messengers (30:9). A verse like this one turns the map into a page of evidence that its audience had been reading in the ordinary course of business.

**The Persistence of a Trace**

The settlements themselves were removed in a single morning. What survived was the fact of their absence, and it survived for centuries, which is the uncomfortable part of the verse. The Book does not say that the stones of the towns remained as they had been; it says that their ruins lie on a travelled road, meaning that a place once full of people had become a feature of the landscape. The chapter's own name, the stone valley, comes from another community that cut its dwellings out of rock, and the survival of those hollows is the same phenomenon on a larger scale. Where a town's people have been removed, the trace they left continues to speak.

**Two Kinds of Remembrance**

The verse invites a distinction the Book makes repeatedly. One kind of remembrance is the ordinary work of a community keeping up the memory of its ancestors. The other is the use of a trace as a warning, and the Book means the second when it points at these ruins. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt states that a clear lesson for people of understanding was left behind at the site (29:35), and the phrase is a definition of what the sūrah is asking its readers to do with the road. The ruins are not there to satisfy interest in ancient events. They are there so that somebody standing where the town used to be can consider what bringing a community to that end.

**A Sign That Requires No Excavation**

The Book's method of proving its warnings is not the uncovering of new evidence. It assumes its audience is already familiar with a landscape of ruins and with the accounts attached to them, and it asks only for the use of faculties everyone possesses. Sūrah Yūsuf ends its long narrative with the observation that in the stories of the messengers there is a lesson for people of understanding, describing the account as confirmation of what came before it and a detailed explanation of all things (12:111). The verse in this sūrah adopts the same stance toward the traces on the road: everything necessary is available, and the only question left open is what the traveller does with what he passes.

**What the Book Does Not Ask of Its Readers**

Nothing in this verse directs anyone to visit the site, perform a rite there, or treat the ruins as objects of veneration. The Book's instruction is consistently about recognition rather than pilgrimage: it tells its hearers to travel through the land and observe what became of those who denied, and elsewhere it reports that a messenger was sent to every community with the same call (6:11; 16:36). The trace on the road is a witness, not a shrine. A community that keeps its warnings attached to ordinary geography, to be encountered on the way to somewhere else, is not asking its people for ceremonies. It is asking them to notice.
verses.77:
> Surely in this is a sign for those who believe

**A Second Closing Line With a Difference**

Three verses after the first refrain, the sūrah says the same thing again and changes one word. The audience of the first line was those who contemplate; the audience of this one is the believers. The variation is not stylistic padding. Contemplation names a capacity that anybody may exercise, and belief names a commitment that shapes what the person is able to see. The Book puts both before its readers within a few lines, which allows a reader who has only paid attention to the story to notice that attention by itself was never the end the narrative was aiming at.

**Why a Sign Needs a Believer**

A sign points beyond itself, and pointing requires a reader who accepts that there is something to point to. A person convinced that the world is a sequence of accidents will look at a ruined city and register a ruin; a person who holds that the world is administered and that communities answer for their conduct will look at the same stones and read a warning. The Book states the principle positively when it says that the signs have been made clear for people of sure faith (2:118), and it states the alternative when it describes those who have no knowledge demanding a sign on their own terms. The difference between the two readings of a ruin lies in what the observer already takes the world to be.

**Belief as the Condition of Perceiving**

The Book nowhere suggests that the evidence is thin or that the believer is asked to accept less than the facts allow. What it says is that the capacity to profit from the signs is connected to the state of the person who approaches them. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf records the declaration that God will turn away from His signs those who behave unjustly with arrogance in the land, adding that even if such people were to see every sign they still would not believe, and that if they saw the right path they would not take it (7:146). The verse is the severest statement of the principle in the Book: perception is a gift, and arrogance is the disposition that forfeits it.

**Those Who Pass the Ruins and Expect Nothing**

The sūrah's audience was familiar with the sites described in the previous verses, and the Book tells them plainly what their reaction had been. Sūrah al-Furqān says of the same city that it was showered with a dreadful rain, asks whether the people had not seen its ruins, and then explains their indifference: they do not expect to be resurrected (25:40). That final clause is the diagnosis the sūrah's refrain assumes. People who have decided that there is no accounting after death can walk past the rubble of a punished community without disturbance, because for them nothing was happening in that account. The sign is not hidden from such readers; it has simply been ruled out in advance.

**The Believers Named in This Sūrah**

The term appears at strategic points in the chapter. Lot's household is exceptioned from the destruction and the believers among them are said to have been evacuated from the city, and the Book records that God found in that place but one family that had submitted (51:35-36). The stone valley's people will be told, in a few verses, that in their story there is a sign for the believers as well. The sūrah therefore keeps two categories of reader in view from beginning to end: those who mock and those who accept. Its narratives are arranged so that the outcome of each community illustrates which of the two responses actually described the world.

**A Lesson Left for People of Understanding**

The Book does not leave the impression that judgment happened in a sealed past. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt states that ruins were left behind at the site as a clear lesson for people of understanding (29:35), which places the readers of later centuries inside the intended audience of the event. The line in this verse makes the same move in a single sentence. What happened to the towns of Lot was not an incident that concluded when the dust settled; the site and the account together form a standing instruction, and the Book expects its readers to be the people the instruction reaches.

**The Refrain as a Judgement on the Reader**

Ending a narrative with a line about who benefits from it places the reader in a position where neutrality is not available. The sūrah has shown a city refusing its prophet, and it now tells its audience which kind of person takes something from the record. A reader who has followed the account of the night and the morning has been handed a test rather than a tale, and the verse names the two outcomes. Those outcomes will be shown again in the third case that the sūrah is about to present, where a people who were given signs turned away from them.

**Two Ways of Reading the Same Stones**

The two closing lines of this section of the sūrah describe two people standing at the same place. One considers, and the other believes, and the sūrah holds both descriptions up without ranking them against each other, since in its arrangement the second grows out of the first. A person who has genuinely contemplated the account of a community that was warned for years and ended in a morning has already begun to move toward the position the verse describes as belief, and a person who holds that position will find the account of that morning intelligible rather than strange. The Book keeps the two words close together because it does not regard insight and faith as rivals, and its narratives are written for the reader in whom the one leads to the other.
verses.78:
> And the residents of the Forest were truly wrongdoers

**A Third Case in the Same Chapter**

The sūrah has told of the cities of Lot, and it now introduces another community with a single line before passing sentence on it. The order in which these examples are presented is worth noticing: the cities of Lot, then the people of the forest, then the people of the stone valley. The Book's way of establishing its warnings is cumulative. A single story might be dismissed as an unusual case, so the sūrah gives its readers a sequence, and each entry in the sequence confirms the pattern of the one before it. The verse's brevity is part of the effect; after the long account of Lot's night, the next community is named and condemned within half a line.

**Who Lived in the Forest**

The community named here is the one associated in the Book with a wooded territory and with the prophet Shuʿayb. Commentators identify the site with the region of Madyan, the Midianites, a people of northwestern Arabia whose livelihood came from trade, and some exegetes noted that the dwellers of the forest might be a distinct group from the Midianites themselves. The names are preserved in more than one place in the Book: the residents of the forest are listed alongside other destroyed peoples, and Sūrah Ṣād joins them with the people of Lot among the forces that had gathered against the messengers (26:176; 38:13). What the Book establishes beyond doubt is that they were a real community with a prophet sent to them.

**A Trading People, Examined in Their Ledgers**

Shuʿayb's message to his people is preserved across several sūrahs, and the thread that runs through all of them is commercial honesty. He begins with the worship of God and moves directly to the balances: the command to worship Allah and to avoid giving short measure and weight, and the injunction to give full measure, weigh with an even balance, and not to defraud people of their property or spread corruption in the land (7:85; 11:85). What the Book presents is not a list of unrelated offences. A community whose prosperity depended on the roads and the marketplace had a specific temptation available every day, and its prophet named the temptation.

**The Argument Shuʿayb Made for Honesty**

The Book records a remarkable sentence from him. After instructing his people to measure and weigh fairly, he tells them that what remains as lawful gain by God is better for them, and adds that he is not a keeper over them (11:86). The reasoning is that a person's true profit is what God leaves with him rather than what he can extract by manipulating a scale. The verse reframes the whole question the merchants were weighing in their minds: not how much can be obtained, but what portion of a livelihood can be trusted. The Book places this economic argument beside the appeal to worship because in its order of things the two belong together.

**Why Fraud Appears Among the Gravest Charges**

The severity with which the Book treats dishonest trade is displayed in the opening of Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn, where a woe is pronounced on those who take full measure when they buy but give less when they measure for others, and who are asked whether they think they will not be resurrected (83:1-4). The sin named there is precisely the practice for which Shuʿayb's people were condemned. The Book's treatment of it is a warning against the assumption that the offences which harm hundreds of ordinary people quietly are less serious than spectacular crimes. A scale adjusted by a fraction takes something from everyone who comes to the counter, and the Book puts the practice inside the same category as the abuses of the cities of Lot.

**The Meaning of the Word "Wrongdoers"**

The sūrah calls this community unjust, and the term covers both directions of what they did. Injustice is done to the buyers and employees they shortchanged, and it is also done to the messengers whose guidance they refused. The Book uses the same word across its accounts of punished nations: the people of Lot are described as wrongdoers in the verse that follows their ruin, and the warning about the marked stones says that they are not far from the wrongdoers of later generations (11:83). The vocabulary permits no distinction between malpractices in the market and the rejection of the message; in the sūrah's reckoning, a community that cheats on the scale and a community that ignores its prophet is one community.

**A People Destroyed Like the Rest**

The Book preserves the ruin of this community in the language it used for the others. Sūrah Hūd records the coming of the command, the rescue of Shuʿayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from God, and the blast that overtook the unjust so that they lay lifeless in their homes (11:94). The same instrument that took the towns of Lot took the merchants of the forest, and the same mercy that carried one family out of the first city carried one prophet and his followers out of the second. The sūrah's reader, arriving at this verse, has just been told that such signs are for those who believe. The account is already teaching by repetition.

**How the Sūrah Moves From One Case to the Next**

The transition into this verse is abrupt, and the abruptness is itself a feature of the chapter's construction. After the extended treatment of Lot's night, the sūrah names another community in a single clause and moves straight to the punishment, because its audience already knew the narrative of Shuʿayb. The Book varies its level of detail according to what its hearers needed told: it gives a full scene where the account carries the argument, and a compressed notice where the story is common knowledge. The reader who notices that variation learns how the Qur'an uses the material its audience possessed, whether that material was a well-known history, a familiar landscape, or a prophet whose name was already in the mouths of the townspeople.
verses.79:
> so We inflicted punishment upon them. The ruins of both nations still lie on a well-known road

**The Sentence Passed on a Trading People**

The verse states that punishment was carried out, and the Arabic verb carries the sense of a retribution that answers a wrong rather than an irritation that vents itself. The Book uses this vocabulary for people who were warned, given time and argument, and then met with the consequence of what they had decided. In the case of the forest-dwellers, the same sentence is recorded with a detail the sūrah does not repeat here: the blast overtook the wrongdoers after their prophet and those who believed with him had been carried to safety by a mercy from God (11:94). The verse's brevity does not thin the account; it assumes the reader has heard the fuller version and moves to the consequence.

**Two Peoples on One Road**

The exegetes read the reference to "both nations" as the people of Shuʿayb and the people of Lot, joined here partly because they were neighbours in place and partly because their missions belonged to the same stretch of history. The sūrah had named the two communities within a few lines of each other and had already told its readers that the settlements of Lot's people lay along a route people travelled. The closing sentence now gathers the two cases into one statement about geography, which is the sūrah's way of insisting that the warning material was available and continuous rather than scattered and forgotten.

**A Road That Anyone Could Find**

The phrase translated as a well-known road matches the description the sūrah gave a few verses earlier of the route the other ruins lay on, and the commentators noted the correspondence, treating the two expressions as references to the same visible thoroughfare. What the Book is describing is not an obscure site known only to specialists but a road with traffic on it. The location is given because its accessibility is the argument: whatever the reader's view of the account, the landscape it points to was public. Other verses in the Book address the same audience with the same confidence, telling them they pass by these ruins day and night and asking whether they will not then use their understanding (37:137-138).

**Ruins Left As a Deliberate Lesson**

The Book is explicit that the survival of such sites is not an oversight. It says of one of them that a clear lesson for people of understanding was left behind, and it says of another that the homes of a destroyed people stand in complete ruin because of their wrongdoing, as a lesson for people of knowledge (29:35; 27:52). The remains in this verse belong to that same category. A civilisation that had been removed in a morning left behind walls, hollows and tracks, and the Book treats those leftovers as an instruction placed on the ground for whoever came later. Nothing about the arrangement is accidental, including the fact that the road stayed in use.

**The Prophet's Words and the Soil's Testimony**

There is a correspondence in these chapters between what the messengers said and what happened afterward. Shuʿayb told his people that they were in prosperity and that he feared for them the torment of an overwhelming day, and that a swift punishment would overtake those who harmed the sign they had been given (11:84; 11:64). The Book then records the arrival of exactly what he had described. The line in this verse closes the loop by pointing at the site where the words were spoken and the event occurred, so that the record and the route support each other. The Book's warnings elsewhere rely on the same pairing of statement and trace.

**Why the Book Keeps Grouping Its Communities**

A reader who counts the cases in this sūrah notices how many of them are presented in sequence: the cities of Lot, the dwellers of the forest, the people of the stone valley. The effect of the arrangement is that no single example has to carry the whole argument. Each community differed from the others in its circumstances, its livelihood and the form its wrongdoing took, and each met the same end after the same kind of refusal. The verse's reference to two nations on one road is one of the chapter's devices for making that point concrete, and it gives a reader something a list of names would not: a journey that passes both sites.

**One Instrument for Two Peoples**

Sūrah Hūd already described the destruction of Shuʿayb's people with the same word this sūrah used for the cities of Lot: the blast overtook the wrongdoers and they fell lifeless in their homes (11:67; 11:94). The vocabulary of judgment in the Book is narrow by design. Whatever the community, whatever its tools and industries, the end recorded for it tends to arrive as a single overwhelming event rather than as a gradual decline. The merchants who manipulated their scales and the men who mobbed a prophet's house received the same sentence from the same quarter, and the sūrah says so in a handful of words before turning to its third and most detailed survivor community.

**The Reader Standing on the Route**

The sūrah's first audience travelled these roads and recognised the names of the places it mentioned. A reader in any later century still receives the same instruction through the account, which is why the verse does not end with the punishment but with the road. The record of a destroyed nation and the physical trace of its absence are held up together, and the sentence is left for the one who is doing the travelling. What the Book asks of such a reader is what it asked of the men of Makkah who passed the sites with their camels: to look at what is lying there and to draw the obvious conclusion about who is in charge of the ground they are walking on.
verses.80:
> Indeed, the residents of the Stone Valley also denied the messengers

**The Chapter Named After the Place in This Verse**

The word used here for the stone valley gives the sūrah its title, and this line is the reason the chapter is called al-Ḥijr. The term refers to a rocky tract or enclosure, and the community named by it lived in a stony region that the Book locates in the territory between the Ḥijāz and Syria. The naming of the sūrah from a single word in one of its verses is one of the ways the chapter's structure reveals itself: the stories it collects are attached to specific grounds, and one of those grounds supplies the name that the whole revelation will be known by afterward.

**Thamūd and the Prophet Sent to Them**

The people of the stone valley are the tribe of Thamūd, and the prophet sent to them was Ṣāliḥ. The Book introduces him as their brother, a man from among them rather than a stranger, and his opening call is the one the sūrah's readers know from every messenger in the Qur'an: worship God, for you have no god besides Him (7:73; 11:61). What follows in the fuller accounts is a people already settled and prosperous, made successors to a previous nation and established in the land with palaces on its plains and homes carved into its mountains (7:74). The sūrah's single reference to their denial presupposes all of that background.

**Whose Denial Is Meant**

The commentators discussed the plural in this verse, since Thamūd had one prophet rather than several. One reading takes the reference to be their denial of Ṣāliḥ himself, since rejecting a messenger is rejecting the message he carries and, in the Book's reckoning, the whole series of messengers behind him. Another reading expands the reference to Ṣāliḥ together with the believers who were with him, so that the tribe is described as having denied the truth in every form in which it stood before them. The Book uses the same plural when it reports the story in another sūrah, saying that the people of Thamūd rejected the messengers (26:141), which supports the broader reading.

**A Successor Nation With a Short Memory**

Thamūd's own scriptures in the Book include a reminder of how it came to hold its land. Ṣāliḥ tells his people to remember the time when God made them successors after ʿĀd and settled them in the territory where they built and carved (7:74). The warning depends on that memory: the tribe occupied ground from which another community had been removed, and the Book presents that fact as the plainest possible instruction. The verse in this sūrah places them third in a sequence of exactly such peoples, which makes the chapter's point by arrangement rather than by commentary. Each generation in the sequence warned, denied, and left the same kind of trace.

**Denial Recorded as Conduct**

The Book does not describe the tribe's rejection as a difference of opinion. In the fuller accounts, the denial takes the form of an act: they hamstrung the she-camel that had been given to them as a sign, in defiance of their Lord's command, and then challenged their prophet to bring on what he had warned them about (7:77; 11:65). The sūrah's line about denying the messengers is therefore a summary of behaviour that everyone in the audience could recall, including the part where the tribe's own leaders planned to destroy Ṣāliḥ and his family by night and cover the deed with an oath (27:48-49). The Book's final word on their planning is that they made a scheme and God made a scheme while they were unaware (27:50).

**The Lands the Meccans Travelled Through**

The territory of Thamūd lay on routes that the Prophet's townspeople used, and the Book's descriptions assume familiarity with the remains. Sūrah al-Fajr names Thamūd as the people who carved rocks in the stone valley (89:9), and the exegetes noted that the Arabs of the Prophet's lifetime knew these mountain dwellings from their journeys. The sūrah's audience therefore stood in the position of a people who had seen the trace and heard the account and could compare the two. The warning in this verse arrives with that geography behind it: the residents of the stone valley are not an anecdote being imported from a distant land but neighbours who had already been dealt with.

**Guidance Offered and Refused**

The Book states that the tribe had been shown guidance and chose otherwise: it says that Thamūd were offered the way and preferred blindness to it, so that a disgracing punishment overtook them for what they had been doing (41:17). The verse in this sūrah matches that account by placing the denial after the arrival of messengers and signs, and the verse that follows it will supply the specific evidence they turned away from. What the sūrah records is a stage in which the community had everything it needed to decide correctly and decided otherwise, which is the state the Book describes for every generation it names in this part of the chapter.

**A Third Community and a Fourth Observation**

By the end of this line the sūrah has placed three ruined peoples in a row and given each of them a different shape: a city visited by angels, a merchant nation warned by a prophet of its own, and a tribe of rock-cutters that had inherited another people's land. The reader who has followed the chapter from its first theme, the mockery of the Prophet in Makkah, will see in the third case the closest resemblance to the audience being addressed: a settled people with wealth, buildings and a sense of security, hearing an account of their predecessors and not believing it. The verses that follow record what happened next.
verses.81:
> We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them

**Signs Were Given, Not Merely Available**

The verse says that the signs were handed to the community, which is a stronger statement than saying that evidence existed in their surroundings. The Book's narratives of Thamūd are specific about what they received. They were shown proofs and wonders, and the accounts name a she-camel as the clearest of them: the Book calls it a clear proof from their Lord, and elsewhere it is described as a sign and as a test for the people (7:73; 11:64; 54:27). The tribe's problem was therefore not a shortage of information. What the verse records is an offer made plainly and refused persistently, and the tense of the refusal, which the Book puts in the form of a habit, says that the turning away was repeated rather than momentary.

**The She-Camel as a Sign With Terms Attached**

The sign given to Thamūd was unusual in that it came with a behavioural arrangement attached. Ṣāliḥ instructed his people to leave the animal to graze freely on God's land and to do her no harm, warning them that a swift punishment would overtake them otherwise (11:64), and the Book records a further provision that the water of the town was to be divided between her and them, each taking a turn to drink on an appointed day (26:155; 54:28). A sign of that kind cannot be admired from a distance and left alone. It enters the daily economy of a town, requires an adjustment to habit, and puts every person who draws water on notice about what they owe to a creature they did not make.

**A Sign That Demanded Obedience Rather Than Admiration**

The Book's treatment of signs is consistently behavioural. Earlier in this sūrah, the mockers demanded a display from heaven as a condition of belief, and the answer they received was that God does not send signs for entertainment. Thamūd was given one, and the record of what happened shows what such an arrival can produce in a community that has already decided not to change. The Book reports that they hamstrung her and then used the moment to demand the punishment their prophet had warned them about, which is a refusal so complete that the sign itself became the occasion for a challenge (7:77). The verse in this sūrah summarises the whole episode in the language of habit.

**The Vocabulary of Turning Away**

The Arabic term used here for turning away describes a deliberate movement of the back rather than a failure to notice, and the Book applies it to the response of whole communities to revelation. In this sūrah it has already described the mockers who asked why the Prophet had not brought angels, and the Book's accounts of previous nations rarely record an argument that was actually answered; the response to the messengers is a shrug, a dismissal, or a demand. Sūrah Fuṣṣilat reports the same tribe in the same terms, saying that they preferred blindness over guidance even after the way had been shown to them (41:17), which is the mirror image of the verse before the reader.

**A Sign Set Before a People Who Knew Its Cost**

One detail in the accounts shows how little the tribe's decision depended on ignorance. After they killed the animal, Ṣāliḥ told them they had only three days left to enjoy their homes, and the Book calls that promise unfailing (11:65). The tribe then had a short window in which the consequence of their act was announced to them in advance. Nothing in the account suggests they used the interval to reconsider.
