The Prophet's part is to proclaim and to disengage; God's part is to be sufficient. A messenger who refused either half of his instruction would be bargaining for a protection he had not been given terms for, and a community that reads the passage learns that the assurance of divine help in the Book is attached to the performance of the commission rather than offered as a blanket immunity. The sūrah's earlier narratives of protected households illustrate the same structure, since Noah was told to build, Lot to leave and Abraham to act before the rescue arrived.

**The Reassurances in the Book's Difficult Passages**

The Qur'an's consolations to the Prophet recur throughout the Makkan sūrahs, and they are usually attached to a specific distress. He is told not to let the words of his opponents grieve him (10:65), not to let his life be destroyed by sorrow over those who refuse to believe (35:8), and to remain patient with what they say while glorifying his Lord (50:39). The line in this verse belongs to that family of statements, and it names the hostile activity it addresses. A reader who follows the sequence can see the sūrah moving from history to instruction and then to comfort, and the comfort is specific enough to be useful to anyone facing the same kind of opposition.

**A Promise Made in the Present Tense**

The words describe an ongoing sufficiency rather than a single intervention, and the tense matters for the community that would inherit the message. The mockers of Makkah were not dealt with in one stroke on the day this verse was recited, and the Prophet continued to face ridicule for years afterward. What the sentence establishes is that the outcome is in hands that do not tire, which is the assurance the sūrah's readers have been prepared for by eighty verses describing how the nations of the past were handled in the end. The next line names the specific offence behind the mockery.
verses.96:
> who set up ˹other˺ gods with Allah. They will soon come to know

**The Charge Behind the Laughter**

The verse identifies the religion of the men who mocked. They were not skeptics; they were worshippers who had added other authorities alongside God, and the Book calls that arrangement by the name it uses throughout: setting up partners. The Makkan pantheon consisted of deities whose standing was bound up with the town's status, its pilgrimage traffic and the prestige of its leading families, and the Prophet's message removed them. What the verse does, then, is place the mockery inside a religious position rather than a neutral one, which changes the way the sūrah's reader hears the laughter described earlier in the chapter.

**What "Setting Up" a God Involves**

The Arabic expression describes a person constructing an object of worship by his own act rather than receiving it from the One who created him. The Book puts the same phrase to work in its argument with the Makkans elsewhere, where it asks whether the idolaters have taken their own desires as the god they obey (25:43) and describes the man who takes his desires as his deity and whom God has left astray in knowledge (45:23), a passage that also warns those who follow their own desires to consider where their path is going. The point of the phrase is that worship of this kind begins in human preference, and the resulting object is a creature of the worshipper's convenience.

**Mockery as Practical Idolatry**

The Book treats the mockery of the messenger and the worship of manufactured gods as one position rather than two. A community that laughs at the revealed message has already decided that its own arrangements are the final authority, and the deities it maintains are the public expressions of that decision. The sūrah's readers have watched the same logic in the cities of Lot and the stone valley, where the offence was a practice the community would not allow to be questioned. The men of Makkah standing in the street and laughing at the Prophet were defending an order in which their own gods had a place and the living God had none.

**"They Will Soon Come to Know"**

The closing clause is one of the Book's most frequently used warnings, and its brevity is part of its effect. The verse does not say what they will come to know, because the answer is contained in everything the sūrah has said. Elsewhere the Book tells the disbelievers that they have denied the truth and will soon face the consequences of their ridicule (26:6), and it hands the timing of the reckoning to God alone while stating that its arrival is certain. The word rendered as soon belongs to a timescale that cannot be judged by human expectation; the sūrah has already used the same phrase when it told the mockers to eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by false hopes, warning them that they would soon know (15:3).

**The Difference Between Knowing Now and Knowing Then**

The men addressed in this verse had been given the opportunity to understand the message while there was time to change their conduct. The knowledge announced for them arrives at a point where it cannot be put to use, and the Book's judgment scenes consistently present the guilty as understanding their situation only when the account has been closed. The sūrah's earlier verses state that the disbelievers will wish they had been Muslims when they see the reckoning (15:2), a line that describes the same delayed recognition. The difference between the two kinds of knowledge is the whole difference between the two outcomes the Book sets before its readers.

**Why the Sūrah Joins These Two Ideas**

Placing idolatry and mockery in a single sentence is the sūrah's way of explaining what the laughter in its opening verses was really about. The men who asked why the Prophet had not been given a treasure were not indifferent to religion; they had a religious establishment to protect, and the message he carried threatened it at the level of its foundations. A reader who grasps that connection can understand why the sūrah spends so much of its length on destroyed nations. The communities of the past had also been defending arrangements of their own, and the sentence pronounced over them in verse after verse is the one repeated here in four words.

**The Book's Recurring Promise to Its Opponents**

The warning in this line is repeated at intervals throughout the Makkan sūrahs, and its frequency indicates how much of the message was addressed to people who were not going to accept it. The Book never presents the reckoning as a possibility in these passages; it states it as a fact whose timing is unknown. The same phrase closes the sūrah's own opening exhortation and returns here near the end, which gives the chapter a frame. The mockers who are told to enjoy themselves at the beginning are told at the close that they will come to know, and the reader has passed through eighty verses of evidence in between.

**What the Messenger Is Not Required to Do**

The promise in the previous verse and the verdict in this one settle the question of what the Prophet owes his opponents. He announces the warning; he does not execute the sentence, and he is not asked to force agreement. The Book's teaching in these final verses is that the case belongs to God, who is sufficient for His messenger and who will inform every community of what it used to do. The sūrah's closing instructions turn from the mockers to the messenger's own practice, and the next verse shows how closely his distress was being observed.
verses.97:
> We certainly know that your heart is truly distressed by what they say

**A Verse That Names the Prophet's Grief**

The Book here states that God knows the distress caused to the Prophet by the speech of his opponents, and the wording places the knowledge in the emphatic form used for matters that need no proof. The verse does not reproach him for the feeling and does not treat it as a weakness. It records that the grief exists, that it has a specific cause in what was being said, and that it is known to the One who is addressing him. The sūrah's consolation works by naming the wound rather than by arguing that it should not hurt, which is a pattern that runs through the Book's reassurances to its messenger.

**What They Were Saying**

The sūrah has preserved a sample of the speech in question. Its opening verses describe people who will wish they had submitted, and it goes on to record the mockers asking why the reminder had been sent down to a man from among them and calling him possessed (15:6). The Book records their further demands in other sūrahs: that he produce a tangible sign, that a treasure be sent down to him, that angels accompany him, and their various labels for the recitation, from poetry to sorcery to ancient fables (21:5; 25:5). The verse's reference to what they say covers an ongoing campaign of public mockery that was aimed at the Prophet's standing in his own community.

**Grief Without Blame**

The Book treats the Prophet's sorrow as a natural response that has to be managed rather than a fault to be corrected. Sūrah al-Kahf asks whether he will destroy himself with grief over a people who refuse to believe the message (18:6), and Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ opens with the same image of a messenger tormenting himself over their refusal (26:3). The record of his prayer is preserved in another sūrah: "O my Lord! Indeed, these are a people who persist in disbelief" (43:88). What the Book never does in these passages is tell the Prophet that the people's conduct does not matter or that he is wrong to care about it.

**The Comfort of Being Fully Known**

The reassurance in this line lies in the knowledge it attributes to God. A person bearing a private burden often finds that the hardest part is being read wrongly by everyone around him, and the Book tells the Prophet that nothing he feels has escaped notice. Elsewhere he is told not to let the words of his opponents grieve him, on the ground that all honour and power belong to God and that He hears and knows everything (10:65), and another passage states that God is fully aware of what his opponents conceal and what they reveal (36:76). The consolation is not that the situation is painless but that it is completely understood.

**Why the Sūrah Records the Prophet's Interior Life**

Later generations received this sūrah as a text, and the line about the Prophet's grief tells them something about the man they are following. He is presented in the Qur'an as a human being who was hurt by mockery and who had to be reminded that his distress was known and would be taken care of. The Book's readers are shown a messenger who felt what anyone in his position would feel and who continued the work he had been given in spite of it. The community that inherited the message inherited a record that included this verse, and its presence in the sūrah is part of the Book's presentation of prophecy.

**From Grief to Instruction**

The verse's function in the sūrah is to make the next instruction necessary. Having stated that the Prophet is distressed by what is said, the text immediately tells him how to spend the hours and days during which the mockery continues. The instruction that follows is not a denial of the grief; it is a practice to live inside while the grief is present, and the arrangement of the two verses is a piece of practical guidance that has been applied by religious communities ever since. The Book's pattern in these closing verses is to acknowledge the difficulty first and then prescribe the conduct that carries a person through it.

**The Sūrah's Accumulated Consolations**

By the time a reader reaches this line, the chapter has supplied consolation in several forms. The Prophet has been told that God is sufficient for him against the mockers, that those mockers will soon come to know, that his enemies will be questioned about everything they used to do, and that the grief he carries is known to God. The instructions that follow add the practice that accompanied those reassurances, and the sequence shows how the Book deals with a messenger under pressure: it tells him what the outcome will be, tells him what he is feeling is understood, and gives him something to do with his days. The final verses of the sūrah are that something.

**A Sorrow That Was Told to Keep Working**

The Book's record of the Prophet's grief is inseparable from its record of what he did while carrying it. He was mocked, called names, told that his message was a collection of old stories, and asked to produce signs of his opponents' choosing, and the account of his response in the sūrahs of this period is neither anger nor withdrawal but continued speech. The verses of this sūrah put him in the position of a man who is told that his distress is known and then told to keep proclaiming anyway, to keep praying, and to keep at it until the end of his life. The grief is acknowledged in one line and given a schedule in the next, and the entire closing movement of the chapter is built on that combination. What the sūrah preserves for its readers is not a hero who felt nothing, but a messenger who was told what he was feeling was understood and who continued the work regardless.
verses.98:
> So glorify the praises of your Lord and be one of those who ˹always˺ pray

**The Remedy Prescribed**

The verse gives the Prophet an activity in place of the distress described in the line before it. The Book's counsel to a messenger under attack is to turn his attention upward in glorification and to place himself among those who pray, and the instruction is repeated in several Makkan sūrahs in nearly the same terms. Sūrah Qāf tells the Prophet to be patient with what his opponents say and to glorify the praises of his Lord before sunrise and before sunset (50:39), and Sūrah Ṭā-Hā expands the same command to include the hours of the night and the two ends of the day, so that the day itself is organised around remembrance (20:130). What the Book offers its messenger is a schedule.

**Glorification as a Standing Practice**

The Arabic command for glorification describes a continual acknowledgement of God's freedom from every deficiency, and the Book's use of it ranges across the created order. The same activity is attributed in other passages to the angels and to all creation, and the Prophet is being told to join a chorus that never stops rather than to perform an occasional ritual. The instruction comes with the phrase about praising his Lord, which attaches gratitude to the declaration. A person who spends his day declaring God perfect and thanking Him for what He has provided has been given a form of attention that leaves little room in which mockery can echo unopposed.

**"Be One of Those Who Pray"**

The second clause is worded in a way that deserves attention. The Prophet is not told simply to pray; he is told to be among those who pray, which places him inside a company rather than in a private relationship with the instruction. The community that surrounded him in Makkah was small, poor and constantly under pressure, and the verse gives its leader the task of standing with it in prostration. The Book's picture of the prophetic life in these years is full of such company: a household, a few believers, and a practice of worship that continued in a city where the worship was not welcome.

The mockers aimed to make the Prophet look small, and the Book's remedy is an action in which he is placed on the floor in front of his Lord. Judged by the standards of Makkan society, prostration is the posture of a defeated man; in the scales of the revelation, it is the position of the one who is in the right place. The sūrah's reader is shown a messenger being asked to spend the hours that his enemies used for ridicule in worship, and the contrast is the point. Nothing in the instruction requires him to win the argument in the street. It requires him to keep his face on the ground in the presence of the One whose knowledge of the whole affair has just been affirmed.

**The Shape of a Day Given to Worship**

The details supplied by other passages show that the practice commanded here was not confined to one time. The Book mentions glorification before sunrise and before sunset, the dawn prayer that is witnessed by the angels (17:78), devotion during parts of the night (76:26), and the command to devote oneself to God wholeheartedly (73:8). Read together, these instructions describe a life that has been divided into portions of remembrance, and the verse in this sūrah is the general command from which those details follow. The Prophet's answer to the campaign against him was, among other things, a daily routine that his opponents could not interrupt.

**The Community That Prays With Its Messenger**

The wording that places the Prophet among those who pray also describes the community's future. The people who joined him in worship in Makkah became the nucleus of a society whose calendars would later be built around the prayers, and the verse's company of the prostrating is that gathering in its earliest form. A sūrah that has spent so much of its length describing the destruction of one community after another closes with a description of a small community being formed by an instruction, and the contrast between the two is one of the chapter's quietest effects.

**The Practice That Outlasted the Mockers**

The men who laughed at the Prophet in Makkah did not continue to do so indefinitely, and the practice commanded in this verse did continue, in a form that has been maintained by the community he gathered across fourteen centuries. The verse therefore does two things at once: it supplies the Prophet with a remedy for a specific distress and it establishes the activity that would define the community he was building. What the sūrah leaves its readers is an instruction that has no expiry date and a picture of how the message was carried through a difficult period, one prayer at a time, until the next verse's final term was reached.

**The Last Instructions of the Chapter**

The sūrah's closing verses are short and they are all addressed to the Prophet. He is told what to proclaim, what to avoid, what God will do for him, what God knows about his heart, and now how to spend his time. The chapter that began with the Book itself and passed through the ruins of nations ends with the daily practice of a single man and the community gathering around him. A reader who reaches this point has been shown the whole arc of the sūrah's concern, and the verse that follows completes it by naming the horizon against which the practice was to be performed.
verses.99:
> and worship your Lord until the inevitable comes your way

**The Term That Closes the Chapter**

The sūrah ends by naming a limit for the practice it has just prescribed. The Prophet is to worship his Lord until the arrival of what the translation calls the inevitable, a word that in Arabic usage here describes certainty, and which the commentators understood as the death that no person escapes. The verse therefore sets the horizon of the instruction at the furthest possible point. The worship commanded in the previous line was not a remedy for a season or a mood to be maintained until conditions improved. It was to continue for the remainder of the Prophet's life, whatever the city did in the meantime.

**Why Death Is Called Certainty**

The Arabic word used in this verse names the reality that cannot be doubted, and the Book applies it to the arrival of what every person is promised. Sūrah al-Muddaththir puts the same phrase on the lips of the guilty when they describe what came to them at the end, saying that the certainty came to us (74:47), and the Book's warnings about the afterlife are expressed in the language of knowledge that grows certain: those who were heedless will see the fire and then see it with the eye of certainty (102:5-7). Calling death the certainty is a statement about the one event in a person's future that is not open to dispute, and the sūrah's instruction is anchored to it.

**Worship Until the Last Moment**

The command's shape makes worship a lifelong occupation rather than an achievement to be completed. The Book's picture of the Prophet in his final years includes continuing devotion, and the community that received this sūrah understood it as a directive about endurance. A reader who has followed the chapter's treatment of cities that were given warnings and used them to bargain will see the contrast the verse makes. Those communities were asked for a change of conduct and offered a period in which to make it, and the Prophet is shown asking for nothing for himself, simply continuing in the practice he was given until the term appointed for him arrived.

**A Chapter That Ends Where It Began**

The sūrah opened by naming the Book and promising that those who disbelieved would one day wish that they had submitted, and it closes with an instruction to worship the Lord of that Book until the end of life. In between it has gathered the narratives of nations that were destroyed, a series of declarations about creation and the appointed hour, consolations given to a messenger under attack, and a description of the revelation as a gift that exceeds everything the wealthy of Makkah possessed. The last verse returns the reader to the relation between a servant and his Lord, which is the ground on which the whole chapter has been standing.

**The Horizon That Frames the Daily Practice**

Without this line, the practice described in the previous verse could be read as a technique for managing stress. With it, the practice is given an orientation toward the end of a life and the account that follows. The Book elsewhere states the purpose of human existence in a single sentence, declaring that jinn and humans were not created except to worship God (51:56), and this sūrah's closing instruction is that declaration put into the form of a personal command to one man. The verse's brevity is what gives it reach: there is nothing in it that applies only to the Prophet's circumstances.

**What the Chapter Leaves With Its Reader**

A reader who reaches the end of al-Ḥijr has been shown three destroyed communities, a catalogue of natural provisions, a promise about the preservation of the revelation, instructions about forgiveness and conduct, a messenger's grief and its remedy, and a final command to persist in worship until death. The material is arranged so that the histories lead to the instructions, and the instructions lead to this line. What the sūrah asks of the person reading it is not to reconstruct the geography of ruined cities or to master the chronology of forgotten nations but to take the posture described in its final verses and hold it for the rest of his life.

**The Practice and the Prophecy Together**

The sūrah's treatment of the communities of the past is not detached from the practice commanded at its close. Every account of a destroyed people in the chapter is evidence for the account that the worshipper expects at the end of his own life, and every prompt to reflect on those ruins is an invitation to live in the light of that expectation. The Prophet's worship until the inevitable arrives is therefore the proper response to everything the sūrah has said about the way the world is run, and the reader who finishes the chapter has been given both the evidence and the use to which it is meant to be put.

**The Closing Word of the Sūrah**

The last word of the chapter in the Arabic is the word for the certainty, and it leaves the reader at the boundary of the life in which the worship takes place. Everything the sūrah has said about the past, the provision of the earth, the preservation of the message and the appointed time of every community converges on that boundary, and the instruction about how to spend the time before reaching it is the single sentence with which the chapter ends. The reader closes a sūrah that has described a great deal of human history and finds himself addressed by one command about his own remaining days. That is the shape of the whole chapter: a wide survey of the world and its ruins, and a narrow instruction about how to spend the hours after the reading ends.
